claim: The '80 percent of export proceeds through normal banking channels' condition was never part of s.154A. It was a proviso to s.65F(1)(c), which the Finance Act 2022 omitted. There is therefore no 80 percent statutory condition attached to the 0.25 percent rate.

note: RESOLVED and it closes a blocker open since guide 2. Read verbatim from footnote 6 to s.65F in the consolidated Ordinance. The mechanism makes the point structurally too: s.154A operates at the moment an authorised dealer realises foreign exchange, so the proceeds are already through a banking channel and an 80 percent test there would be meaningless. No evidence was found that the condition migrated into PSEB's certification criteria. Every source asserting it as live law collapses to this one repealed clause: coverage of one, not five. Guide 6 (PSEB) can now be written, and the correction is its strongest section.

note: DEFERRED by the owner on 9 Sep 2026: guides come first, tools later. Recorded so the gap is not forgotten. Note the build differs in kind from the 22 existing calculators, which are pure in-browser arithmetic with a privacy promise attached. Verification needs an external data source: FBR publishes a downloadable ATL file and IRIS has an online verification page, SECP has company-name search, IPO Pakistan has trademark search (its site failed TLS verification during this research), PSEB has a member directory. Three routes when this is picked up: (1) deep-link with guidance, cheapest and honest, captures the informational half of the intent; (2) ingest FBR's published ATL file, useful but owns a freshness problem where a stale answer costs trust; (3) live server-side proxy, most useful and most fragile. Route 1 first is the recommendation.

claim: The 'Late Filer' category, introduced by the Finance Act 2024 via Rule 1A of the Tenth Schedule and applying only to s.236C and s.236K, was abolished by the Finance Act 2026 through the omission of Rule 1A. Late filers now pay the same withholding rates as on-time filers.
source: KPMG Brief of Finance Act 2026, p.22
note: Quoted in the brief. Our property calculator's comment already notes the late-filer tier existed only for TY2025-2026, so the code is current. Most competitor pages still show three tiers.

claim: Section 7E (tax on deemed rental income from immovable property) was held unconstitutional by the Federal Constitutional Court on 7 May 2026 in C.P.L.A. 1442-K/2022, and the Finance Act 2026 omitted both s.7E and its rate entry at Division VIIIC of Part I of the First Schedule.
source: KPMG Brief of Finance Act 2026 ('The Act has abolished tax rate for section 7E, which is in line with the omission of section 7E'); FBR Salient Features relief measures
note: HIGH VALUE. s.7E is still present in the Ordinance PDF amended to 31.07.2025, the same pattern as the 154A sunset: the consolidated text predates the Act. Most ranking property pages still explain how to obtain a 7E exemption certificate for a tax that no longer exists. We never modelled 7E, so no code change is needed.

claim: The Finance Act 2026 raised the s.182A late-filer ATL surcharge from Rs 20,000 to Rs 100,000 for a company, Rs 10,000 to Rs 50,000 for an AOP, and Rs 1,000 to Rs 25,000 for an individual. The surcharge does not apply to an individual who furnishes an undertaking with the concerned Commissioner that he will not purchase, acquire or otherwise obtain ownership or beneficial interest in any property for six months from the date of the undertaking.
source: Finance Act 2026 gazette, s.182A amendment (34)(i), read verbatim
note: MATERIAL AND HIGH RISK IF WRONG. The individual surcharge is 25x its previous level. The widely cited Rs 1,000 / 10,000 / 20,000 figures are TY2026 and are now WRONG for TY2027: they still appear in FBR's consolidated Ordinance dated 20 Feb 2026 because that consolidation predates the 1 July 2026 effective date. The property undertaking waiver was not in the Bill and was added by the Act, so it is absent from every Bill-stage commentary. GAZETTE-CONFIRMED: the Act substitutes 'twenty' with 'one hundred', 'ten' with 'fifty' and 'one' with 'twenty-five' in the s.182A(1)(a) proviso, so the figures are Rs 100,000 company, Rs 50,000 AOP, Rs 25,000 individual. Sub-section (3) adds the property undertaking. Downloaded the 40MB gazette that exceeded the research agent's fetch limit and extracted with pdftotext.

claim: s.236C(2): where a property is purchased and sold in the same tax year, the 236C collection is treated as minimum tax, not adjustable and not refundable.
source: specialist tax blog only
note: A real content gap for property flippers if true. VERIFY against the bare Act text before publishing; not confirmed from statute. | SUPERSEDED by s236c2-minimum-tax-verified. RESOLVED. Read verbatim from the consolidation amended to 30 June 2026: the s.236C(2) proviso, inserted by the Finance Act 2017, does make the collection minimum tax on a same-year acquisition and disposal. The claim was right; it is now sourced to statute rather than to a blog.

claim: KPK stamp duty, CVT and registration fee rates for property transfers
source: only tier 4-5 sources found; the only official document located was the KP Finance Act 2025
note: DO NOT PUBLISH. The firm is in KPK so this matters most, and it is the least sourced. Needs kpcode.kp.gov.pk or the KP Revenue Authority directly. Punjab's cut from 3% to 1% was by Ordinance (~10 April 2026) which lapses after 90 days unless enacted; its current status is also unverified.

claim: TM-55, request for a search under Rule 87, costs PKR 1,000 per mark per class.
source: Gazette notification, Trade Marks Rules First Schedule item 54
note: Was flagged as tier 2/3 by the research; now read directly from the gazette PDF already on disk. Completes the fee table: the minimum realistic official spend for one class is TM-1 3,000 + TM-11 9,000 = 12,000, plus 1,000 if a search is done.

claim: Gazette form mapping: TM-1 application 3,000; TM-5 notice of opposition 9,000; TM-6 counter-statement 1,500; TM-11 registration 9,000; TM-12 renewal under s.35 15,000; TM-12 additional fee under rule 52(1) for late renewal 900; TM-13 restoration under s.35(6) 3,000; TM-55 search under rule 87 1,000.
source: Gazette notification, Trade Marks Rules First Schedule
note: TWO distinct conflation errors circulate. (1) TM-11 registration and TM-5 opposition are both 9,000 and get merged. (2) The widely syndicated S.S. Rana table labels renewal as TM-13; the gazette says TM-12 is renewal at 15,000 and TM-13 is restoration at 3,000. Note the PDF's OCR renders TM-12 as 'TM-I2' in places.

claim: Rule 13 of the Trade Marks Rules 2004: every application for registration shall be in respect of goods or services in one class only. Pakistan does not permit multi-class applications.
source: WIPO Lex, Trade Marks Rules 2004 full text
note: The money insight for the guide: cost scales linearly per class. Three classes is 3 x TM-1 plus 3 x TM-11 = PKR 36,000 in official fees alone. Almost no competitor models this.

claim: Trade Marks Rules 2004: Rule 50 the Registrar sends notice not earlier than six months nor later than one month before expiry; Rule 51 renewal may be filed within the six months ending on the expiry date; Rule 52 a six-month grace period follows expiry on payment of the additional fee; Rule 53 restoration on Form TM-13 within six months of the date of removal. Term is ten years from the filing date under s.35, renewable indefinitely.
source: WIPO Lex, Trade Marks Rules 2004
note: Competitors state restoration as 'within 12 months of expiry'. Rule 53 runs from the date of REMOVAL, not expiry, and those are different dates. Also note the term runs from the filing date, not the registration date.

claim: Opposition may be filed within two months from the date of advertisement or re-advertisement, extendable by the Registrar but not exceeding two months in the aggregate.
source: WIPO Lex, Trade Marks Rules 2004 Rule 30; Trade Marks Ordinance 2001 ss.28-29
note: Counter-statement follows on TM-6 at PKR 1,500.

claim: Pakistan acceded to the Madrid Protocol with effect from 24 May 2021, but the domestic enabling chapter on International Registration of Trade Marks (including s.92I) arrived only with the Trade Marks (Amendment) Act 2023, assented 11 August 2023. Pakistan declared an 18-month refusal period, an individual fee, a required declaration of intention to use, and that licence recordings in the International Register have no effect in Pakistan.
source: WIPO Information Notice No. 4/2021
note: Outbound filing from Pakistan was usable from 2021; inbound designations lacked a domestic legal basis until the 2023 Act. Competitors present Madrid as simply 'available'.

claim: No trademark fee revision later than the 4 March 2019 notification (effective 9 March 2019) has been located.
source: Negative evidence: WIPO Lex records no superseding amendment; IPO's own fee page links only the 2019 notification
note: NEGATIVE EVIDENCE ONLY. Publish as 'as at <date>, the 2019 schedule remains in force; no later revision has been notified', with a last-verified stamp. Do not write that the fees will not change.

claim: Trademark fees of PKR 2,000 first class, 1,500 additional class, 500 search, 1,500 gazette, 1,000 certificate
source: multiple Pakistani consultant sites
note: REJECTED: flatly contradicted by the 2019 gazette. Either pre-2019 or invented, and propagated by content mills. Worth actively debunking in the guide.

claim: Pakistan trademark filing activity grew 14.7% in 2024
source: WIPO World Intellectual Property Indicators 2025
note: The separate claim of 59,073 Pakistani applications in 2024 could NOT be confirmed on the page fetched. Do not publish that figure without the WIPO IP Statistics Data Center.

claim: There is no FBR fee for an NTN. The Ordinance as originally enacted required one under old s.181(2), but Part IX was substituted in its entirety by the Finance Act 2008 and the replacement s.181 contains no fee provision. FBR's own registration prerequisites and its 14-step IRIS guide contain no payment step.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.181 with footnote 1; FBR Requirements before Registration; FBR Registration of Individual on Iris
note: Provable from statute rather than asserted, which no competitor does. Any fee charged is a consultant's service charge, not a government charge.

claim: s.181(4), inserted by the Finance Act 2015: 'From tax year 2015 and onwards, in case of individuals having Computerized National Identity Card (CNIC) issued by the National Database and Registration Authority, CNIC shall be used as National Tax Number.'
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.181(4)
note: The nuance competitors miss: the CNIC IS the number, but holding one does not mean you are registered. Registration under s.181(1) via Form 181 in IRIS is separate, and ATL membership is separate again. Three distinct states that are never explained together.

claim: FBR's own IRIS guide warns: 'just after login you cannot file Tax Return unless the registration process is completed by submitting the registration application'. Registration completes only when Form 181 is submitted from the Draft folder; the grant or refuse order appears in Completed Tasks after about 5 minutes.
source: FBR, Registration of Individual on Iris (official guide)
note: The most common structural failure: people create the login, see a dashboard, assume they are registered, and never submit Form 181. Also note the cell format FBR shows is 00923211234567, and at login the CNIC goes in a field labelled 'Registration No'.

claim: FBR's IRIS registration guide lists only three attachments, all marked 'business individuals only': business letterhead, paid utility bill of business premises not older than 3 months, and evidence of tenancy or ownership of business premises. A salaried individual with no business attaches nothing.
source: FBR, Registration of Individual on Iris, step 13
note: Competitors publish a long universal document list that pushes salaried readers toward hiring a consultant. Correcting this is both accurate and useful.

claim: FBR states that an individual can register online through the IRIS portal, but the principal officer of an AOP or a company must visit the Regional Tax Office.
source: FBR, Register for Income Tax
note: Contradicts the many 'register your company NTN online in 10 minutes' pages. Also note FBR requires the company principal officer's SIM to be registered against his own CNIC AND not already registered with FBR.

claim: FBR's press release of 18 October 2024 states the ATL is updated on a daily basis, replacing weekly updates, and that taxpayers filing by the due date are included immediately, replacing the previous annual March shift.
source: FBR Press Release, 18 October 2024
note: CONTENT OPPORTUNITY: FBR's own ATL landing page still says 'every Monday', contradicting FBR's own press release. Nobody has written about this. It changes the practical answer to 'I filed today, when do I get filer rates' from 'up to a week' to 'immediately'. The ATL download page showed 'Updated on 09 Sep 2026', consistent with daily.

claim: The Tenth Schedule (see s.100BA) governs persons not on the ATL. Rule 1 increases the deduction rate by 100 percent (doubling) by default, with three carve-outs: s.231B motor vehicles increased by 200 percent (tripled), s.236K property purchase on a fixed band table (10.5/14.5/18.5 percent), and a named table for 236C at 11.5 percent, 236G at 2 percent and 236H at 2.5 percent. Rule 10 excludes s.149 salary, s.231AB cash withdrawal, s.235 electricity, s.236 telephone and internet, s.154 and s.154A from the Schedule entirely.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001, Tenth Schedule and s.100BA
note: Three corrections to the common framing: vehicles are TRIPLED not doubled; electricity, telephone and internet are excluded from the Schedule so any differential there is written directly into the First Schedule rather than derived by doubling; and Rule 1 has a proviso shielding a person with a clean three-year filing record from the punitive property table. Almost nobody cites s.100BA, which is the hook that makes the Schedule bite.

claim: s.231AB cash withdrawal: the rate for a person on the ATL is 0 percent, and 0.8 percent for a person not on it, on daily withdrawals above Rs 50,000. s.231AB is excluded from the Tenth Schedule by Rule 10, so 0.8 percent is a standalone statutory rate rather than a doubling.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.231AB and First Schedule; cross-checked against lib/tax/withholding.ts CASH_WITHDRAWAL
note: The most visceral number available for the filer guide: the cost is not 'double', it is infinite in relative terms, since a filer pays nothing at all. Our calculator already models filerRate 0 and nonFilerRate 0.008.

claim: s.114C (Threshold for Economic Transactions, Fifteenth Schedule), inserted by the Finance Act 2025, bars ineligible persons from buying vehicles above Rs 7 million, property above Rs 100 million, securities above Rs 50 million and cash withdrawals above Rs 100 million. Per FBR's own circular it comes into force only from a date notified by the Federal Government in the official Gazette, and no such notification was found as of September 2026.
source: FBR circular reported 5 Aug 2025; National Assembly panel deferral reported
note: BIGGEST COMPETITIVE GAP AND BIGGEST RISK. Many ranking pages report these bans as current law and tell readers non-filers cannot buy a car or property. That appears to be wrong today. But this rests on ABSENCE of evidence for the notification. Before publishing, check FBR's SRO listings directly. If confirmed, saying so is both accurate and responsible, since the error pushes readers into panic decisions.

claim: s.182A: a person who does not file by the due date shall not be included in the ATL for that year, shall not be allowed to carry forward any loss under Part VIII of Chapter IV for that tax year, shall not be issued a refund during the period they are off the ATL, and shall not be entitled to additional payment for delayed refund under s.171.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.182A
note: Loss carry-forward denial is permanent for that year and can dwarf every withholding differential combined. Almost no consumer-facing page mentions any of (b) to (d).

claim: FBR's Overseas Pakistanis FAQ describes a route by which a non-resident POC or NICOP holder obtains the filer rate on s.236C and s.236K without being on the ATL and without filing: the authority handling the transaction uses the Overseas Pakistanis link on FBR's portal to create a PSID, uploads POC/NICOP and residency proof, and a Commissioner verifies and approves payment at filer rate.
source: FBR, FAQs on filer rate under section 236C or 236K
note: High search intent, essentially absent from competitor content, and directly relevant to the diaspora segment identified via s.82 residency.

claim: Official ATL checks: SMS 'ATL <space> 13-digit CNIC' to 9966 for individuals, 'ATL <space> 7-digit NTN' for AOPs and companies, 'AJKATL <space> CNIC' or 11-digit NTN for Azad Jammu and Kashmir; plus the online ATL status page, the ATL search utility, the taxpayer profile inquiry and the full ATL download. The AJK ATL is at par with the income tax ATL following the Finance Act 2018.
source: FBR, Check Active Taxpayer status
note: Directly serves the 208 verification-intent queries in the harvest, and is the honest version of the deferred verification tool: explain the official route rather than build a lookup.

claim: Companies Act 2017 Seventh Schedule, w.e.f. 21 April 2025: registration of a company with share capital of nominal capital up to Rs 100,000 costs Rs 6,050 electronically or Rs 11,000 physically; each additional Rs 100,000 or part costs Rs 847 up to Rs 5bn then Rs 200; the fee is capped at Rs 40 million electronic and Rs 50 million physical; a company limited by guarantee costs Rs 22,000 electronic or Rs 33,000 physical; name reservation costs Rs 1,000 electronic or Rs 2,000 physical.
source: SECP-hosted Seventh Schedule PDF, header 'W.E.F 21ST APRIL, 2025'
note: MAJOR. Live competitor pages quote Rs 1,800-2,200 incorporation and Rs 200 name reservation, roughly a third of the real figures, because they predate SRO 1806(I)/2024 which raised name reservation from Rs 200 to Rs 1,000. Even invest.gov.pk, a government site, still quotes the old numbers. Note SECP's own page is mislabelled 'Sixth Schedule' in its URL and title while the document is the Seventh.

claim: The Seventh Schedule contains an escalation clause at Item I sub-item (2): the fee shall be increased by 10 percent after the lapse of one year from the date of the notification. It applies to Items I to IV and expressly not to the enhancement-of-capital fee.
source: SECP-hosted Seventh Schedule PDF
note: The clause is verbatim in the schedule and the schedule is effective 21 April 2025, so an uplift would be due from 21 April 2026, inside the period this guide covers. NO SRO, circular or SECP page confirming application was found, and no revised figure. If applied, the up-to-Rs-100,000 electronic fee would be about Rs 6,655. DO NOT print a 2026 figure without confirming with SECP. Publishing the clause and the open question is more honest, and more useful, than pretending certainty.

claim: SECP FAQ, verbatim: 'There is no minimum requirement of authorized capital. However, minimum fee is charged according to authorized capital of Rs.100,000/-'
source: SECP FAQs on Incorporation
note: Kills the widely repeated 'minimum capital of Rs 100,000' myth. Rs 100,000 is the lowest FEE SLAB, not a capital requirement.

claim: Companies Act 2017 s.14(1): three or more persons may form a public company, two or more a private company, and one person a single member company. s.154(1): a single member company needs at least one director, every other private company not less than two, an unlisted public company not less than three, and a listed company not less than seven. s.154(2): only a natural person shall be a director.
source: Companies Act 2017, Gazette of Pakistan Act XIX of 2017
note: Competitors conflate two distinct rules, publishing 'minimum 3 directors and 7 shareholders' for a public company. Seven is the DIRECTOR minimum for a LISTED company under s.154(1)(d); three is the SHAREHOLDER minimum for any public company under s.14(1)(a).

claim: Companies Act 2017 s.197(3): Form 29 reporting a change in directors or officers must be filed within 15 days of the appointment or change, and the proviso excludes the first appointment made at incorporation. s.130(3): Form A or B is filed within 30 days of the AGM, with a registrar extension not exceeding 15 days available to listed companies only.
source: Companies Act 2017 ss.130, 197
note: CORRECTS MY OWN EARLIER RECORD. I had Form 29 at 15 days but described the 30/45-day split as listed vs other companies. The 45 days is an EXTENSION CEILING for listed companies (30 plus up to 15), not a separate deadline class. Competitors commonly state Form 29 as 30 days.

claim: Companies Act 2017 s.130(5): nothing in the section applies to a company where there is no change of particulars in the last annual return filed, provided that a company OTHER THAN a single member company or a private company having paid-up capital of not more than three million rupees shall inform the registrar that there is no change.
source: Companies Act 2017 s.130(5), read verbatim
note: SUPERSEDES the cruder version in my earlier secp-annual-filing-chain record. The correct structure: the exemption from FILING is available to any company with unchanged particulars. The proviso adds a positive duty to NOTIFY 'no change', from which SMCs and private companies with paid-up capital not over Rs 3m are carved out. So a small company with no changes files nothing at all; a larger one must still tell the registrar.

claim: Companies Act 2017 s.10: name reservation lasts not more than sixty days (s.10(4)); refusal may be appealed to the Commission within thirty days and that order is final (s.10(6)-(7)). SECP publishes 56 prohibited words and a rule that any deviation in dictionary spellings will not be accepted. SECP's published turnaround: an application submitted by 10:00 a.m. on a working day is disposed of the same day, otherwise the next working day. Three names may be proposed in order of priority.
source: Companies Act 2017 s.10; SECP Company Name Reservation and Prohibited Words pages
note: The 60-day validity is almost never mentioned, so nobody warns readers a reserved name can lapse before incorporation. Competitors also claim reservation takes 1-3 working days against SECP's published same-day SLA.

claim: Companies Act 2017 s.17(2): subscription money payable in cash is due within 30 days of incorporation, and unpaid shares are deemed cancelled with the subscriber removed from the register. s.17(3): receipt of subscription money must be reported to the registrar within 45 days, with a certificate from a practising chartered accountant or cost and management accountant.
source: Companies Act 2017 s.17
note: Essentially absent from every competitor guide. New companies do not realise they must actually pay in share money within 30 days and file a CA/CMA certificate within 45. A real compliance trap and a natural section nobody else has.

claim: SECP's eZfile went live to the public on 15 February 2024, and an enhanced release on 27-28 March 2025 moved foreign company registration, mortgages and charges, change in principal line of business, and series of debentures to eZfile exclusively. SECP reports 99.9 percent of company registrations are now completed entirely online.
source: SECP eZfile User Manual (17 Feb 2024); Business Recorder 28 Mar 2025; The Nation 12 Jan 2026
note: IMPORTANT NUANCE: SECP has published no formal eServices retirement notice, and its own legacy /eservices/company-incorporation/ page was still live in September 2026 describing the old flow and citing the REPEALED Companies Ordinance 1984. So 'eZfile is mandatory' is true in practice and for named processes but is not backed by a dated cut-over notification. Saying that plainly is a differentiator.

claim: That a paid NIFT digital signature certificate is required to incorporate a company
source: consultant sources only (Rs 2,500-5,000); SECP's own getting-started page describes a PIN sent by SMS and email plus a Rs 100 charge at submission
note: LIKELY A COMPETITOR ERROR. No SECP page reachable in this research supports a mandatory purchased DSC for standard incorporation. Do not repeat the claim; if the guide addresses it, address it as an open question.

claim: SECP and FBR operate a one-window facility under which an applicant registering on the SECP portal has the company's NTN issued automatically to the company email address. As of January 2026 SECP states eZfile is integrated with FBR, EOBI and provincial departments. Companies Act s.153(1)(h) disqualifies a person from being a director if he does not hold a National Tax Number.
source: SECP press release; FBR event page; Companies Act 2017 s.153
note: Links the SECP cluster directly to the NTN cluster: incorporation now produces the NTN automatically, which changes the answer to 'do I need to register for an NTN separately after incorporating'.

claim: SECP registered 4,761 new companies in August 2026, taking the cumulative registry to 311,765. Private companies were 2,762 (58.01 percent) and single member companies 1,846 (38.78 percent). By province: Punjab 53 percent, ICT 18 percent, Sindh 15 percent, KP 9 percent. IT led sectors at 872 new companies. Of 134 foreign investors, 106 were Chinese.
source: PhoneWorld reporting SECP data, 4 September 2026
note: SMC at nearly two in five new companies argues for treating the single member path as first-class in the guide rather than a footnote. IT leading sectors reinforces the convergence positioning.

claim: Under the Seventh Schedule effective 21 April 2025, electronic submission is the CHEAPER option: Rs 6,050 electronic against Rs 11,000 manual for registering a company with nominal capital up to Rs 100,000.
source: SECP-hosted Seventh Schedule PDF, cross-checked against Business Recorder's own framing
note: SETTLED against a second agent that read the same article and concluded the opposite. The article contains THREE relevant passages and two of them agree with us: (1) its general rule, 'the amount of fee is double or more in case of submission of documents manually'; (2) its guarantee-company figures, 'Rs 20,000 (electronic submission of documents)' against 'in case of documents submission manually, the SECP will charge Rs 33,000'. Only the Rs 6,050 sentence reverses the labels, so that sentence is the outlier and the article is internally inconsistent. Electronic is cheaper. Our published guide 4 is correct. A third figure, Rs 5,500 electronic under SRO 1806(I)/2024, was reported to us but not verified and may be the pre-21-April-2025 rate.

claim: SECP has published a document titled 'CIRCULAR NO.13 2024 - Increase of Fee in Seventh Schedule to the Companies Act, 2017', confirming that the Commission issues a circular when the Seventh Schedule fee increases.
source: SECP document listing page (PDF itself not retrievable)
note: RELEVANT TO secp-fee-escalator. The existence of a dedicated circular for a fee increase suggests the 10 percent escalator, if applied from 21 April 2026, would also be announced by circular. No such 2026 circular was found. That strengthens the case that the escalator has NOT been applied, but it remains absence of evidence. SECP PDFs are behind a JS download manager, so the circular text could not be read; see DEAD-ENDS.md.

claim: s.65F now allows a 100 percent tax credit to only two categories: (a) persons engaged in coal mining projects in Sindh, to the extent income derives from supplying coal to power generation projects, and (b) a startup as defined in s.2(62A) for the tax year in which it is certified by the Pakistan Software Export Board and the next two tax years. The IT-export limb at clause (c) was omitted by the Finance Act 2022.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.65F, read verbatim
note: CORRECTS a claim circulating widely that s.65F still gives IT exporters a 100 percent credit. It does not. The only PSEB-adjacent route is the narrow, time-boxed startup limb, which connects directly to PSEB's Rs 5,000 startup registration fee. No competitor links those two.

claim: s.154A(1)(a) originally applied the reduced rate 'in case tax credit under section 65F is not available'. The Finance Act 2022 substituted that trigger with the requirement that the exporter be registered with and duly certified by PSEB, decoupling the two provisions.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.154A footnote 3
note: Explains why the 80 percent myth persists: before 2022 the two sections were linked, so a condition in 65F felt like a condition on 154A. After 2022 they are independent.

claim: PSEB fees from its own site: freelancer registration Rs 1,000 per year and renewal Rs 2,000 per year; company new registration Rs 5,000 per year for an IT/ITeS startup established within 12 months or Rs 10,000 otherwise; company renewal banded by revenue from Rs 10,000 up to Rs 30,000 above Rs 600 million; and a surcharge of Rs 5,000 per year on an expired registration.
source: PSEB official site (pseb.org.pk redirects to techdestination.com)
note: Consultant blogs quote Rs 500, Rs 1,000, Rs 3,500 and Rs 5,000 for the same freelancer category, plus a fabricated USD-export-slab renewal table. All contradicted by PSEB's own pages. Also note pseb.org.pk now redirects: guides still sending readers there are stale.

claim: PSEB requires a freelancer to supply a personal NTN with no business name, along with both sides of the CNIC and a personal bank account letter. Renewal additionally requires a summary of export revenue with the correct IT/ITeS code from the State Bank and the prior year's income tax return.
source: PSEB freelancer registration page
note: The 'personal NTN with no business name' requirement is a real and common rejection cause and is documented nowhere else.

claim: A PKR 12.5 million turnover threshold for sales tax registration of retailers
source: tier-3 consultant source; contradicted by the Act
note: REJECTED. s.14 of the Sales Tax Act 1990 contains no turnover threshold at all, and the figure appears in neither s.2(5AB) cottage industry nor s.2(43A) Tier-1 retailer. The real thresholds are different numbers: cottage industry is annual turnover not exceeding Rs 8 million with at most ten workers, and Tier-1 turns on criteria including a 12-month electricity bill above Rs 1.2 million or a shop of 1,000 square feet or more.

claim: Sales Tax Act 1990 s.14(1) requires registration by every person making taxable supplies in Pakistan in the course of a taxable activity who falls in these categories: a manufacturer not running a cottage industry; a retailer liable to pay sales tax, excluding one paying through the electricity bill under s.3(9); an importer; an exporter seeking a refund against zero-rated supplies; a wholesaler, dealer or distributor; and a person required under any other federal or provincial law to be registered for a duty or tax collected as if it were sales tax.
source: Sales Tax Act 1990 as updated to 2025-26, s.14, read verbatim
note: Registration is triggered by category and activity, not by turnover. That is the correction the whole cluster needs.

claim: s.14(1A) and s.14(1B), inserted by the Finance Act 2025, require any person including a non-resident selling digitally ordered goods from within Pakistan through an online marketplace, website or software application to register for sales tax, and require online marketplaces and couriers not to allow anyone to use their services for e-commerce unless that person holds an NTN and, where s.14(1A) applies, sales tax registration.
source: Sales Tax Act 1990 s.14(1A)-(1B); FBR Circular 02 of 2025-26 para 3(vii)
note: RESOLVES part of ecommerce-tax-not-cancelled. The domestic e-commerce registration obligation is real and in force. Mechanism: for online payment the acquiring bank is the payment intermediary and withholds; for cash on delivery the courier carries the obligation.

claim: Sales Tax Act ss.14AC (bar on bank account operations), 14AD (bar on transfer of immovable property) and 14AE (sealing premises, seizing moveable property, appointing a receiver), all inserted by the Finance Act 2025, each come into force only on a date the Board notifies in the official Gazette.
source: Sales Tax Act 1990 ss.14AC-14AE
note: The sections exist verbatim; whether the commencement notifications have issued could not be verified. Same shape as s.114C. Do not tell a reader their bank account can be frozen today without checking for the SRO. Note s.14AC also requires three consecutive opportunities of being heard and staged suspensions before a permanent bar.

claim: KPK services sales tax is governed by the Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Sales Tax on Services Act 2022 (Act XIX of 2022), assented 8 June 2022 and updated through the Finance Act 2024, not by the Finance Act 2013. Under s.29(1) a person must register who provides a taxable service from a registered office or place of business in the Province, is otherwise required to register, is a withholding agent, or meets criteria the Management Committee specifies. s.29(6) requires application not later than fifteen days before becoming liable, and s.29(7) requires the Authority to register within fifteen days.
source: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Sales Tax on Services Act 2022, updated 2024
note: Most KPK guides still cite the 2013 Finance Act, which is superseded. Critically there is NO turnover threshold in s.29: registration turns on providing a taxable service in the Province or being a withholding agent. That refutes the common 'small providers are under the threshold' claim. The firm is in KPK so this is the jurisdiction that matters most.

claim: After sales tax registration a person must visit a NADRA e-Sahulat centre within 30 days for biometric verification; failure to attend or a failed verification results in removal from the Sales Tax Active Taxpayer List. Registration uploads include GPS-tagged photographs of the business premises, and for manufacturers GPS-tagged photographs of machinery and industrial meters.
source: FBR, Register for Sales Tax
note: Concrete, checkable and largely uncovered. Manufacturers may additionally face post-verification, with 15 days to resubmit documents found non-genuine before removal from the ATL.

claim: Companies Act 2017 s.223(5) exempts from audit a private company with paid-up capital not exceeding Rs 1 million, and s.223(9) applies that carve-out to single member companies. s.247(1) is a different rule: it governs WHO may audit, requiring a chartered accountant for a private company with paid-up capital of Rs 3 million or more, with a cost and management accountant also qualifying below that. s.233(3) is a third rule: the section does not apply to a private company with paid-up capital not exceeding Rs 10 million, which files under s.234 instead.
source: Companies Act 2017 ss.223, 233, 234, 247, read verbatim
note: FLAGSHIP CORRECTION for the SMC guide. Competitors routinely cite the s.247 Rs 3m figure as an AUDIT EXEMPTION threshold. It is not: it is an auditor-qualification threshold. Three thresholds do three different jobs (1m audit, 3m auditor type, 10m filing route) and ranking pages collapse them into one number.

claim: The Income Tax Ordinance defines 'Small Company' at s.2(59AB): registered on or after 1 July 2005 under the Companies Act, with paid-up capital plus undistributed reserves not exceeding Rs 50 million, not more than 250 employees at any time in the year, annual turnover not exceeding Rs 250 million, not formed by splitting up or reconstitution of an existing company, and not an SME. s.2(59A) is a different definition, 'small and medium enterprise'.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.2(59AB) and s.2(59A)
note: Most consultant pages cite s.2(59A) for small company. Wrong section, and getting it right is a visible credibility marker.

claim: A single member company is taxed identically to a private limited company. The Ordinance operates on 'company' at s.2(12) read with s.80 and draws no distinction for an SMC, which is a private company under the Companies Act. Both reach the s.2(59AB) small company rate on the same thresholds.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 ss.2(12), 80; Companies Act 2017 s.2
note: A clean answer most pages fudge. The real differences between SMC and private limited are Companies Act compliance differences, not tax differences.

claim: Single Member Companies Rules 2003 rule 6(1) requires an SMC to appoint a company secretary within fifteen days, with a proviso that the sole director shall not be the company secretary.
source: SMC Rules 2003 (SRO 1086(I)/2003) original text
note: A real and frequently missed cost: a one-person SMC still needs a second human. FLAGGED because the text read is the ORIGINAL 2003 version, which references the repealed Companies Ordinance 1984, so it is not the current consolidation. SECP press coverage also reports the nominee director requirement was deleted. Confirm the current SMC Rules before publishing this or the nominee rule.

claim: s.114(1)(b)(vii) of the Income Tax Ordinance requires a return from any person who has obtained a National Tax Number, and s.114(1)(a) requires a return from every company regardless of income or activity.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.114
note: Directly relevant to the NTN guide: obtaining an NTN itself creates a filing obligation. Also refutes the common claim that a company with no income need not file.

claim: There is no SECP registration for a sole proprietorship. The Companies Act 2017 contains no sole-proprietor provision and SECP registers only companies and LLPs. What exists is an FBR NTN under s.181, sales tax registration if applicable, and provincial or local licensing.
source: Companies Act 2017, by absence; SECP registration scope
note: Also settles the conversion question: there is no statutory conversion from sole proprietorship to company. You incorporate a new company and transfer assets; the proprietorship ceases. Several ranking pages imply a conversion procedure exists.

claim: Companies Act 2017 s.9(1): no association or partnership of more than twenty persons may be formed for gain unless registered as a company. s.9(2): those in violation are personally liable for all liabilities incurred in the business. s.9(3)(d) carves out partnerships of lawyers, accountants and other professions where practice as a limited liability company is not permitted.
source: Companies Act 2017 s.9
note: A statutory trigger point for the incorporate-or-not decision, and one nobody covers.

claim: FBR's 'Register for Income Tax' page lists an original certificate of maintenance of a personal bank account among the requirements for an individual, while FBR's IRIS registration guide lists only three attachments, all marked for business individuals only. The two FBR surfaces genuinely disagree.
source: FBR Register for Income Tax page against FBR Registration of Individual on Iris guide
note: IMPORTANT NUANCE for the NTN guide already published. The guide says a salaried person attaches nothing, which is accurate about IRIS uploads. FBR's requirements page asks for a bank certificate as a prerequisite. Frame as: IRIS enforces one set at upload, the facilitation counter asks for another. Do not present either as the whole truth.

claim: FBR's IRIS FAQs state the User ID is the 13-digit CNIC or NICOP for an individual Pakistani, a 7-digit NTN for an individual non-Pakistani, and a 7-digit NTN for AOPs and companies.
source: FBR IRIS FAQs
note: Answers two open questions at once: NICOP is accepted, so overseas Pakistanis register on the same basis as residents, and non-Pakistanis get a separate 7-digit NTN rather than a CNIC-based identifier. Whether a Pakistan-registered SIM is enforced for overseas applicants remains unverified and is the real practical blocker.

claim: Partnership registration is with the Registrar of Firms under s.58 of the Partnership Act 1932 on Form No. 1, not with SECP. For Islamabad Capital Territory: partnership deed on Rs 1,000 stamp paper, affidavit on Rs 5 stamp paper, a Rs 1,000 fee to National Bank under head C-03545, CNICs of all partners and witnesses, all notarised, partners appearing in person, certificate after about ten days. Form No. 1 must be signed by all partners before a witness who is a Gazetted Officer, Advocate, Attorney, Pleader or Honorary Magistrate.
source: ICT Administration firm registration page; Partnership Act 1932 Form No. 1
note: Note the preprinted Form No. 1 still says 'Filing Fee Rs.100/-' while ICT charges Rs 1,000: the form is stale. Registration is province-specific, so ICT figures do not automatically apply in Punjab or KPK.

claim: FBR's IRIS FAQs document the error 'Residence / Head Office / Business Address in Address Tab must be entered before submission', with two causes: the address not being marked as residence, and the business address not being linked to the business.
source: FBR IRIS FAQs
note: A specific, citable failure mode almost no competitor documents. FBR's helpline is also verified from this source: 051-111-772-772, 9am to 11pm Monday to Friday.

claim: The TY2027 corporate rate, small company rate, SME rates and restructured salaried slabs
source: consultant blogs and news only; not read from the Finance Act 2026 gazette
note: DO NOT PUBLISH rate tables from secondary sources. FBR Circular No. 02 of 2026-27 dated 08.09.2026 explains the Finance Act 2026 amendments and would settle most of them; it is referenced in search results but the circular listing page is a JS-driven form. Note one circulated claim, that a 9 percent surcharge above Rs 10m was abolished, conflicts with s.4AB which sets 10 percent. Verified from FBR's own Salient Features: super tax abolished below Rs 500m income and reduced from 10 to 8 percent above it, and the top salaried rate threshold raised from Rs 4.1m to Rs 7m.

claim: The section 4AB surcharge on salary is nil for tax year 2027. It was 10 percent of the tax where taxable income exceeded Rs 10 million in its first year, then 9 percent for salary in the following year, and it no longer applies to salary at all for TY2027.
source: lib/tax/salary-years.ts, which is reconciled against the Ordinance by scripts/check-tax.ts across all 15 salary tax years
note: RESOLVES the contested 9-versus-10 percent question directly. Both figures are real and belong to different years, which is why secondary sources contradict each other: each picked up a different year's rate and reported it as current. Our own codebase already held the answer and check:tax asserts it every build. Note also two related traps recorded in lib/tax/pakistan.ts: section 60C, the profit-on-debt allowance for a house loan, was omitted by the Finance Act 2022 and no longer exists.

claim: The salaried slab table for tax year 2027 has eight bands: nil to Rs 600,000; 1 percent to Rs 1.2m; 11 percent with Rs 6,000 fixed to Rs 2.2m; 20 percent with Rs 116,000 fixed to Rs 3.2m; 25 percent with Rs 316,000 fixed to Rs 4.1m; 29 percent with Rs 541,000 fixed to Rs 5.6m; 32 percent with Rs 976,000 fixed to Rs 7m; and 35 percent with Rs 1,424,000 fixed above that.
source: lib/tax/pakistan.ts SLABS, reconciled against the First Schedule and hand-computed cases by scripts/check-tax.ts on every build
note: SUPERSEDES ty2027-rate-tables-unverified for the SALARIED table specifically. The guide can interpolate these from lib/tax rather than restating them, which is the no-figures rule working as designed. Note the top band starting at Rs 7m corroborates FBR's Salient Features claim that the 35 percent threshold rose from Rs 4.1m. The corporate, small company and SME rates remain unverified.

claim: FBR Circular No. 02 of 2026-27 dated 8 September 2026, para 7, sets out the substituted salaried table in clause (2) of Division I, Part I of the First Schedule with eight bands: nil to Rs 600,000; 1 percent above that to Rs 1.2m; Rs 6,000 plus 11 percent to Rs 2.2m; Rs 116,000 plus 20 percent to Rs 3.2m; Rs 316,000 plus 25 percent to Rs 4.1m; Rs 541,000 plus 29 percent to Rs 5.6m; Rs 976,000 plus 32 percent to Rs 7m; and Rs 1,424,000 plus 35 percent above Rs 7m.
source: FBR Circular No. 02 of 2026-27, para 7; corroborated by the Finance Act 2026 gazette and by KPMG
note: CROSS-CHECKED against lib/tax/pakistan.ts SLABS: all eight bands match exactly, rate and fixed amount. Two genuinely new intermediate slabs at 29 and 32 percent. The circular was retrieved through FBR's homepage download handler rather than its JS-driven listing page.

claim: FBR Circular No. 02 of 2026-27, para 8: under s.4AB surcharge was payable at ten percent where taxable income exceeded Rs 10 million, and at nine percent for a person whose income was chargeable under the head Salary. The Finance Act 2026 withdrew the nine percent surcharge for salaried individuals. The ten percent surcharge continues to apply to other individuals and associations of persons.
source: FBR Circular No. 02 of 2026-27, para 8
note: CONFIRMS what lib/tax/salary-years.ts already encoded. The three-step history explains why sources contradict: FA2024 inserted it at 10 percent, FA2025 added a 9 percent salaried proviso, FA2026 withdrew it for salary entirely. A salaried person's top effective marginal rate for TY2027 is a clean 35 percent, not 38.15.

claim: FBR Circular No. 02 of 2026-27, para 21: after substitution of Division XVIII, advance tax under s.236K on the purchase of immovable property is a flat 1.25 percent of fair market value. FBR's Salient Features for Budget 2026-27 states 1.5 percent.
source: FBR Circular No. 02 of 2026-27 para 21, against FBR Salient Features relief measure (iv)
note: DEFINITIVE. Two FBR-published documents contradict each other and the circular is the one written against the enacted Act. This is the most citable proof available that reading the enacted law beats reading the budget handout, and it is already correct in lib/tax/property.ts.

claim: The Finance Act 2026 did not revise the rates for AOPs and business individuals. Division I clause (1) remains: nil to Rs 600,000; 15 percent above that to Rs 1.2m; Rs 90,000 plus 20 percent to Rs 1.6m; Rs 170,000 plus 30 percent to Rs 3.2m; Rs 650,000 plus 40 percent to Rs 5.6m; and Rs 1,610,000 plus 45 percent above that, with a proviso reducing the top rate to 40 percent for a professional firm prohibited from incorporating.
source: Income Tax Ordinance Division I clause (1); KPMG confirms no revision
note: THE STORY FOR THE SLABS GUIDE. A business individual on Rs 5.6m pays Rs 1,610,000 where a salaried person on identical income pays Rs 976,000. The gap widened this year because salaried rates fell and business rates did not.

claim: Division I clause (2) applies the salaried table where salary exceeds seventy-five percent of taxable income. Separately, FBR's filing page offers the salaried return form where salary is more than fifty percent of income. These are different tests: 75 percent decides which rate table applies, 50 percent decides which return form is offered.
source: Income Tax Ordinance Division I clause (2); FBR File Income Tax Return page
note: Competitors state one figure and imply it governs both. Worth its own callout.

claim: s.116(2): every resident taxpayer being an individual who files a return for any tax year shall furnish a wealth statement and wealth reconciliation statement with it, and every member of an association of persons must do the same. The former Rs 1 million threshold was omitted by the Finance Act 2013.
source: Income Tax Ordinance s.116(2) with footnote
note: Pages still quoting an income threshold for the wealth statement are thirteen years out of date. Due date is the return's due date under s.118(4).

claim: s.182 Table S.No.1: the penalty for failing to furnish a return by the due date is the higher of 0.1 percent of tax payable per day or Rs 1,000 per day, with a minimum of Rs 10,000 for an individual having 75 percent or more income from salary and Rs 50,000 otherwise, capped at 200 percent of tax payable, and reduced by 75, 50 or 25 percent where the return is filed within one, two or three months after the due date.
source: Income Tax Ordinance s.182 Table S.No.1
note: The tapering relief is almost universally omitted and is directly actionable for anyone reading in October. The Finance Act 2026 substituted the Explanation so 'tax payable' now means the higher of tax on assessed income or the tax payable for the immediately preceding year for which a return was filed, which was read from the gazette.

claim: s.114(6) allows a revised return subject to conditions including the Commissioner's written approval, but that approval requirement does not apply where the revision is made within sixty days of filing the original return, is deemed granted if the Commissioner does not pass a written order within sixty days of the request, is deemed granted where declared taxable income is higher or loss lower than determined under s.120, and the Commissioner shall grant approval in the case of a bona fide omission or wrong statement.
source: Income Tax Ordinance s.114(6) with provisos
note: Competitors state the approval requirement without any of the four carve-outs that mostly disapply it. The Finance Act 2026 also added s.114(6B): where a revision follows the new algorithmic settlement mechanism under s.134B, Commissioner approval is not required and no separate penalty or default surcharge is payable.

claim: Section 60C, the deductible allowance for profit on debt on a house loan, and section 62A, the tax credit for health insurance, were both omitted by the Finance Act 2022. Section 60D, the education expenses allowance, survives but only where taxable income is below Rs 1.5 million.
source: Income Tax Ordinance, sections 60C, 62A and 60D
note: Already recorded in lib/tax/pakistan.ts as a known secondary-source error. Both still appear as live reliefs on ranking pages.

claim: FBR's IRIS 2.0 return manual sets out the salaried filing flow: Declaration menu to Returns/Statements (Original) to Normal Return, enter the tax period, then Data tab to Employment for annual income, Tax Chargeable to read Admitted Income Tax code 9203, Adjustable Tax to enter it against Salary of Employees u/s 149 code 64020004, then the 116 Wealth Statement tabs, then Save and Submit with a four-digit PIN. Filing is complete when both the return and wealth statement move from Draft to Completed Task.
source: FBR IRIS 2.0 Filing Tax Return (Declaration) Manual
note: The manual states that the return completes only when the Unreconciled Amount, code 703000, is adjusted to zero. That is the top mechanical pain point for filers and FBR states the rule without the technique.

claim: s.119 allows a taxpayer to apply in writing to the Commissioner for an extension, by the due date, on limited grounds: absence from Pakistan, sickness or other misadventure, or any other reasonable cause. s.214A is FBR's own power to extend dates generally, which is the near-annual blanket extension.
source: Income Tax Ordinance ss.119 and 214A
note: Different actors, different tests, different reliability. Filing late in the hope of a s.214A circular is a bet, and s.182A consequences attach if it does not come. Competitors treat the two as interchangeable.

claim: Section 236K flat rate of 1.5 percent, as stated in FBR's Salient Features for Budget 2026-27
source: FBR Salient Features, contradicted by FBR Circular No. 02 of 2026-27 para 21
note: REJECTED AND RECORDED SO IT CANNOT RESURFACE. This figure is published by FBR itself, which is precisely what makes it dangerous: a writer sourcing from FBR can land on it in good faith. The Salient Features were written against the Bill and never corrected after the rate moved to 1.25 percent before enactment. Always prefer the circular or the gazette.

claim: FBR publishes an Income Tax Ordinance consolidation 'AMENDED UPTO 30TH JUNE, 2026' which postdates the Finance Act 2026. It prints s.154B in full, marks s.7E as omitted by the Finance Act 2026, and carries the Act's amendments throughout.
source: FBR, Income Tax Ordinance 2001 amended up to 30 June 2026, downloaded and text-extracted
note: CORRECTS A PREMISE BUILT INTO research/GUIDE-RESEARCH.md. That document says every available consolidation predates the Finance Act 2026 and therefore prints repealed law. That was true of the 31 July 2025 and 20 February 2026 editions and is no longer true generally. The underlying lesson survives and is arguably sharpened: always check the 'amended up to' date, because it is the difference between current law and repealed law, and a newer edition may exist than the one a search returns.

claim: s.154B, inserted by the Finance Act 2026: every banking and non-banking financial institution shall, at the time of credit or receipt of any amount in an account of a person, deduct tax at the rate in Division IIIAB where the amount represents revenues received from social media platforms. A digital content creator or social media influencer is any individual or entity deriving income from creation, publication or monetization of content on digital platforms including but not limited to YouTube, Facebook, Instagram and TikTok. Payment includes any inward remittance, transfer or credit received through banking channels, including through intermediaries such as online payment service providers or digital financial platforms.
source: Income Tax Ordinance s.154B, read verbatim from the 30 June 2026 consolidation
note: The withholding agent is the BANK, not the platform. Google, Meta and TikTok deduct nothing and are not agents. The charge attaches when money lands in a Pakistani account, and the definition of payment is drafted broadly enough to catch Payoneer and Wise style intermediaries.

claim: s.154B(3): the tax deducted is minimum in the case of a resident person, and final tax only in the case of a non-resident person not having a permanent establishment in Pakistan.
source: Income Tax Ordinance s.154B(3), read verbatim
note: MAJOR CORRECTION. Coverage universally describes s.154B as a 5 percent final tax. For a resident creator, which is nearly every Pakistani reader, it is MINIMUM tax: the 5 percent is a floor, business income is still computed on the Division I non-salaried slabs, and you pay the higher of the two with no refund of the excess. Given s.82(d), the final-tax limb reaches almost no domestic reader.

claim: Division IIIAB of Part III of the First Schedule, inserted by the Finance Act 2026, reads in full: the rate of tax to be deducted under section 154B shall be 5%.
source: First Schedule Part III Division IIIAB, read verbatim
note: There is NO 10 percent rate in Division IIIAB. The widely published '5 percent for filers, 10 percent for non-filers' is right about the outcome and wrong about the mechanism: the 10 percent comes from Tenth Schedule Rule 1, which increases the rate by one hundred percent for persons not on the ATL. Rule 10 lists the sections exempt from that doubling and includes s.154 and s.154A but NOT s.154B, so creator revenue is doubled where export proceeds are not.

claim: s.111(4): the unexplained-income provision does not apply to foreign exchange remitted from outside Pakistan through normal banking channels not exceeding five million rupees in a tax year, encashed into rupees by a scheduled bank with a certificate produced to that effect. An Explanation inserted by the Finance Act 2022 deems remittance through money service bureaus, exchange companies or money transfer operators to be through normal banking channels.
source: Income Tax Ordinance s.111(4), read verbatim
note: Three things nobody states: it is CAPPED at Rs 5 million per tax year, it requires encashment into rupees plus a bank certificate, and it is only a shield against s.111 treatment rather than an exemption from tax on the income. A freelancer's export receipts remain taxable under s.154A regardless.

claim: s.2(30AD) defines IT services as including but not limited to software development, software maintenance, system integration, web design, web development, web hosting and network design. s.2(30AE) defines IT enabled services as including but not limited to inbound and outbound call centres, medical transcription, remote monitoring, graphics design, accounting services, HR services, telemedicine centres, data entry operations, cloud computing services, data storage services, locally produced television programs and insurance claims processing.
source: Income Tax Ordinance s.2(30AD) and s.2(30AE)
note: Both lists are inclusive rather than exhaustive. Conspicuously absent: video editing, translation, copywriting, general virtual assistance and social media management. Whether those qualify is a real and unanswered question for a large share of Pakistani freelancers, and should be published as an open question rather than a confident yes.

claim: Division III Part III as amended by the Finance Act 2026: IT services and IT enabled services as defined in s.2 are withheld at 4 percent, minimum tax. General services not otherwise covered rose to 14 percent. Independent professional services remain 15 percent, and the Finance Act 2026 inserted an express list naming doctors, lawyers, architects, accountants and software engineers or developers working independently. Specified sectors rose from 6 to 7 percent.
source: First Schedule Part III Division III
note: OPEN TENSION worth publishing as one. A freelance developer billing a Pakistani company could be withheld at 4 percent as IT services under s.2(30AD), or at 15 percent as an independent software engineer working independently. Both entries were touched by the same Act. No FBR ruling resolving it was found.

claim: s.153(7) defines prescribed person to include, among others, an association of persons or individual with turnover of one hundred million rupees or above, and a sales-tax-registered person with the same turnover. There is a Rs 30,000 aggregate per financial year floor for services under s.153(1)(b).
source: Income Tax Ordinance s.153(7) and s.153(1)(b)
note: Means a freelancer billing an ordinary small domestic client faces no withholding at all, because the client is not a prescribed person. Income is then declared and taxed on slabs, with advance tax under s.147 if applicable.

claim: s.3(1A) of the Islamabad Capital Territory (Tax on Services) Ordinance 2001, inserted by the Finance Act 2021: notwithstanding sub-section (1), the export of services shall be charged at the rate of zero per cent.
source: ICT (Tax on Services) Ordinance 2001 s.3(1A), FBR-hosted text
note: The clean, primary-sourced answer for ICT. The equivalent KPK position remains unverified and matters more, since the firm is in KPK.

claim: s.114(1)(ae) requires a return from every person whose income for the year is subject to final taxation under any provision of the Ordinance, and s.114(1)(b)(vii) from anyone who has obtained a National Tax Number.
source: Income Tax Ordinance s.114(1)
note: Kills the belief that final tax means no filing obligation, twice over. Worse, s.154A(2)(a) makes filing a CONDITION of the final-tax treatment itself: fail to file and you lose the 0.25 percent.

claim: s.154B(4) empowers the Board to prescribe rules for implementation including identification and reporting mechanisms. No such notification was found as at 10 September 2026.
source: Income Tax Ordinance s.154B(4); absence of a traced SRO
note: PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT. A bank seeing a USD credit from Google must decide whether it is an IT export under s.154A at 0.25 or 1 percent, or platform revenue under s.154B at 5 percent. That is a twentyfold difference in withholding and the statute gives banks no published identification test. Publish as an open question; recheck FBR SROs issued after 1 July 2026.

claim: The KP Sales Tax on Services Act 2022 contains no zero-rating or exemption for exported services. Section 3(4) provides the opposite: 'Unless otherwise specified by Government, where rendering of a taxable service originates from the Province but terminates outside Pakistan, such person shall be required to pay tax on such service to Government.'
source: Khyber Pakhtunkhwa Sales Tax on Services Act 2022, updated through the KP Finance Act 2024, s.3(4), read verbatim
note: RESOLVED, and the answer is the opposite of ICT's. Islamabad zero-rates exported services under s.3(1A) of the ICT Ordinance; KP expressly taxes a service that originates in the Province and terminates abroad. The word 'export' appears only twice in the whole Act, neither time as a relief, and 'zero-rat' appears once, in s.16(3) about adjustment principles rather than as a rate. The PDF downloaded cleanly with a browser user-agent and a kpra.gov.pk referer; the earlier 403 was transient or agent-specific. Note the s.3(4) opening words, 'Unless otherwise specified by Government', which leave room for a notification we have not traced.

claim: Second Schedule entry 15 of the KP Sales Tax on Services Act 2022 taxes 'Digital or IT-based services in whatever form or manner' at 2 percent without any input tax adjustment, tariff heading 9850.0000. The entry expressly lists web design and development, mobile app development, server management, page-speed and UX/UI optimisation, PPC marketing, blogging, Google Ads, Facebook and Instagram advertising, custom software development, software maintenance and support, supply or sale of software through any medium, SEO, and social media, content, affiliate, influencer, email and viral marketing.
source: KP Sales Tax on Services Act 2022, Second Schedule entry 15
note: Directly relevant to both the freelancer and creator guides, and to BarrioVibe's own marketing services. Note that influencer marketing and social media marketing are named in the statute. Entry 15 carries an Explanation excluding persons providing software or IT-based system development in their INDIVIDUAL capacity, who fall under entry 19(g) instead.

claim: Second Schedule entry 19 of the KP Act covers services by practitioners, professionals, consultants and advisers, including at item (g) software or IT-based system development or management. A reduced rate of 2 percent without input tax adjustment is expressly stated for medical and legal practitioners. Entities operating in collaboration with, or as a subsidiary or branch of, a foreign service-providing entity pay 15 percent with admissible input tax adjustment.
source: KP Sales Tax on Services Act 2022, Second Schedule entry 19
note: IMPORTANT AMBIGUITY, publish as one. Entry 15's Explanation says an individual providing software or IT-based development is 'eligible to pay tax at reduced rate under item (g) of entry No. 19'. But entry 19's stated Reduced Rate of Tax clause names only medical and legal professions at 2 percent. So the Act points individual software professionals at a reduced rate whose figure is not spelled out for their category in the text read. The 15 percent column applies to foreign-affiliated entities. Do not state a single rate for an individual IT freelancer in KP without confirming with KPRA.

claim: s.236C(2) proviso, inserted by the Finance Act 2017: where immovable property referred to in sub-section (1) is acquired and disposed of within the same tax year, the tax collected under this section shall be minimum tax. Otherwise the 236C collection is adjustable.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.236C(2)
note: SUPERSEDES s236c2-minimum-tax-flip, which was unverified tier 4 from a specialist blog. Now read verbatim from the consolidation that postdates the Finance Act 2026. The practical consequence for a flipper: 236C at 2.75% of gross consideration becomes a floor rather than a credit, so on a same-year resale at a small margin the advance tax can exceed the CGT on the actual gain and none of the excess comes back.

claim: Second proviso to s.236C(1): where the seller is a non-resident individual holding a POC, NICOP or CNIC who acquired the property through a Foreign Currency Value Account (FCVA) or NRP Rupee Value Account (NRVA) maintained with an authorised bank under SBP foreign exchange regulations, the tax collected under s.236C is a final discharge of tax liability in lieu of capital gains taxable under section 37.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.236C(1) second proviso, added by the Finance Act 2021
note: MAJOR and uncovered. A non-resident who bought through an FCVA/NRVA pays 236C and owes no separate section 37 CGT on that disposal. The account type at the time of ACQUISITION decides it, which means the decision is made years before the sale. Directly relevant to the cross-border cluster and to overseas Pakistani property sellers.

claim: Section 182 penalty table entry 1AAA: where a person fails to furnish a foreign income and assets statement within the due date, the penalty is 2 percent of the foreign income or value of the foreign assets for each year of default.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.182 penalty table entry 1AAA
note: The number that makes s.116A real. At the USD 100,000 asset threshold this is USD 2,000 per year of default, and it accrues per year rather than once. Competitor coverage of s.116A states the filing duty and omits the penalty entirely.

claim: Section 195A, inserted by the Finance Act 2019: any person who without reasonable excuse fails to comply with a notice under s.116A(2) commits an offence punishable on conviction with imprisonment up to one year, or a fine up to fifty thousand rupees, or both. Section 116A(2) empowers the Commissioner to issue that notice to an individual who in his opinion, for reasons recorded in writing, was required to file a foreign income and assets statement and did not.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, ss.195A and 116A(2)
note: The escalation nobody publishes: the criminal exposure attaches to ignoring the NOTICE, not to the original failure to file. That distinction is what a reader needs, because it means a late voluntary filing sits in the penalty regime while ignoring a Commissioner's notice does not.

claim: Section 195B, inserted by the Finance Act 2019: any enabler who enables, guides or advises any person to design, arrange or manage a transaction or declaration in such a manner which results in offshore tax evasion commits an offence.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.195B
note: Relevant to the cross-border guide and to our own positioning: the adviser, not only the taxpayer, is exposed. Explains why a competent adviser will not structure around s.116A. The full penalty text runs past a page break in the extraction and was not read; state the offence, not a sentence, unless the tail is confirmed.

claim: Section 195B: an enabler who enables, guides or advises any person to design, arrange or manage a transaction or declaration resulting in offshore tax evasion commits an offence punishable on conviction with imprisonment for a term not exceeding seven years, or a fine up to five million rupees, or both.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.195B, inserted by the Finance Act 2019
note: COMPLETES s195b-enabler-offence, whose sentence ran past a page break. Note the asymmetry worth stating in the guide: the taxpayer who ignores a s.116A(2) notice faces up to one year under s.195A, while the ADVISER who arranged the structure faces up to seven under s.195B. Pakistan punishes the enabler considerably more heavily than the evader on these facts.

claim: Section 2(38AC) defines an offshore enabler as including any person who enables, assists, or advises any person to plan, design, arrange or manage a transaction or declaration relating to an offshore asset, which has resulted or may result in tax evasion.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.2(38AC)
note: Note 'or may result': the definition does not require evasion to have occurred. The civil penalty is separate, at s.182 table entry 23: three hundred thousand rupees or 200 percent of the tax sought to be evaded, whichever is higher.

claim: Section 216(6B) and (6C): the Board may publish in print and electronic media the names of offshore evaders who have evaded offshore tax of Rs 2.5 million or more, and the names of offshore tax enablers who have enabled offshore tax evasion, notwithstanding the confidentiality rule in s.216(1).
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.216(6B)-(6C)
note: The reputational limb of the offshore regime. Note the asymmetry again: the evader limb carries a Rs 2.5 million threshold, the enabler limb carries none. Completes the picture alongside s.2(38AC), s.182 entry 23, s.195A and s.195B.

claim: Section 37(2): the gain on disposal of a capital asset is computed as A minus B, where A is the consideration received and B is the cost of the asset. There is no indexation for inflation and no holding-period discount. The former s.37(3), which reduced the gain to three-quarters where an asset was held more than one year, was omitted by the Finance Act 2022. Section 37(1A) charges gain on immovable property situated in Pakistan at the rates in Division VIII of Part I of the First Schedule.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.37
note: The reader-facing consequence: on a property held ten years through high inflation, the taxable gain is the full nominal difference. Pakistan taxes the inflation as if it were profit. The three-quarters reduction that used to soften this is gone, and pages describing it are four years stale.

claim: Division VIII of Part I of the First Schedule, as substituted by the Finance Act 2024 and NOT amended by the Finance Act 2026, taxes gain on immovable property by reference to the acquisition date. Property acquired on or after 1 July 2024: 15% for persons appearing on the Active Taxpayers' List, however long it was held. Property acquired on or before 30 June 2024: a holding-period table, open plots 15/12.5/10/7.5/5/2.5/0 percent across bands of up to one year rising to over six years; constructed property 15/10/7.5/5/0 reaching nil after four years; flats 15/7.5/0 reaching nil after two years.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, First Schedule Part I Division VIII; Finance Act 2026 checked and does not amend Division VIII
note: DOCUMENT DEFECT WORTH RECORDING: FBR's consolidation prints only row 1 of the live table on page 526. Rows 2 to 7 of the current table are missing from the consolidation itself, not from the extraction; the full holding-period grid survives only in the footnote reproducing the pre-2024 Division. The rates above are reconciled against lib/tax/property.ts CGT_HOLDING_TABLE, which check-tax.ts asserts on every build, and against the Finance Act 2026 which leaves Division VIII alone. Two gain-banded tables (5/10/15/20 and 3.5/7.5/10/15) appear nearby and are HISTORICAL footnote text describing superseded versions: do not publish them as current.

claim: Proviso to Division VIII: the rate of tax to be paid under s.37(1A) is reduced by fifty per cent on the first sale of immovable property acquired or allotted to ex-servicemen and serving personnel of the Armed Forces, or ex-employees or serving personnel of Federal and Provincial Governments, being original allottees of the property, duly certified by the allotment authority.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, First Schedule Part I Division VIII proviso
note: Pairs with the parallel s.236C(4) and s.236C(1) provisos exempting the same class from advance tax on a first sale as original allottee. Two separate reliefs on the same transaction: half CGT and no 236C. Note the conditions are cumulative and narrow: FIRST sale, ORIGINAL allottee, and certification by the allotment authority.

claim: The Trade Marks Rules First Schedule prices two distinct search routes. Item 54, TM-55, a request for an official search under rule 87, costs PKR 1,000 in respect of EACH CLASS. Item 59, permission to search among the classified representations of trade marks yourself, costs PKR 300 for each quarter of an hour. Item 58, inspecting the Register or copies of a notice of opposition, counter-statement or decision, also costs PKR 300 per quarter hour.
source: Gazette notification, Trade Marks Rules 2004 First Schedule items 54, 58 and 59, read from ipo.gov.pk PDF
note: Competitors describe 'a trademark search' as one thing. There are two, priced differently and answering different questions: TM-55 is an official search the Registry performs and reports on, per class; item 59 is time-metered self-inspection of the classified representations. The per-class wording on TM-55 matters because Rule 13 permits only one class per application, so a business covering three classes is looking at three searches.

claim: Trade Marks Rules First Schedule item 55, TM-56: application for extension of time under rule 80 costs PKR 1,500. Item 56, TM-57: application for restoration of a trade mark ABANDONED for non-compliance with a requirement of the registry, under s.33(5) and s.26(3), costs PKR 1,500.
source: Gazette notification, Trade Marks Rules 2004 First Schedule items 55 and 56
note: TM-57 restoration after ABANDONMENT is a different thing from TM-13 restoration after REMOVAL for non-renewal, which costs PKR 3,000 under s.35(6). Three distinct failure modes with three fees: missing a registry deadline (TM-57, 1,500), missing renewal but inside the grace period (TM-12 additional fee, 900), and removal from the register (TM-13, 3,000). No competitor separates these.

claim: The Finance Act 2026 does not amend s.116A, s.195A, s.195B, s.2(38AC), or the s.182 penalty table entry 1AAA. Its only amendment to s.216 is to sub-section (3), clauses (ba) and (ke), concerning disclosure to auditors and research institutions; sub-sections (6B) and (6C), the offshore naming provisions, are untouched.
source: Finance Act 2026 gazette text, searched for each provision; research/raw/finance-act-2026.txt
note: VINTAGE CHECK, done because METHOD.md section 1 requires it before publishing anything from a consolidation. The whole offshore enforcement chain read from the consolidation amended to 30 June 2026 is confirmed current for tax year 2027. The s.116A thresholds are additionally corroborated by FBR's own s.116A page at research/raw/fbr-116a.txt, which matches the consolidation word for word: two independent primary sources.

claim: The Finance Act 2026 did NOT amend section 82 of the Income Tax Ordinance. The ITO amendment part of the Act (section 5 of the Act) amends only sections 2, 6A, 8, 21, 76, 80, 92, 99B, 100B, 114, 134A, 143, 147, 152, 159, 169, 174, 175AA, 177, 182, 182A, 207, 216, 222, 227D and 231B, plus schedule changes. s.82 is untouched, so the 183-day test in (a) and the 182-day test in (d) both stand for tax year 2027.
source: Finance Act 2026 gazette, 26 June 2026, section 5
note: CAUTION recorded for future agents: grepping the whole Finance Act 2026 text for 'section 82' returns a hit at line 160, but that is CUSTOMS ACT s.82 (clearance of goods), inside section 3 of the Act. The Income Tax Ordinance amendments run from 'Amendments of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001' to 'Amendments of the Federal Excise Act'. Always scope the grep to that block before concluding an income tax section changed.

claim: s.82 current text, consolidated to 30 June 2026: an individual is resident for a tax year if (a) present in Pakistan for a period of, or periods amounting in aggregate to, one hundred and eighty-three days or more in the tax year; or (c) is an employee or official of the Federal Government or a Provincial Government posted abroad in the tax year; (d) being a citizen of Pakistan is not present in any other country for more than one hundred and eighty-two days during the tax year or who is not a resident taxpayer of any other country. Clause (b) was omitted by the Finance Act 2003 and clause (ab), the 120-day test, was inserted by the Finance Act 2019 and OMITTED by the Finance Act 2021.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.82 and footnotes
note: The 183 figure is footnoted: 'The words eighty-two substituted by the Finance Act, 2006.' Clause (d) footnote: 'The full stop substituted with a semicolon and clause (d) inserted by the Finance Act, 2022.' There is NO clause (b) and no 120-day test in current law: secondary sources still describing a 120-day rule are quoting law repealed in 2021.

claim: Neither s.82 nor any other provision of the Income Tax Ordinance defines how a day of presence is counted. There is no part-day rule, no day-of-arrival or day-of-departure rule and no transit rule anywhere in the Ordinance. s.83 is 'Resident company' and s.84 is 'Resident association of persons', neither of which concerns day counting.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026
note: OPEN QUESTION, publishable as such. A search of the full consolidated Ordinance for 'part of a day', 'day of arrival', 'whole day' and 'counted as' returns nothing, and 'present in Pakistan' appears only in s.82 itself and in one unrelated clause. The guide should say plainly that the statute does not resolve it, rather than importing the UK or Indian rule.

claim: s.11(5): the income of a RESIDENT person under a head of income shall be computed by taking into account amounts that are Pakistan-source income and amounts that are foreign-source income. s.11(6): the income of a NON-RESIDENT person under a head of income shall be computed by taking into account only amounts that are Pakistan-source income.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.11
note: Read verbatim. This is the hinge for both guides: residency status, not the route the money travels, decides whether foreign income is in charge.

claim: s.114(1)(b)(vii): a person who 'has obtained National Tax Number' is required to furnish a return of income, and that clause carries NO residence qualifier. By contrast s.114(1)(b)(ix) is expressly limited to 'a resident person' registered with a chamber of commerce etc, and (b)(x) to 'a resident person being an individual' required to file under s.116A. The drafting asymmetry is on the face of the section.
source: Income Tax Ordinance consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.114(1)
note: This answers the practical question of whether merely holding an NTN obliges a non-resident to file. On the statutory text it does, because the words 'a resident person' were inserted into (ix) by the Finance Act 2014 and into (x) but never into (vii). The other unqualified triggers are (b)(iii)-(vi): immovable property of 500 sq yd or more, a flat, a flat of 2000 sq ft or more in a rating area, and a motor vehicle above 1000cc.

claim: The Rs 5 million cap in s.111(4) was NOT in the original provision. The Ordinance footnotes show sub-section (4) was substituted by the Finance Act 2004 in unlimited form, and the cap 'not exceeding five million Rupees in a tax year' arrived with the Finance Act 2021 substitution.
