A PSEB-registered IT exporter whose proceeds are withheld at 0.25% under s.154A is outside s.6A entirely, so the e-commerce charge does not stack on top of the export regime. The carve-out keys on the proceeds being SUBJECTED TO WITHHOLDING under those sections, not merely on the person being an exporter, which matters where a receipt is routed outside the s.154A channel.

claim: s.6A(3), notwithstanding s.8: the tax imposed under s.6A on a person whose turnover in a tax year exceeds two hundred million rupees shall be ADJUSTABLE. A proviso allows a person with turnover up to two hundred million rupees to opt out of the final tax regime at the time of filing the return for tax year 2027 and onwards.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.6A(3)
note: The default for a smaller seller is FINAL tax, which is unusual and is the opposite of the s.154B creator position where residents get minimum tax. Above Rs 200 million turnover it is adjustable automatically; below that it is final unless the person opts out on filing, and the opt-out is available from tax year 2027. A small seller with thin margins may be much better off opting out, since 1 or 2 percent of GROSS can exceed the tax on actual profit.

claim: s.79(1) provides that no gain or loss shall be taken to arise on the disposal of an asset: (a) between spouses under an agreement to live apart; (b) by reason of transmission to an executor or beneficiary on death; (c) by reason of a gift of the asset TO A RELATIVE as defined in s.85(5); (d) on compulsory acquisition under any law where the consideration is reinvested in a like asset within one year; (e) by a company to its shareholders on liquidation; (f) by an association to its members on dissolution in accordance with their interests. s.79(3): where (a), (b), (c), (e) or (f) applies, the acquirer is treated as acquiring an asset of the same character AND at a cost equal to the disposer's cost at the time of disposal.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.79
note: The carry-over cost basis in s.79(3)(b) is the part that matters and is almost never explained. A gift to a relative is not a tax-free step-up: the recipient inherits the giver's original cost, so the whole accrued gain is preserved and lands on the recipient when they eventually sell. Gifting an asset before selling it therefore defers nothing and shifts the gain to a different person. Note the restriction added by the Finance Act 2018: the gift limb was narrowed to a gift TO A RELATIVE, so a gift to a friend or an unrelated party is a disposal at market value.

claim: An Explanation inserted into s.79(1)(b) by the Finance Act 2026 clarifies, for removal of doubt, that transmission of immovable property to a beneficiary on the death of a person shall ALSO INCLUDE the transmission of assets by reason of a family settlement amongst the family members consequent upon the death of the person.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.79(1)(b) Explanation, footnoted as inserted by the Finance Act 2026
note: NEW THIS YEAR and uncovered. It closes a real and common problem: heirs who redistribute inherited property among themselves by agreement, rather than taking exactly what the succession certificate allocates, were arguably making taxable disposals to one another. The Explanation brings that family settlement inside the non-recognition rule, provided it is consequent upon the death. Note the limits on its face: it speaks of IMMOVABLE property and of a settlement consequent upon death, so a rearrangement among living family members is not within it.

claim: The live s.85(5)(i) defines 'relative' in relation to an individual as (a) an ancestor, a descendant of any of the grandparents, or an adopted child, of the individual or of a spouse of the individual; or (b) a spouse of the individual or of any person specified in clause (a). Sub-section (5) was substituted by the Finance Act 2023, which restructured it and added a definition of 'jurisdiction with zero taxation regime'.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.85(5), live text read above the footnote apparatus
note: FOOTNOTE TRAP AVOIDED, and worth recording as a worked instance. The consolidation prints the pre-2023 definition inside footnote 1 immediately below the live text, and the two are materially identical in the relative limb, so quoting the footnote would have produced a correct-looking claim from the wrong text. Applying the METHOD.md rule, the live text is the one above the marker. The practical scope: descendants of any grandparent reaches siblings, uncles, aunts and first cousins, which is wider than most readers assume.

claim: Sales Tax Act 1990 s.2(9) defines 'due date' in relation to furnishing a return under s.26 as the 15th day of the month following the end of the tax period, or such other date as the Board may specify by notification, AND expressly permits 'different dates may be specified for furnishing of different parts or annexures of the return'. The '15th' was substituted for '20th' by the Finance Act 1998; the annexure-splitting words were inserted by the Finance Act 2016.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/20267171373418951SalesTaxAct1990updatedupto30.06.2026.pdf s.2(9), consolidation amended to 30 June 2026
note: The statutory anchor. Note s.2(9) is the FILING definition; the PAYMENT date is separate and comes from rule 18(9). The annexure-splitting clause is why Annex-C has its own 10th-of-month deadline.

claim: Sales Tax Rules 2006 rule 18(9): 'In cases where due date has been prescribed as 15th of a month, the tax due shall be deposited by the 15th and the return shall be submitted electronically by 18th of the same month.' Payment and filing are therefore NOT the same date for the ordinary monthly return: pay by the 15th, file by the 18th.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/2025881385446623STR-2006-UpdatedUpto06-08-2025(ver-iv).pdf rule 18(9)
note: FLAGSHIP CORRECTION for the sales tax return guide. Competitors overwhelmingly state a single '15th' or single '18th' deadline. Both halves are wrong on their own. Rule 18(8) requires payment into a designated NBP branch on challan STR-11 or through the electronic payment system.

claim: Sales Tax Rules 2006 rule 18(9) proviso, Table: seven categories have their own payment and filing dates. Electricity distribution companies pay by the 18th and file by the 21st; Independent Power Producers pay 22nd, file 25th; gas transmission and distribution companies pay 15th, file 18th; petroleum exploration and production companies pay 18th, file 21st; CNG dealers (quarterly) pay 15th, file 18th after quarter end; brick manufacturers under the Tenth Schedule (quarterly) pay 15th, file 18th; WAPDA hydroelectric pay 18th, file 21st.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/2025881385446623STR-2006-UpdatedUpto06-08-2025(ver-iv).pdf rule 18(9) proviso Table
note: S.No.6 inserted by SRO 1203(I)/2019, S.No.7 by SRO 169(I)/2022. Rule 14(2): a person operating in several sectors with different dates files ONE return by the date applicable to his MAJOR activity.

claim: The monthly sales tax return is form STR-7 (Sales Tax Rules 2006 rule 14(1)), filed 'along with all its annexure provided therein'. The annexures in the prescribed form, with their own headings: Annex-A (PURCHASES), Annex-B (IMPORTS), Annex-C (Domestic Sales / DOMESTIC SALES INVOICES), Annex-C1, Annex-D (EXPORTS), Annex-E (EXCISES), Annex-E1 (NATURAL GAS), Annex-F (CARRY FORWARDS), Annex-G (ARREARS), Annex-H (STOCKS), Annex-H1 (STOCK), Annex-I (DEBIT CREDIT NOTES), Annex-J (PRODUCTION), Annex-K (STATEMENT OF PRODUCTION AND SUPPLIES FOR STEEL PRODUCTS), Annex-L (For Petroleum Development Levy (PDL)), and Annex-P (BREAKUP OF SERVICES, 'TO BE COMPLETED BY THE SERVICE PROVIDER', showing province or area from which the service is provided, value of services excluding sales tax, and sales tax charged).
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/2025881385446623STR-2006-UpdatedUpto06-08-2025(ver-iv).pdf rule 14 and form STR-7
note: Annex-C was SUBSTITUTED and Annex-C1 INSERTED by SRO 578(I)/2025 dated 8 April 2025, so any competitor page describing Annex-C from before April 2025 is stale. Annex-K added by SRO 918(I)/2019; Annex-L inserted by SRO 1185(I)/2023 dated 5 September 2023. Rule 14(1) provisos (SRO 55(I)/2025, 24 January 2025): registered manufacturers must furnish Annex-J; registered commercial importers, distributors and wholesalers must furnish Annex-H1. ANNEX-P IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS FOR A SERVICES BUSINESS: it breaks services down by the province or area from which the service is provided, which is the federal return's interface with provincial sales tax on services. Rule 18(1) proviso: if a registered person fails to fill in relevant data in ANY applicable column of the return or any annexure, the return SHALL BE TREATED AS INVALID.

claim: Sales Tax Rules 2006 rule 18(3): a registered person enters supplies data in Annexure-C and debit/credit notes in Annexure-I and must submit that data BY THE 10TH day of the month following the tax period. As soon as the supplier submits Annex-C/Annex-I data, it becomes immediately available to the buyer in his 'Purchase Data' and 'Debit or Credit Note Data', and the buyer LOADS that data into his Annexure-A and Annexure-I. Purchases from unregistered persons are entered manually in Annexure-A.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/2025881385446623STR-2006-UpdatedUpto06-08-2025(ver-iv).pdf rule 18(3)
note: ANSWERS 'which annexures are auto-populated'. Annex-A is populated FROM the counterparty's Annex-C, it is not typed. This is also the reason the Annex-C deadline (10th) is earlier than the return deadline (18th): the buyer needs the seller's data to build his own return. Directly supported by s.2(9)'s clause allowing different dates for different annexures.

claim: Sales Tax Rules 2006 rule 18(3), second proviso (added by SRO 350(I)/2024 dated 7 March 2024): a buyer's return for a tax period is taken as a PROVISIONAL return in IRIS until the seller files his return for the same tax period up to the last day of the month in which the due date of filing falls. (a) Where the seller fails to file by that day, IRIS computes the buyer's liability AFTER DELETING the non-filer seller's invoices and the corresponding input tax, and the provisional return is then taken as valid after payment of the liability so computed. (b) Where the seller does file with payment by that day, the provisional return is taken as valid WITH the claim of those invoices and input tax.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/2025881385446623STR-2006-UpdatedUpto06-08-2025(ver-iv).pdf rule 18(3) second proviso
note: THE ANSWER to the biggest practical pain point, and precisely sourced. There IS a provisional/suspended input mechanism and it is automatic in IRIS. Rule 18A (SRO 1130(I)/2024, 1 August 2024) carves out six categories from this proviso, including invoices from gas and electricity distribution companies, IPPs/WAPDA and petroleum E&P companies where they have paid, and manufacturer-to-distributor invoices where the manufacturer has paid, and buyers whose suppliers pay the recomputed liability within six days from the end of the month in which their returns were taken as provisional.

claim: Three distinct Sales Tax Act 1990 provisions deny input tax by reference to the supplier: s.8(1)(ca) denies input tax on goods or services 'in respect of which sales tax has not been deposited in the Government treasury by the respective supplier' (inserted by the Finance Act 2006); s.8(1)(caa) denies input tax on 'purchases in respect of which a discrepancy is indicated by CREST or input tax of which is not verifiable in the supply chain'; and s.8(1)(l) denies, 'from the date to be notified by the Board', input tax on goods and services which at the time of the buyer's filing 'have not been declared by the supplier in his return or he has not paid amount of tax due as indicated in his return'. The parallel proviso to s.7(2)(i) is also expressed to run 'from the date to be notified by the Board'.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/20267171373418951SalesTaxAct1990updatedupto30.06.2026.pdf ss.7(2)(i), 8(1)(ca), 8(1)(caa), 8(1)(l)
note: CREST is defined at s.2(5AC) as the computerised program for analysing and cross matching sales tax returns, COMPUTERISED RISK-BASED EVALUATION of SALES TAX, inserted by the Finance Act 2013. IMPORTANT: rule 18(2) of the Sales Tax Rules 2006 states that the proviso to s.7(2)(i) and clause (l) of s.8(1) 'shall be applicable for sales tax and federal excise returns for the tax periods from July, 2016 and onwards', which is the Board notification those two provisions were waiting on. Clauses (ca) and (caa) are NOT conditional on a notification.

claim: Sales Tax Act 1990 s.8A makes a registered person receiving a taxable supply, who is in the knowledge or has reasonable grounds to suspect that some or all of the tax on that supply or any previous or subsequent supply would go unpaid, JOINTLY AND SEVERALLY liable with the supplier for the unpaid tax. The words ', of which the burden to prove shall be on the department' were inserted by the Finance Act 2015.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/20267171373418951SalesTaxAct1990updatedupto30.06.2026.pdf s.8A
note: The burden-of-proof words matter and are usually omitted by competitors: the department must prove the buyer's knowledge or reasonable grounds. The Board may exempt transactions from s.8A by notification.

claim: Sales Tax Act 1990 s.8B(1): a registered person shall not be allowed to adjust input tax in excess of NINETY PER CENT of output tax for that tax period. First proviso: the restriction does not apply in the case of fixed assets or capital goods. Second proviso: the Board may exclude any person or class of persons by notification. THIRD PROVISO, ADDED BY THE FINANCE ACT 2026: the Board may by notification 'reduce or enhance the limit provided in this sub-section for any registered person on the basis of compliance or non-compliance with the production monitoring, digital invoicing, e-bility, POS, or any other electronic system prescribed by the Board for digital integration of data.'
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/20267171373418951SalesTaxAct1990updatedupto30.06.2026.pdf s.8B
note: CURRENT for tax periods from 1 July 2026. The 90% figure itself is unchanged; what is NEW for TY2027 is that the cap is now explicitly tunable per registered person by reference to digital-integration compliance. s.8B(2) allows adjustment or refund of the disallowed excess on furnishing audited accounts certified by auditors showing value addition below the limit; s.8B(3) makes that a yearly exercise in the second month following the end of the financial year. s.8B(4) lets the Board use a data-based automated risk management system to defer input tax or fix higher or lower limits, with a right to contest by application to the Commissioner who must decide within thirty days. s.8B(6): a Tier-1 retailer who fails to integrate loses 60% of adjustable input tax for the period.

claim: Sales Tax Act 1990 s.33, Table, S.No.1: a person who fails to furnish a return within the due date shall pay a penalty of FIFTY THOUSAND rupees, with a proviso that where the return is filed within TEN days of the due date the penalty is TWO THOUSAND rupees for each day of default. The Finance Act 2026 substituted 'ten' with 'fifty' thousand and, in the proviso, 'hundred' with 'thousand'.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/20267171373418951SalesTaxAct1990updatedupto30.06.2026.pdf s.33 Table S.No.1; confirmed against Finance Act 2026 gazette 26 June 2026, amendments to the Sales Tax Act, item (12)
note: MAJOR AND TIME-SENSITIVE: the fixed penalty rose 5x (Rs 10,000 to Rs 50,000) and the daily penalty rose 10x (Rs 200 to Rs 2,000/day) with effect from the Finance Act 2026. Every competitor page written before July 2026 states the old figures. VERIFICATION NOTE: the consolidation's footnote 484 reads 'the word "fifty" Substituted through Finance Act, 2026', which under the usual FBR footnote convention would mean fifty was REPLACED. The enacting gazette settles it the other way: 'for the word "ten", the word "fifty" shall be substituted'. The consolidation's footnote wording is unreliable here; the gazette is definitive. This is a live example of why the enacted Act must be checked.

claim: The Sales Tax Act 1990 contains NO express provision requiring a 'null' or 'nil' return, and no such words appear in the Act. The obligation arises from the general words of s.26(1), 'Every registered person shall furnish not later than the due date a true, complete and correct return', which is not conditioned on having made supplies. This contrasts with the Income Tax Ordinance s.165, which carries an EXPRESS proviso that a withholding statement must be filed 'even where no withholding tax is collected or deducted during the period'.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/20267171373418951SalesTaxAct1990updatedupto30.06.2026.pdf s.26(1); searched the full Act for 'null return', 'nil return', 'no supplies' and 'even where no', zero hits
note: Publishable as a precise point: the duty is real but it is implied from 'every registered person', not spelled out, and the s.33 S.No.1 penalty attaches to failure to furnish A RETURN without any carve-out for a period of no activity. The contrast with the express s.165 proviso is a good teaching device. Words 'making taxable supplies' were OMITTED from s.26(1) by the Finance Act 1999, which strengthens the reading that the duty does not depend on activity.

claim: Sales Tax Act 1990 s.26(3): a registered person may file a revised return within ONE HUNDRED AND TWENTY days of filing, subject to approval of the Commissioner Inland Revenue. s.26(3A) (inserted by the Finance Act 2025): approval is NOT required if the revised return is filed within sixty days of filing and the tax payable is more, or the refund claimed is less, than in the original, unless restricted by the Board's compliance risk management system. s.26(2A) (inserted by the Finance Act 2024): an officer may by notice require a non-filer to furnish a return within fifteen days, and such notice may only be issued within fifteen years from the end of the financial year in cases of tax fraud and five years in all other cases. Sales Tax Rules 2006 rule 14(3): a return not filed within six months after the due date may be filed only after approval of the Commissioner.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/20267171373418951SalesTaxAct1990updatedupto30.06.2026.pdf s.26; Sales Tax Rules 2006 rule 14(3)
note: The six-month rule in rule 14(3) is the practical trap for a dormant registered person who stops filing: after six months he cannot self-serve, he needs the Commissioner. Useful for the null-return section.

claim: Sales Tax Rules 2006 rule 17: as stipulated in the second proviso to s.26(1) of the Sales Tax Act 1990, every registered person BEING A PRIVATE OR PUBLIC LIMITED COMPANY shall file an annual sales tax return in form STR-10 for a financial year by the 30th SEPTEMBER of the following financial year.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/2025881385446623STR-2006-UpdatedUpto06-08-2025(ver-iv).pdf rule 17
note: Widely omitted by competitor guides, which cover only the monthly return. Applies to companies only, not to individuals or AOPs. Form STR-10, distinct from the monthly STR-7.

claim: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.165(1) requires every person collecting tax under Division II of Part V of Chapter X, or Chapter XII, or the Tenth Schedule, or deducting tax under Division III, to furnish to the Commissioner a QUARTERLY statement in the prescribed form. The word 'biannual' was substituted (i.e. replaced) by the Finance Act 2020 dated 30 June 2020, and 'half year' was likewise replaced by 'quarter' throughout clauses (a) to (c). s.165(2) sets the due dates: quarter ending 31 March, on or before 20 April; quarter ending 30 June, on or before 20 July; quarter ending 30 September, on or before 20 October; quarter ending 31 December, on or before 20 January.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/ Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.165(1) and s.165(2)
note: Footnote 9 to s.165(2) reproduces the SUBSTITUTED clauses, which read 'in respect of the half-year ending on the 30th June, on or before the 31st day of July; and ... 31st December, on or before the 31st day of January.' Those are the OLD dates and must not be published as current. History: annual (pre-2010) then biannual then quarterly from the Finance Act 2020. Contrast the stale Income Tax Rules 2002 rule 44(2) which still prescribes a MONTHLY statement, recorded separately as contested.

claim: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.165(1), first proviso (inserted by the Finance Act 2010): 'every person as provided in sub-section (1) shall be required to file withholding statement even where no withholding tax is collected or deducted during the period'. Second proviso (added by the Finance Act 2020): 'this section shall not apply where information required under sub-section (1) has been furnished under section 165A.'
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.165(1) provisos
note: A NIL withholding statement is expressly required. This is the direct answer to whether a dormant withholding agent must still file, and it is stated in the statute rather than inferred, unlike the sales tax null return.

claim: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.165 imposes several distinct statements beyond the quarterly one. s.165(1A) (Finance Act 2020): every person engaged in economic transactions as prescribed by the Board shall furnish a quarterly statement. s.165(2A) (Finance Act 2017): a revised statement may be filed within SIXTY days of filing the original. s.165(2B): the Commissioner may by written notice require a statement for any period specified. s.165(4): a person may apply in writing to the Commissioner for an extension of time to furnish the statement, and the Commissioner may grant it by written order if satisfied a reasonable cause exists. s.165(6): every person deducting tax from a payment under s.149 (salary) shall furnish an ANNUAL statement. s.165(7): a prescribed person shall e-file an annual statement for the relevant tax year within THIRTY DAYS of the end of the tax year, IN ADDITION to the s.165(6) statement. s.165(8): such a person shall also e-file a RECONCILIATION statement reconciling the amounts in the annual statement under s.165(7) with the amounts declared in the return, audited accounts or financial statements, by the due date of filing the return of income under s.118.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.165(1A), (2A), (2B), (4), (6), (7), (8)
note: ANSWERS the s.149 relationship. The employer's salary deduction is reported BOTH in the quarterly s.165(1) statement and in a separate annual statement under s.165(6). Income Tax Rules 2002 rule 44(5) prescribes the s.165(6) annual statement by the 31st day of July after the end of the financial year, in the form set out in Part IX of the Second Schedule. Most competitor content covers only the quarterly statement and misses (6), (7) and (8) entirely, which is a real content gap.

claim: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.182(1), Table, entry 1A covers failure to furnish a statement required under s.165, 165A, 165B or 165C within the due date. The penalty: Rs 50,000 if the person had already paid the tax collected or withheld within the due date for payment AND the statement is filed within ninety days from the due date for filing; in ALL OTHER CASES, Rs 2,500 for each day of default from the due date, subject to a minimum penalty of Rs 10,000. Proviso (Finance Act 2021): where it stands established that no tax was required to be deducted or collected during the relevant period, the minimum amount of penalty shall be TEN THOUSAND rupees.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.182(1) Table entry 1A
note: The Rs 50,000 figure is CURRENT: footnote 5 to the entry reads 'The figure "5000" substituted by the Finance Act, 2025', and under the FBR footnote convention the QUOTED figure is the one REPLACED, so Rs 5,000 came out and Rs 50,000 went in. The expression '165, 165A, 165B or 165C' was itself substituted by the Finance Act 2025. The proviso is the important practical point: a NIL statement filed late still attracts a Rs 10,000 minimum. Entry 1A was inserted by the Finance Act 2013.

claim: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.159(1): where the Commissioner is satisfied that an amount to which Division II or III of Part V of Chapter X, or Chapter XII, applies is (a) exempt from tax, (b) subject to tax at a rate LOWER than that specified in the First Schedule, or (c) subject to hundred percent tax credit under this Ordinance, the Commissioner SHALL, upon application in writing by the person in the prescribed form, issue the person with an exemption OR lower rate certificate. s.159(2): a withholding agent must deduct or collect the FULL amount specified unless there is in force a certificate under sub-section (1), in which case he shall comply with the certificate.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.159(1) and (2)
note: BOTH an exemption certificate and a lower-rate certificate, in one section. Clause (c) was added by the Finance Act 2014, and the expression 'section 100C' was replaced with 'under this Ordinance' by the Finance Act 2021, widening it. The decision-maker is the Commissioner. Note the wording is 'shall ... issue' once satisfied, so the discretion is in the satisfaction, not in the issuing. s.159(2) is what makes the certificate binding on the payer.

claim: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.159(1), provisos added by the Finance Act 2021: (i) 'in case of A COMPANY, the Commissioner shall issue exemption or lower rate certificate under this section within fifteen days of filing of application by the company'; (ii) 'the Commissioner shall be DEEMED to have issued the exemption certificate upon the expiry of fifteen days from filing of application by the aforesaid company and the certificate shall be automatically processed and issued by Iris'; (iii) 'the Commissioner may modify or cancel the certificate issued automatically by Iris on the basis of reasons to be recorded in writing after providing an opportunity of being heard.'
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.159(1) first, second and third provisos
note: MAJOR CORRECTION. The automatic-issuance-on-silence rule is REAL but it is confined to COMPANIES: the second proviso says 'the aforesaid company'. It does NOT apply to an individual or an AOP, and secondary sources routinely state the fifteen-day deemed issuance as though it were general. An individual freelancer or a sole proprietor applying under s.159 has NO statutory deadline for the Commissioner to decide and no deemed issuance on silence. Also note the deemed certificate is expressly revocable: the Commissioner may modify or cancel it with reasons recorded in writing after a hearing, so it is not unconditional.

claim: The Finance Act 2026 inserted s.159(1C) and s.159(1D) into the Income Tax Ordinance 2001. (1C): where a person has distributed ninety percent or more of its accounting income among unit or certificate holders or shareholders in accordance with clauses (99) and (99C) of Part I of the Second Schedule for the year immediately preceding the last tax year, the person is eligible for an exemption certificate under sub-section (1) and 'the certificate shall be issued for the subsequent WHOLE TAX YEAR', with a proviso for a person who has started business for the first time issuing on the basis of an undertaking to distribute ninety percent. (1D): where a person has been issued approval under sub-clause (c) of clause (36) of section 2 for a tax year, the person is eligible for an exemption certificate under sub-section (1) and 'the certificate shall be issued for the said whole tax year'.
source: Finance Act 2026 gazette 26 June 2026, amendments to the Income Tax Ordinance item (27); confirmed in the consolidation at s.159(1C) and (1D) with footnote 'Sub-sections (1C) and (1D) inserted by the Finance Act, 2026'
note: NEW for tax year 2027 and almost certainly not covered by any competitor. Read verbatim from the enacting gazette AND cross-checked against the consolidation, which is the standard METHOD.md sets. Relevant to collective investment schemes, REITs and clause 2(36)(c)-approved non-profits rather than to the typical IT exporter, but it is the clearest statutory instance of a WHOLE-TAX-YEAR validity period, which matters for the validity question.

claim: Neither Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.159 nor Income Tax Rules 2002 rule 40 prescribes a general validity period for an exemption or lower-rate certificate. Rule 40 prescribes only the FORMS: an application under s.159(1) in the form specified in Part VII of the First Schedule, and the certificate itself in the form in Part VIII, with Part VII(a) and Part VIII(a) for the SRO 947(I)/2008 system-based import certificate. The certificate form at Part VIII(A) contains a field 'Validity period From: ____ To: ____', so the duration is set by the Commissioner on the face of each certificate rather than fixed by law. The only statutory whole-tax-year durations are the new s.159(1C) and (1D), and s.159(1B) which provides that a s.236C certificate for a long-held personal residence 'shall be issued once in fifteen years'.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026 s.159; Income Tax Rules 2002 consolidated to 24 NOVEMBER 2023, rule 40 and First Schedule Parts VII, VII(a), VIII, VIII(A): https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/2023112416114319348IncomeTaxRules2002AmendedUpto24.11.2023.pdf
note: ANSWERS the validity question honestly: there is no single statutory answer, and any competitor stating a flat 'valid for one year' as a general rule is asserting something the statute and Rules do not say. The publishable line is that validity is whatever the certificate states, except where the Ordinance fixes it. VINTAGE CAVEAT REMOVED: re-verified against FBR's NEWEST Rules consolidation (24 November 2023), not the stale 2017 file. Rule 40 is UNCHANGED between the two: it still prescribes forms only and no duration. Corroborated by FBR's Iris FAQs, which say that for import quota certificates the Commissioner does not write the validity period into the order because it 'is already fixed by the System'.

claim: Both s.153 (payments for goods, services and contracts) and s.154A (export of services) sit in DIVISION III of Part V of Chapter X of the Income Tax Ordinance 2001, per the Ordinance's own table of contents which places Division III 'Deduction of Tax at Source' over sections 149 to 158. s.159(1) applies to 'an amount to which Division II or III of this Part or Chapter XII applies'. A s.159 certificate is therefore capable in principle of reaching both a s.153 services deduction and a s.154A export-of-services deduction.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, table of contents for Part V Divisions II to IV, and s.159(1)
note: Establishes the statutory route rather than asserting it. The practical obstacle is separate and is recorded as s153-minimum-tax-blocks-159: s.153(3) makes the deduction MINIMUM tax for a resident, and s.154A(2) makes the deduction FINAL tax where the conditions are met, so there is generally no 'exempt or lower rate' finding for the Commissioner to be satisfied of. The certificate route is not a general escape from a minimum or final tax regime.

claim: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.153(3): the tax deductible under s.153(1) and (2) on the income of a resident person shall be MINIMUM tax, subject to provisos which make it not-minimum for sale or supply of goods by a manufacturer company or a listed public company, and adjustable for a listed public company on execution of contracts. The word 'final' was substituted by the Finance Act 2019, i.e. the regime moved from final to minimum. s.154A(2) makes the s.154A deduction a FINAL tax on fulfilment of conditions, one of which, clause (b), is that 'withholding tax statements for the relevant tax year have been filed if required under the Ordinance'.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.153(3) and s.154A(2)
note: THE HONEST ANSWER for the IT exporter and services provider. A s.159 certificate presupposes the Commissioner being satisfied the amount is exempt, taxable at a lower rate, or subject to 100% tax credit. Where s.153(3) imposes a minimum tax the liability cannot fall below the deduction, so there is normally nothing for the Commissioner to certify. Note also the direct Topic 2 to Topic 3 linkage: s.154A(2)(b) makes final-tax treatment for a PSEB-registered IT exporter CONDITIONAL on having filed the s.165 withholding statements. That single cross-reference is the strongest reason the three guides should link to each other.

claim: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.154A(1)(a) requires every authorised dealer in foreign exchange to deduct tax at realisation of foreign exchange proceeds on exports of computer software or IT services or IT enabled services 'where the exporter is registered with and duly certified by the Pakistan Software Export Board (PSEB)'. That PSEB expression was substituted by the Finance Act 2022 for the earlier expression 'in case tax credit under section 65F is not available'. s.154A(2) makes the deduction final tax on three conditions: (a) return has been filed; (b) withholding tax statements for the relevant tax year have been filed if required; (c) sales tax returns under Federal or Provincial laws have been filed if required, with a proviso disapplying condition (c) for a clause (a) exporter.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.154A(1) and (2)
note: RE-VERIFICATION of the pre-existing store finding s154a-pseb-condition against the consolidation to 30 June 2026. The earlier record stands and is CORROBORATED, not contradicted. This record adds two things the earlier one did not carry: the s.154A(1)(a) condition that the exporter be 'registered with and duly certified by the Pakistan Software Export Board (PSEB)', substituted by the Finance Act 2022 for the earlier expression 'in case tax credit under section 65F is not available'; and the express proviso disapplying condition (c) (sales tax returns) for a clause (a) exporter. The s.165 linkage in condition (b) is the direct bridge between the withholding-statement guide and the IT-exporter guide.

claim: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 First Schedule Part III Division III, sub-paragraph (i) proviso: 'the rate of tax shall be 4% in case of IT services and IT enabled services as defined in section 2', against a 7% headline rate for the listed service categories which expressly include software development services, IT services and IT enabled services. Sub-paragraph (ii), substituted by the Finance Act 2026: '15% in the case of independent professional services such as doctors, lawyers, architects, accountants, software engineers or developers, working independently'. Sub-paragraph (v): '14% of the gross amount in the case of services other than those covered in sub-paragraphs (i), (ii), (iii) and (iv)'.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, First Schedule Part III Division III
note: INDEPENDENTLY CORROBORATES the rates supplied as already verified, and refines them. Two refinements worth publishing: the 15% is specifically for INDEPENDENT PROFESSIONAL services by named professions 'working independently', and it expressly names software engineers or developers, so a solo Pakistani developer invoicing a local client is at 15% under (ii) rather than 4% under (i) unless the payment is for IT or ITeS as defined in s.2. The 14% in (v) is the RESIDUAL category, not a general services rate. The headline for the (i) list was 3% until the Finance Act 2023 and 4% until the Finance Act 2025, which is why older pages quote lower numbers.

claim: FBR's own public-facing sales tax return page at https://www.fbr.gov.pk/sales-tax-return-filing/51147/131159 does not state the monthly return due date, the payment date or the annexures. Its only substantive statement on timing is 'Failure to pay tax, payable on due date will attract penalty or default surcharge or both.'
source: https://www.fbr.gov.pk/sales-tax-return-filing/51147/131159
note: A useful negative result and a content-gap argument: the regulator's own page for the task does not answer the two questions a filer actually has. It also means the 15th/18th split cannot be corroborated from that page and rests on Sales Tax Rules 2006 rule 18(9), which is the correct primary source in any case.

claim: CORRECTED. The withholding statement under s.165 is QUARTERLY and this is settled, not contested. Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.165(1)-(2) (consolidated to 30 June 2026) requires a quarterly statement due 20 April, 20 July, 20 October and 20 January. FBR's own Circular No. 03 of 2020 (Income Tax) confirms it at the point of change: 'An amendment has been made in section 165 of the Ordinance whereby obligation to file withholding tax statements on biannual basis has been changed to quarterly basis', and tabulates the four quarters matching the statute. The Income Tax Rules 2002 have NOT been conformed: rule 44(2) in FBR's newest consolidation (AMENDED UPTO 24TH NOVEMBER, 2023) still prescribes a BIANNUAL statement due 31 July and 31 January, and the Second Schedule Part-X form is still titled 'Biannual Statement of collection or deduction of income tax under section 165(2)'. The residual conflict is therefore QUARTERLY (statute) versus BIANNUAL (Rules), NOT quarterly versus monthly.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026 s.165(1)-(2); https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/2020931892445579CircularNo.3of2020.pdf (Circular No. 03 of 2020, page 17); https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/2023112416114319348IncomeTaxRules2002AmendedUpto24.11.2023.pdf rule 44(2) and Second Schedule Part-X
note: SUPERSEDES this record's earlier 'monthly versus quarterly' framing, which rested on FBR's 10 February 2017 Rules consolidation. That file is TWO vintages stale: SRO 849(I)/2019 dated 24 July 2019 had already changed rule 44 from monthly to biannual before the Finance Act 2020 made the statute quarterly. Footnote convention confirms the direction and was checked directly: footnote 2 to Second Schedule Part-X reads 'The word "Monthly" substituted through SRO 849(I)/2019', and the QUOTED word is the one REPLACED, so monthly came out and biannual went in. PUBLISH QUARTERLY. The Ordinance governs: rule 44 is subordinate legislation under s.237 while s.165(2) fixes the dates in primary law, and FBR's own circular states the quarterly position. The unconformed Rules are a genuinely publishable observation about FBR's drafting hygiene, not a reason to hedge the due dates. Independently re-verified rather than accepted on report: cover date, both rule 44 occurrences and the circular passage were each read from the saved files. Note FBR published a consolidation on 8 September 2020, AFTER the Finance Act 2020, that still read biannual, so this is not a publication-lag artifact. The 24 November 2023 consolidation is the newest FBR publishes; nothing exists for 2024 to 2026, and of the 13 SROs amending the Rules after November 2023 none touches rule 44.

claim: Sales Tax Act 1990 s.33, Table, S.No.5: a person who fails to deposit the amount of tax due or any part in the time or manner laid down shall pay a penalty of FIFTY THOUSAND rupees or five per cent of the amount of tax involved, whichever is higher. First proviso: if the tax or part is paid within TEN days from the due date, the defaulter shall pay FIVE THOUSAND rupees for each day of default. Second proviso: NO penalty shall be imposed when any miscalculation is made for the FIRST TIME during a year. Third proviso: if the tax is still unpaid sixty days after a notice by an officer of Inland Revenue not below Assistant Commissioner, the defaulter is liable on conviction by a Special Judge to imprisonment up to three years, or a fine up to the amount of tax involved, or both. The Finance Act 2026 substituted 'ten thousand rupees or five per cent ...' with 'fifty thousand rupees or five per cent ...' and, in the first proviso, 'hundred' with 'thousand'.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/20267171373418951SalesTaxAct1990updatedupto30.06.2026.pdf s.33 Table S.No.5; Finance Act 2026 gazette 26 June 2026, Sales Tax Act amendments item (12)(d)
note: CONFIRMS that late FILING (S.No.1) and late PAYMENT (S.No.5) are separately penalised, which is the practical consequence of the 15th/18th split in rule 18(9): a person who pays on the 18th has met the filing date but missed the payment date and is exposed under S.No.5. The first-time miscalculation relief in the second proviso is genuinely useful to readers and is almost never mentioned by competitors. Verified against the enacting gazette, not only the consolidation.

claim: Annex-P of the sales tax return (BREAKUP OF SERVICES, 'TO BE COMPLETED BY THE SERVICE PROVIDER') lists five rows: Balochistan, Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Punjab, Sindh, and 'Capital Territory & Others', against value of services excluding sales tax and sales tax charged. Its own notes state: '(1) On the basis of this information, the tax paid by the Service Provider will be proportionately distributed among the provinces. (2) The system will fill this annexure AUTOMATICALLY according to the province wise sales of services declared by registered person in Annex-C. (3) The tax share will be credited to the designated account of the Provinces.'
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/2025881385446623STR-2006-UpdatedUpto06-08-2025(ver-iv).pdf form STR-7, Annex-P
note: DIRECTLY RELEVANT to the IT and services audience. Annex-P is a SECOND auto-populated annexure alongside Annex-A: it is filled by the system from the province-wise services data in Annex-C, so the accuracy of Annex-P depends entirely on how the service provider codes the province in Annex-C. It is also the mechanism by which the federal return apportions services tax to provinces. Ties to the already-verified store findings that ICT s.3(1A) zero-rates export of services and that KP has no export zero-rating: where a service is coded to matters. Note s.2(20)(c) of the Sales Tax Act includes within 'output tax' the sales tax levied on services rendered under the Islamabad Capital Territory (Tax on Services) Ordinance 2001, which is why an Islamabad services provider accounts for ICT services tax through this same federal return.

claim: Sales Tax Rules 2006 rule 18(1), first proviso (added by SRO 776(I)/2020 dated 25 August 2020): 'in case a registered person fails to fill-in relevant data or information in any applicable column of the sales tax return or any annexure thereto in his case, such return shall be treated as INVALID.' A second proviso (SRO 350(I)/2024) provides that where the sales declared by an individual, an AOP, or a company having only one shareholder or member, other than a manufacturer, are five times more than the sum of the capital and liabilities declared in the balance sheet, electronic filing is allowed only with prior authorisation by the Commissioner through IRIS.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/2025881385446623STR-2006-UpdatedUpto06-08-2025(ver-iv).pdf rule 18(1) provisos
note: HIGH PRACTICAL VALUE and rarely covered. A return with an incomplete annexure is not a late return, it is an INVALID one, which means the s.33 S.No.1 penalty for failing to furnish a return within the due date can attach even though the filer believes he submitted on time. The five-times-capital rule is a real trap for a single-member company or a sole proprietor whose declared capital is small relative to turnover: filing is blocked pending Commissioner authorisation, which can cause a missed deadline. Rule 18(1) Explanation: the electronic return designed per Change Request Forms and made available on the Board's web portal is DEEMED to be the prescribed return, which is how the form can change without a rule amendment.

claim: Sales Tax Act 1990 s.7(1) makes the right to deduct input tax expressly 'subject to the provisions of section 73'. s.73(1): payment for a transaction exceeding fifty thousand rupees 'in aggregate to a single supplier in a tax period' (words inserted by the Finance Act 2024), excluding payment against a utility bill, must be made by crossed cheque, crossed bank draft, crossed pay order or other crossed banking instrument showing transfer of the amount of the sales tax invoice in favour of the supplier FROM THE BUSINESS BANK ACCOUNT OF THE BUYER. A proviso (Finance Act 2005) treats online transfer from the buyer's business account to the supplier's business account, and payments by credit card, as banking-channel transactions provided they are verifiable from both parties' bank statements. s.73(2): the buyer is NOT entitled to input tax credit, adjustment, deduction, refund, repayment, drawback or zero-rating if payment is made otherwise, 'provided that payment in case of a transaction on credit is so transferred within ONE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY DAYS of issuance of the tax invoice'. s.73(3): the amount must be deposited in the SUPPLIER'S business bank account, failing which the SUPPLIER loses those same entitlements.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/20267171373418951SalesTaxAct1990updatedupto30.06.2026.pdf ss.7(1) and 73
note: THE THIRD CONDITION on input tax, alongside holding a tax invoice (s.7(2)(i)) and the supplier having declared and paid (s.8(1)(ca)/(caa)/(l)). Frequently omitted by competitor guides, and the 180-day rule for credit transactions is a hard deadline that silently destroys an otherwise valid input claim. Note the Finance Act 2024 change: the Rs 50,000 test is now an AGGREGATE per supplier per tax period, not per transaction, so splitting invoices no longer avoids it. The Finance Act 2021 proviso permits set-off of mutual payables and receivables with the same party, but ONLY where sales tax has been charged and paid by both parties AND the registered person has sought PRIOR approval of the Commissioner. s.73(3) is the trap that catches a buyer who pays into a supplier's personal rather than business account.

claim: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.153(7)(i) defines 'prescribed person', i.e. who must withhold under s.153 and therefore who must file s.165 statements in respect of those deductions: (a) the Federal Government; (b) a company; (c) an association of persons constituted by or under law; (d) a non-profit organization; (e) a foreign contractor or consultant; (f) a consortium or joint venture; (g) an exporter or export house for the purposes of s.153(2); (h) an association of persons having turnover of ONE HUNDRED MILLION rupees or above in any of the preceding tax years; (i) an individual having turnover of ONE HUNDRED MILLION rupees or above in any of the preceding tax years; (j) a person registered under the Sales Tax Act 1990 having turnover of one hundred million rupees or more in any of the preceding tax years; (k) a person deriving income from the business of construction and sale of residential, commercial or other buildings (builder).
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.153(7)(i)
note: THE SCOPING ANSWER competitors skip, and it is the first thing a reader needs. A COMPANY is a prescribed person at ANY turnover: clause (b) has no threshold. An individual or an AOP only becomes one at Rs 100 million turnover in any preceding tax year. So a small IT company withholds from day one and must file quarterly s.165 statements, while a sole-proprietor freelancer of the same size generally does not. The Rs 100m figures were raised from 'fifty' million by the Finance Act 2020 (footnote convention: the QUOTED word is the one replaced), and the test was widened from 'tax year 2007/2009 or any subsequent year' to 'any of the preceding tax years' by the Finance Act 2018. Clause (j) is a trap: sales tax registration alone does NOT make a person a prescribed person, the Rs 100m turnover condition was added to it by the Finance Act 2020.

claim: No statutory or prescribed time limit could be found for the Commissioner to decide a s.159 application made by a person OTHER than a company. The fifteen-day decision requirement and the deemed-issuance rule in the second proviso to s.159(1) are expressed to apply to 'a company' and 'the aforesaid company'. A search of the Income Tax Rules 2002 (FBR consolidation to 10 February 2017) found no rule imposing a decision deadline on a s.159 application: rule 40 prescribes only forms. Separately, rule 223 prescribes a 'TAX EXEMPTION CERTIFICATE UNDER SECTION 145', which is a DIFFERENT certificate (persons leaving Pakistan) and not a s.159 certificate.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.159(1) provisos; Income Tax Rules 2002 consolidated to 24 NOVEMBER 2023, rules 40, 221 and 223: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/2023112416114319348IncomeTaxRules2002AmendedUpto24.11.2023.pdf
note: A NEGATIVE FINDING stated as such, per METHOD.md section 8. For an individual or an AOP the statute gives no deadline and no remedy on silence. Publish it as an open question rather than importing the company rule by analogy. VINTAGE CAVEAT REMOVED: re-checked against FBR's newest Rules consolidation (24 November 2023). The s.159 rules block contains no deadline language at all (no 'within fifteen', 'within thirty' or 'deemed'), so the absence is confirmed against current Rules and is not an artifact of a stale file. The rule 223 / s.145 confusion persists in the 2023 consolidation and is worth calling out: a reader searching FBR's Rules for 'tax exemption certificate' lands on the s.145 certificate for persons LEAVING PAKISTAN, not the s.159 withholding certificate.

claim: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 s.182A is triggered ONLY by failure to file a RETURN OF INCOME under s.114 by the due date specified in s.118 (or as extended under s.214A or s.119). Its consequences are (a) exclusion from the active taxpayers' list for that year, subject to a proviso allowing inclusion on late filing if a surcharge is paid (Rs 100,000 for a company, Rs 50,000 for an association of persons), (b) no carry-forward of losses for that tax year, and (c) no refund during the period the person is not on the ATL. Failure to file a WITHHOLDING STATEMENT under s.165 is not among the triggers of s.182A.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.182A(1)
note: A PRECISION POINT competitors blur. Filing a s.165 withholding statement late attracts the s.182(1) Table entry 1A penalty but does NOT by itself remove a person from the Active Taxpayers List: ATL status under s.182A turns on the s.114 return. Worth stating plainly because 'you will be removed from the ATL' is a common and incorrect scare line in vendor content about withholding statements. Note the separate and REAL linkage that does exist: s.154A(2)(b) makes final-tax treatment for an IT exporter conditional on the withholding statements having been filed, so the consequence of a missing statement lands there rather than on the ATL.

claim: Sales Tax Act 1990 s.28 (Final Return): 'If a person applies for de-registration in terms of section 21, he shall before such de-registration, furnish a final return to the Commissioner in the specified form in such manner and at such time as directed by the Commissioner.' s.29: a return purporting to be made on behalf of a person by his duly appointed representative is deemed for all purposes to have been made by that person or under his authority unless proved to the contrary.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/20267171373418951SalesTaxAct1990updatedupto30.06.2026.pdf ss.28 and 29
note: THE PRACTICAL ANSWER to the null-return problem: the way out of filing nil returns indefinitely is de-registration under s.21 with a final return under s.28, not simply stopping. Until de-registration takes effect the s.26(1) duty continues and the s.33 S.No.1 penalty (now Rs 50,000, raised by the Finance Act 2026) accrues per period. Note the form and timing of the final return are 'as directed by the Commissioner' rather than prescribed, so no form number should be published for it. s.29 matters for anyone filing through a consultant or e-intermediary: the return is treated as the registered person's own, so responsibility does not shift to the agent.

claim: Sales Tax Act 1990 s.11G (Limitation for assessment), inserted with ss.11D to 11G by the Finance Act 2024: (1) a show cause notice under ss.11D to 11F 'shall be issued within FIVE YEARS, from the end of the financial year in which the relevant date falls'. (2) an order under ss.11D, 11E and 11F shall be made within ONE HUNDRED AND EIGHTY DAYS of issuance of the show cause notice, or within such extended period as the Commissioner may specify for reasons recorded in writing, provided the extension shall in no case exceed ninety days; time during which proceedings are adjourned for a stay order or ADR, or adjournment taken by the registered person not exceeding sixty days, is excluded. (3) 'relevant date' means (a) the time of payment of sales tax or charge as provided under s.6, (b) the time of payment for goods or services on which sales tax was to be withheld under s.3(7), and (c) where sales tax has been erroneously refunded, the date of its refund.
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/Docs/20267171373418951SalesTaxAct1990updatedupto30.06.2026.pdf s.11G
note: Gives the guide a defensible answer to 'how long can FBR come back at me'. Note the limitation runs from the end of the FINANCIAL YEAR in which the relevant date falls, not from the tax period, so the real exposure on a monthly return is longer than five years from the return itself. Contrast the DIFFERENT limitation in s.26(2A) for compelling a return from a non-filer: fifteen years in cases of tax fraud and five years in all other cases, running from the end of the financial year in which the return was to be filed.

claim: FBR's explanatory circular on the Finance Act 2020 EXISTS and expressly covers the s.165 change. It is Circular No. 03 of 2020 (Income Tax), C. No. 4(65)IT-Budget/2020-145988-R, Islamabad, 3rd September 2020, subject 'FINANCE ACT, 2020 - EXPLANATION OF IMPORTANT AMENDMENTS MADE IN THE INCOME TAX ORDINANCE, 2001'. At page 17, under the heading 'Requirement for filing of withholding tax statements on a quarterly basis [Section 165]', it states verbatim: 'An amendment has been made in section 165 of the Ordinance whereby obligation to file withholding tax statements on biannual basis has been changed to quarterly basis.' It then tabulates the due dates: quarter ending 30th September, on or before 20th October; quarter ending 31st December, on or before 20th January; quarter ending 31st March, on or before 20th April; quarter ending 30th June, on or before 20th July. It further records that a proviso was inserted in s.165(1) exempting financial institutions including banks from filing quarterly withholding statements where the information has already been furnished under s.165A, and that a new s.165(1A) obliges persons engaged in economic transactions as prescribed by the Board to furnish a quarterly withholding statement.
source: FBR Circular No. 03 of 2020 (Income Tax), 3 September 2020, page 17
note: Tier 2 (FBR circular: FBR's own explanation of the law, not the law itself; the statute is s165-quarterly-statute at tier 1). Independently corroborates the tier 1 statutory finding on the biannual-to-quarterly change and supplies the citable URL that finding lacked. Retrieval: the circular listing at fbr.gov.pk/Orders/Income-Tax-Circulars/231 is a DataTables grid and is empty to curl, but the grid's own AJAX source returns the whole index as JSON: POST https://www.fbr.gov.pk/Home/ShowOrdersFiltered with body CategoryID=231&Parent=true (773 rows). Verified: HTTP 200, 9533704 bytes, head -c 5 = %PDF-, 19 pages, real text layer (43773 chars extracted). PDF internal metadata Title '2020-09-03' and CreationDate 'Thu Sep 3 05:58:26 2020 PKT' match the printed date. Grep terms that verified it: 'biannual' (single hit, page 17) and 'quarterly'. Local copy: research/raw/fbr-circular-3-of-2020-finance-act-2020.pdf. NOTE the circular is SILENT on Income Tax Rules 2002 rule 44, so it does NOT resolve the contested monthly-vs-quarterly Rules conflict recorded as s165-rules-vintage-conflict. Beware the numbering trap: 'Circular No.4 of 2020/IR Operations' is a DIFFERENT document about extending return filing dates, not the Finance Act explanation.

claim: FBR's own Iris FAQs document the s.159 application as an electronic Iris filing, and for import cases describes a two-stage quota process. The taxpayer e-files a single 'Application u/s 159(1) / 148 for reduced rate of withholding tax on Import (FOR QUOTA ALLOCATION)' for the whole year, indicating annual raw-material requirement including HS Codes and quantity consumed in the previous year, with the current year's requirement capped at up to 110% of previous year's consumption. The system supplies the taxpayer's prior-year import data under an 'Import History' tab. The Commissioner IR allows HS Codes and quantities at reduced rate by an Order after due diligence. Critically: 'The Commissioner IR will not indicate validity period of exemption in body of Order under “Content” Tab, as it is already fixed by the System.' Thereafter the taxpayer e-files 'FOR IMPORTS ADDITION' applications with LC details, which 'the System will auto-process ... on the basis of quota allocation granted by the Commissioner IR without assigning them to the Commissioner IR'.
source: https://e.fbr.gov.pk/SOP/IRIS/Iris_FAQs.pdf
note: PROVENANCE NOW ESTABLISHED and independently re-verified: re-downloaded from the live URL, byte-identical to the file on disk (cmp clean, SHA-256 77569f40...), and grep-checked for four must-contain terms. Linked as 'FAQs (PDF)' from the Iris login help index at https://e.fbr.gov.pk/SOP/IRIS/help/index.html. SCOPE LIMIT, important: this FAQ describes s.159(1)/148 applications for reduced withholding on IMPORTS. It is NOT evidence about s.153 or s.154A certificates and must not be generalised to them. Its value for the s.159 guide is twofold: (1) it is FBR's own confirmation that the s.159 route runs through Iris as an e-filed application decided by the Commissioner, and (2) the validity-period sentence shows that for this class of certificate the duration is set by the SYSTEM rather than written into the Commissioner's order, which corroborates the separate finding that no general statutory validity period exists. VINTAGE CAVEAT: the document is undated internally; the server Last-Modified is 20 January 2023, so it predates the Finance Acts 2025 and 2026 and must be cited as process guidance current as retrieved, never as authority for a rate or a date.

claim: The Sales Tax Act consolidation amended to 30 June 2026 does NOT follow the same footnote convention as the Income Tax Ordinance consolidation, and the two are inconsistent in a way that inverts meaning. In the Ordinance, a footnote naming a word means that word was REPLACED (e.g. 'The word "company" substituted by the Finance Act, 2021' means company came out). In the Sales Tax Act at s.33 Table entry 1, footnote 484 reads 'the word "fifty" Substituted through Finance Act, 2026' while the live text reads '[fifty] thousand rupees', and the Finance Act 2026 gazette says 'for the word ten, the word fifty shall be substituted'. So here the footnote names the word that went IN.
source: Sales Tax Act 1990 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.33 Table entry 1 and footnote 484, checked against Finance Act 2026 gazette s.(12)(a)(i) at research/raw/finance-act-2026.txt line 680
note: NEW TRAP, and it defeats the rule recorded in METHOD.md from the Income Tax side. The safe procedure is now: do not rely on the footnote convention in either direction. Read the LIVE TEXT inside the bracket, which is the operative word, and where the figure is load-bearing confirm it against the enacting Finance Act gazette. Both consolidations were checked and they genuinely differ; this is not a misreading of one footnote. Consequence for the guide: the late sales tax filing penalty is Rs 50,000 with Rs 2,000 per day where filed within ten days, both raised by the Finance Act 2026 from Rs 10,000 and Rs 200.

claim: The full amendment history of the s.165 statement periodicity is three-stage, not two. (1) Rule 44(2) of the Income Tax Rules 2002 originally prescribed a MONTHLY statement. (2) SRO 849(I)/2019 dated 24 July 2019, made under s.237(1) and signed by the Secretary (Income Tax Budget) [F.No.1(69) R and S/2018], substituted 'biannual' for 'monthly' in rule 44, omitted the 15th-day deadline and added the 31 July / 31 January timelines; it also substituted the word 'Monthly' in the Second Schedule Part-X form title and omitted the word 'MONTHLY' from the Division IV heading. (3) The Finance Act 2020 dated 30 June 2020 then amended s.165 of the Ordinance itself from biannual to QUARTERLY, with the four 20th-of-the-month due dates. Rule 44 was never conformed to stage (3).
source: https://download1.fbr.gov.pk/SROs/2019724137946542SRO849of2019.pdf; footnotes to rule 44 and Second Schedule Part-X in the Income Tax Rules 2002 consolidated to 24 November 2023
note: Explains WHY FBR's own documents disagree, which is more useful to a reader than the bare rule. The 2017 Rules consolidation on disk predates even stage (2), which is why it reads monthly. CAVEAT ON THE SRO ITSELF: SRO 849(I)/2019 is a SCANNED IMAGE with no text layer, read by rendering pages; a negative grep on that file proves nothing. The substituted-word direction was confirmed independently from the footnotes in the 2023 consolidation, which are machine-readable, so the claim does not rest on the scan alone.

claim: The name of the form used in IRIS to file the s.165 withholding statement could not be established from any official FBR source. The only officially prescribed title is the Income Tax Rules 2002 Second Schedule Part-X heading, 'Biannual Statement of collection or deduction of income tax under section 165(2) [See rule 44(2)]', which is itself out of step with the quarterly statute. The body of that form is an embedded image with no extractable field names. The IRIS portal requires login, and a sweep of FBR's circular index found no circular or user guide naming the statement form.
source: Income Tax Rules 2002 consolidated to 24 November 2023, Second Schedule Part-X; FBR circular index (POST /Home/ShowOrdersFiltered)
note: A NEGATIVE FINDING published as such, per METHOD.md section 8. Do NOT invent or repeat a form name for the s.165 statement. The honest guide line is that FBR does not publicly document the IRIS form name, that the only prescribed form title is the Part-X heading, and that the reader should expect the portal label to differ from it. Note the Part-X title still says Biannual, so a reader who searches FBR's Rules for the form will find a title that contradicts the quarterly filing dates they must actually meet: worth calling out explicitly.

claim: s.127(5): an appeal shall be preferred to the Commissioner (Appeals) within THIRTY DAYS of, where the appeal relates to an assessment or penalty, the date of service of the notice of demand, and in any other case the date on which the order to be appealed was served. A proviso allows the Commissioner (Appeals) to admit a late appeal where satisfied the appellant was prevented by sufficient cause. s.127(4) prescribed fee: on an appeal against an assessment, five thousand rupees for a company and two thousand five hundred rupees otherwise; in any other case five thousand rupees for a company. s.127(1) also excludes a State-Owned Enterprise from the right of appeal, inserted by the Tax Laws (Amendment) Act 2024.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.127(1), (4) and (5)
note: Note the clock runs from SERVICE OF THE NOTICE OF DEMAND for an assessment or penalty appeal, not from the date of the order itself, which are different dates and the distinction is the one most likely to cost a reader their appeal. The fee is small enough that cost is not the barrier; the thirty days is.

claim: Section 126A, which split appellate jurisdiction by value (Commissioner (Appeals) where the value of assessment or refund did not exceed twenty million rupees, Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue above that), was OMITTED by the Finance Act 2025. It had been inserted by the Tax Laws (Amendment) Act 2024.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.126A footnote recording the omission by the Finance Act 2025
note: A short-lived provision that is still widely described as current. It was live for roughly a year, and coverage written in that window states a Rs 20 million threshold deciding which forum hears an appeal. That threshold no longer exists. Anyone advising on forum choice from a 2024 or early-2025 source is working from repealed law.

claim: s.170(2)(c): an application for refund must be made within THREE YEARS of the later of the date the Commissioner issued the assessment order for the tax year to which the refund relates, or the date on which the tax was paid. s.170(3): where satisfied tax has been overpaid, the Commissioner shall first apply the excess against other tax due under the Ordinance, then against outstanding liability for other taxes, and refund only the remainder. s.170(4): the Commissioner shall pass an order within SIXTY DAYS of receipt of a refund application. s.170(5): a person aggrieved by that order, OR by the Commissioner's failure to pass one within the time specified, may appeal.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.170
note: Three practical points nobody sets out together. The three-year clock runs from the LATER of assessment or payment, which is more generous than it first reads. The refund is applied against other liabilities before any money moves, so a taxpayer with arrears elsewhere may see nothing. And s.170(5)(b) gives an express appeal against SILENCE, so a Commissioner who simply does not decide within sixty days is appealable, which is unusual and useful.

claim: s.171(1): where a refund due to a taxpayer is not paid within three months of the date on which it becomes due, the Commissioner shall pay a further amount by way of compensation at KIBOR plus 0.5 per cent per annum of the refund, computed from the end of the three month period to the date of payment. A proviso suspends the compensation provision where there is reason to believe a person has claimed a refund not admissible to them.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.171(1)
note: The state pays interest on a late refund and almost no taxpayer knows it. Worth pairing with s.205, under which the taxpayer pays default surcharge at twelve per cent or KIBOR plus three per cent for late payment: the asymmetry between what the taxpayer pays and what the state pays is itself a publishable observation, and both figures are read from the same statute.

claim: s.170A, 'Electronic processing and electronic issuance of Refunds by the Board': notwithstanding s.170, and commencing from tax year 2021, the Board may process and issue a refund to a taxpayer who has filed a return of income WITHOUT REQUIRING A REFUND APPLICATION, to the extent of tax credit verified by the Board's computerised system as may be prescribed.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.170A
note: Explains why some refunds arrive unprompted and others require the s.170 application: s.170A is limited to credit the Board's own system can verify, so withholding properly reported by the deductor can be refunded automatically while anything requiring evidence the system does not hold still needs an application. s.170(6) separately empowers the Board to make rules for expeditious processing and automatic payment through a centralised system from a notified date.

claim: Third Schedule Part I sets depreciation rates on the written down value for the purposes of s.22: buildings not otherwise specified 5 per cent (general rate); factory, workshop, cinema, hotel, hospital 10; residential quarters for labour 10; furniture including fittings 10; machinery and plant not otherwise specified 10 (general rate); COMPUTER HARDWARE including printer, monitor and allied items 30; technical or professional books 20; new ships 5. s.22(2): the deduction is computed by applying the Part I rate against the written down value at the beginning of the year.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.22(2) and Third Schedule Part I
note: Computer hardware at 30 per cent against a 10 per cent general machinery rate is directly relevant to a software house or IT services firm, which is our audience: the same rupee spent on a workstation is written off three times faster than the same rupee spent on generic plant. Note the rate applies to WRITTEN DOWN VALUE, so it is reducing balance rather than straight line, and the asset never fully depreciates by the rate alone.

claim: Third Schedule Part II, initial allowance and first year allowance: buildings all types 10 per cent; furniture including fittings and machinery and plant not otherwise specified, motor vehicles all types, ships, technical or professional books 15 per cent; COMPUTER HARDWARE including printer, monitor and allied items, machinery and equipment used in manufacture of IT products, aircrafts and aero engines 30 per cent.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, Third Schedule Part II
note: The initial allowance is in ADDITION to the ordinary depreciation deduction and is taken in the year the asset is first used. Note that the words 'machinery and equipment used in manufacture of I.T. products' were inserted into the 30 per cent class, so the IT-favourable treatment reaches manufacturing equipment for IT products as well as the hardware itself. Do not conflate Part I and Part II: the 30 per cent figure appears in both but they are different allowances doing different jobs.

claim: A proviso to s.22(1) provides that depreciation expense shall NOT be allowed for the amount paid for the addition of capital assets to a seller, in all relevant tax years, where the tax deductible under s.152 or s.153 in respect of those payments has not been deducted and deposited in the treasury. The mechanism is that such amounts are not added to the assets for computation of tax depreciation.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.22(1) proviso
note: HIGH VALUE and largely uncovered. Failing to withhold on a capital purchase does not merely attract a withholding penalty: it permanently removes the asset's cost from the depreciation base, IN ALL RELEVANT TAX YEARS. So a company that bought equipment from a supplier without deducting under s.153 loses the write-off on that equipment for its entire life, which can dwarf the withholding itself. This is the sharpest reason for a business to take its s.153 obligations seriously, and it ties directly to the s.165 statement guide.

claim: s.6(1): tax is imposed at the Division IV rates on every non-resident person who receives any Pakistan-source ROYALTY, fee for OFFSHORE DIGITAL SERVICES, fee for MONEY TRANSFER OPERATIONS, CARD NETWORK SERVICES, PAYMENT GATEWAY SERVICES, INTERBANK FINANCIAL TELECOMMUNICATION SERVICES, or fee for TECHNICAL SERVICES. s.6(2) computes it on the GROSS amounts of receipts. The money transfer, card network, payment gateway and interbank telecommunication heads were inserted after the offshore digital services head.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.6(1) and (2)
note: The payment gateway and card network heads are why this matters to our audience beyond the obvious: fees charged by a foreign payment processor on Pakistani-source receipts are within the charge. Note the charge is on GROSS receipts, so there is no netting of the non-resident's own costs. The withholding mechanism is s.152(1), which requires every person paying royalty or fees for technical services to a non-resident chargeable under s.6 to deduct at the Division IV rate.

claim: First Schedule Part I Division IV: the rate of tax imposed under s.6 on payments to non-residents is 15% of the gross amount of the royalty or fee for technical services, and 5% of the gross amount of the fee for offshore digital services. The 5% offshore digital services limb was inserted by the Finance Act 2025.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, First Schedule Part I Division IV
note: A threefold difference turning on characterisation, which is exactly the kind of fork that produces disputes. The same payment to a foreign supplier can be 15% as a fee for technical services or 5% as a fee for offshore digital services depending on what it is for, and the s.2(22B) definition is the thing that decides it.

claim: s.2(22B) defines 'fee for offshore digital services' as any consideration for providing or rendering services by a non-resident person for online advertising including digital advertising space, designing, creating, hosting or maintenance of websites, digital or cyber space for websites, advertising, e-mails, online computing, blogs, online content and online data, providing any facility or service for uploading, storing or distribution of digital content including digital text, digital audio or digital video, online collection or processing of data related to users in Pakistan, any facility for online sale of goods or services or any other online facility.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.2(22B)
note: HIGH RELEVANCE to a Pakistani software house, because the list reads like an invoice from its own suppliers: hosting, online computing, storage and distribution of digital content, and online advertising. It closes with 'any other online facility', which is about as wide as drafting gets. The practical question this raises for a firm paying AWS, a CDN or an ad platform is whether it should have been withholding at 5 per cent, and the answer turns on whether the fee is Pakistan-source under s.101, which this record does not resolve.

claim: s.138(1): to recover tax due, the Commissioner serves a notice in the prescribed form requiring payment within a specified time. s.138(2): if unpaid within that time or any further time allowed, the Commissioner may recover by one or more modes including attachment and sale of movable or immovable property of the taxpayer, appointment of a receiver for the management of that property, ARREST OF THE TAXPAYER AND HIS DETENTION IN PRISON FOR A PERIOD NOT EXCEEDING SIX MONTHS, and the modes in s.48(1)(a), (ca) and (d) of the Sales Tax Act 1990. s.138(3): for these purposes the Commissioner has the same powers as a Civil Court under the Code of Civil Procedure 1908 for recovery under a decree.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.138
note: The arrest and detention power is real, statutory and almost never mentioned in taxpayer-facing content, which tends to stop at attachment. Note the sequence though: recovery under s.138(2) only opens after a s.138(1) notice has gone unanswered within the time specified, so the notice is the point at which to act rather than the point at which to worry.

claim: s.138(3A), notwithstanding anything in the Ordinance or any other law or rule or any decision or judgment of any court, forum or authority: tax payable under any provision or any assessment order becomes IMMEDIATELY PAYABLE subject to conditions including (a) that the case has been decided in favour of the department at three appellate forums including the High Court, and (b) that recovery shall only be made to the extent of the lowest amount of demand confirmed by any of those forums.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.138(3A)
note: A strong override clause, and the conditions are the reader-facing point rather than the override. It bites only after the department has won at THREE appellate forums including the High Court, and even then recovery is capped at the LOWEST demand any of those forums confirmed. So it is not a power to collect during an ongoing dispute; it is a power to collect once the dispute has substantially gone against the taxpayer.

claim: s.140(1): to recover tax due, the Commissioner may by notice in writing require any person owing or who may owe money to the taxpayer, holding or who may hold money for or on account of the taxpayer, or holding or who may hold money on account of some other person for payment to the taxpayer, to pay that money to the Commissioner.
source: Income Tax Ordinance 2001 consolidated to 30 June 2026, s.140(1)
note: This is the provision behind a frozen bank account, and the drafting is wider than a bank: it reaches anyone who OWES money to the taxpayer or MAY owe it, which on its face includes a customer with an unpaid invoice. The reader-facing point is that recovery does not require the department to find the taxpayer's assets, only to find someone who owes them money, and that a notice can land on a client rather than on the taxpayer.

claim: The three major automation platforms bill on three different units for the same work. n8n bills per workflow EXECUTION regardless of step count: 'An execution is a single run of your entire workflow. It doesn't matter how many steps are in the workflow or how much data it processes. It's still a single execution.' Zapier bills per TASK, counted per acting step: 'A task is counted whenever Zapier successfully completes a unit of work for you. Failed actions are not counted.' Triggers and polling do not consume tasks. Make bills per CREDIT, formerly called operations, where one module run processing one bundle equals one operation equals one credit.
source: n8n.io/pricing, zapier.com/pricing, make.com/en/pricing and help.make.com, all fetched with scrapling StealthyFetcher 11 Sep 2026
note: THE load-bearing finding for the automation comparison post. The unit, not the headline price, is what produces the cost divergence: a 5-step workflow run 10,000 times is 10,000 n8n executions but 50,000 Zapier tasks and 50,000 Make credits. Verified by two independent routes (a WebFetch research agent and direct scrapling browser automation) which agreed on Zapier exactly.

claim: Make renamed its billing unit from 'operations' to 'credits'. Make's help centre states: 'credits replaced operations as the term for make's billing unit your existing plan and pricing, including the cost of credits, remain unchanged'. Conversion is 1 operation = 1 credit for non-AI apps; AI Provider features may consume more.
source: help.make.com/operations and help.make.com/credits
note: CAUGHT MY OWN STALE PREMISE. I briefed the research agent that Make bills in 'operations' and the agent corrected me from the live docs. Any 2026 post using 'operations' as Make's billing unit reads as stale, which is precisely the defect the comparison post exists to correct. Also: one module can generate SEVERAL operations because the count depends on bundles processed, so '5 steps = 5 credits' holds only if each module processes a single bundle per run.
