Iterators and aggregators break it. Trigger modules run once regardless of bundles returned; routers and error handlers consume nothing.

Free tier is 1,000 credits. Enterprise is custom. The tier ladder runs 10k, 20k, 40k, 80k, so THERE IS NO 50,000-CREDIT TIER.

claim: For a workflow with 5 acting steps run 10,000 times a month, the same work costs $50/mo on n8n (10,000 executions, Pro tier), $289/mo on Zapier (50,000 tasks) and $55/mo on Make Core (50,000 credits, which buys the 80,000 tier because no 50,000 tier exists). Zapier is 5.8x n8n and 5.3x Make Core for identical work, at annual billing.
source: Computed from n8n-pricing-sep2026, zapier-pricing-sep2026 and make-pricing-curve-sep2026
note: The divergence is produced by the BILLING UNIT, not by the headline price: n8n's Pro tier is only 1.1x Make Core, and the gap opens because Zapier multiplies by step count where n8n does not. The comparison holds only for a workflow whose steps each process one bundle per run; iterators and aggregators in Make, and multi-bundle modules generally, break the 1:1 step-to-credit assumption. State the step count and the bundle assumption whenever this arithmetic is published.

claim: n8n Community Edition is source-available, not OSI open source. n8n's README states it is 'fair-code distributed under the Sustainable Use License and n8n Enterprise License' and self-describes as 'Source Available'. The licence restricts: 'You may use or modify the software only for your own internal business purposes or for non-commercial or personal use. You may distribute the software or provide it to others only if you do so free of charge for non-commercial purposes.' Files with .ee. in the filename or .ee in the dirname are excluded and require a paid Enterprise licence.
source: raw.githubusercontent.com/n8n-io/n8n/master/LICENSE.md, full text retrieved; n8n README
note: Matters for an agency audience specifically: 'internal business purposes' permits running it for your own operations, and distributing it to others for a fee does not fall within the grant. An agency that self-hosts n8n on a client's behalf should read the licence rather than assume 'open source'. Also: n8n publishes NO execution limit for self-hosted Community, listing only absent features (SSO, environments, projects). Report that as 'no published limit', never as 'unlimited', which the vendor does not say.

The page states: 'You can use Shopify Payments to accept payments at checkout if your business is located in one of the supported countries listed on this page' and 'If your country isn't listed, or if Shopify Payments doesn't support your business category, then you need to use a third-party payment provider.'
source: help.shopify.com/en/manual/payments/shopify-payments/supported-countries, fetched with scrapling 11 Sep 2026
note: A SOURCED NEGATIVE, not a failed search: the complete list renders on one page, so absence is a finding. This is the root cause of every downstream Pakistani Shopify payment problem, and it is why unresolved Shopify Community threads rank for these queries. Everything else follows from it: third-party gateway required, third-party transaction fee applies, no PKR payouts.

claim: Shopify charges a third-party transaction fee whenever a merchant uses any gateway other than Shopify Payments. Shopify's documentation states: 'Third-party transaction fees apply on all third-party and alternate payment gateways even when [Shopify Payments] is activated. However, if you have Shopify Payments activated, then PayPal and manual payments are excluded from third-party transaction fees.' Because Shopify Payments is unavailable in Pakistan, a Pakistani merchant cannot obtain that exclusion.
source: help.shopify.com third-party payment providers page; shopify.com/pricing FAQ
note: THE STRUCTURAL POINT worth publishing: the fee waiver is conditional on activating Shopify Payments, which a Pakistani merchant cannot do, so the fee is unavoidable rather than a choice. CAVEAT, and it must be stated: the actual PERCENTAGE is not published on either the global or the /pk pricing page. Shopify says only 'The rate depends on your plan' and directs to a location-specific table. Do NOT publish a percentage taken from a blog. Manual payment methods such as cash on delivery and bank deposit are a separate route, and the doc's wording on PayPal/manual exclusions turns on having Shopify Payments active.

Searching it for PayFast, JazzCash, Easypaisa, Keenu, PayPro and Alfa returns zero matches each. Shopify App Store searches for safepay, payfast, jazzcash and easypaisa return unrelated apps (countdown timers, trust badges, analytics) rather than a gateway of that name.

OpenAI: GPT-6 Astra $10/$50; GPT-5.6 Sol $4/$20 (promotional, previously $5/$30, stated available at least through 21 November 2026); GPT-5.6 Terra $2/$12; GPT-5.6 Luna $0.20/$1.20. Anthropic offers 50% batch processing; OpenAI shows Batch -50% and a Data residency +10% mode. Anthropic notes US-only inference at 1.1x and a fast mode for Opus 5 at 2x standard pricing.
source: anthropic.com/pricing and openai.com/api/pricing, scrapling StealthyFetcher

OpenAI also notes its rates reflect context lengths under 272K, so long-context agent runs may price differently. Gemini pricing fetched separately and its tiered table was not extracted per-model.

claim: Both major vendors price cached input far below fresh input. Anthropic: cache READ is one twentieth of input price at every tier (Fable 5.1 $0.25 read vs $10 input; Opus 5 $0.50 vs $5; Sonnet 5 $0.20 vs $2; Haiku 4.5 $0.10 vs $1), while a cache WRITE costs 1.25x the input price (Fable $12.50, Opus $6.25, Sonnet $2.50, Haiku $1.25). OpenAI: cached input is one tenth of input on most models (Astra $1.00 vs $10.00; Terra $0.20 vs $2.00; Luna $0.02 vs $0.20) and Sol $0.40 vs $4.00. Anthropic states its cache pricing reflects a 5-minute TTL with extended caching available.
source: anthropic.com/pricing, openai.com/api/pricing
note: THE load-bearing finding for the agent-cost post, and the reason model choice is the wrong first question. An agent re-sends its system prompt and tool definitions every single turn, so that prefix is the largest repeated cost in the run. Caching it moves that prefix from 1x to 0.05x (Anthropic) or 0.1x (OpenAI). The write costs MORE than an uncached read (1.25x on Anthropic), so caching is a loss on a prefix used once and a large win on one reused across turns: the break-even is roughly the second read. This is an architecture decision, not a procurement decision, which is exactly the framing the cost cluster is missing.

claim: Faithfulness, as defined by the Ragas evaluation framework, 'measures how factually consistent a response is with the retrieved context. It ranges from 0 to 1, with higher scores indicating better consistency. A response is considered faithful if all its claims can be supported by the retrieved context.' It is computed by identifying all claims in the response, checking each against the retrieved context, and dividing the number of supported claims by the total number of claims.
source: Ragas documentation, docs.ragas.io, v0.4.3, fetched with scrapling 11 Sep 2026
note: The load-bearing definition for the RAG-trust post. Its value is that it makes 'is it making things up' a measurable quantity with a published formula rather than a reassurance. IMPORTANT DISTINCTION to publish: faithfulness measures whether the answer follows from what was RETRIEVED, not whether it is true in the world. A system can score 1.0 on faithfulness while being wrong, if retrieval returned a wrong document. That is exactly why it must be read alongside the retrieval metrics rather than alone.

claim: The Ragas metric suite separates RAG failure into distinct, separately measurable stages. Context Precision 'evaluates the retriever's ability to rank relevant chunks higher than irrelevant ones', calculated as the mean of precision@k. Context Recall 'measures how many of the relevant documents were successfully retrieved. It focuses on not missing important results', and always requires a reference to compare against. Noise Sensitivity 'measures how often a system makes errors by providing incorrect responses when utilizing either relevant or irrelevant retrieved documents', scored 0 to 1 with lower being better. Faithfulness measures consistency of the response with the retrieved context.
source: Ragas documentation, context_precision, context_recall, noise_sensitivity and faithfulness metric pages
note: THE STRUCTURE FOR THE DIAGNOSTIC POST, and it replaces the circulating percentages POSTS.md bans ('80% of failures trace to chunking', '73% retrieval failure') which trace to no named study. The publishable insight is that 'the chatbot gave a wrong answer' is not one failure but at least four, each with a different fix: the right document was never retrieved (recall), it was retrieved but ranked below noise (precision), it was retrieved and the model ignored it (faithfulness), or irrelevant context derailed an otherwise answerable question (noise sensitivity). A team without these numbers is guessing which one they have. Note these are framework definitions, not empirical claims about failure rates, and must be published as such.

claim: Whether an AI provider trains on submitted data is decided by the product TIER, not by the vendor. OpenAI's own document states both halves: 'When you use our services for individuals such as ChatGPT, Codex, and Sora, we may use your content to train our models' and 'By default, we do not train on any inputs or outputs from our products for business users, including ChatGPT Business, ChatGPT Enterprise, and the API.' Anthropic's Commercial Terms (effective 17 June 2025) state 'Anthropic may not train models on Customer Content from Services'. OpenAI states 'As of March 1, 2023, data sent to the OpenAI API is not used to train or improve OpenAI models (unless you explicitly opt in).'
source: OpenAI help centre article on data use; Anthropic Commercial Terms; fetched 11 Sep 2026
note: THE thesis finding for the data-training post. Same company, opposite defaults, stated in one document: consumer is opt-OUT, API is opt-IN. The right question is never 'do you use OpenAI' but 'which product, which tier, which billing status'. NOTE ON SOURCING: openai.com and help.openai.com return 403 to both WebFetch and curl; the OpenAI quotes came from Wayback captures of OpenAI's own pages (2026-09-09, 2026-02-06), which is primary content but non-live retrieval. Re-check in a browser before publishing. Anthropic's commitment is the strongest form: a prohibition in the operative commercial contract rather than a policy statement on a marketing page.

claim: Google's Gemini API terms (effective 23 March 2026) split the SAME API into two materially different data regimes by billing status alone. Unpaid tier: 'Google uses the content you submit to the Services and any generated responses to provide, improve, and develop Google products and services' and 'human reviewers may read, annotate, and process your API input and output'. Paid tier: 'Google doesn't use your prompts (including associated system instructions, cached content, and files such as images, videos, or documents) or responses to improve our products' and logs are kept 'solely for detecting and preventing violations of the Prohibited Use Policy'.
source: ai.google.dev/gemini-api/terms, effective 23 March 2026
note: THE SHARPEST TRAP FOUND, and sharper than the consumer-versus-business framing the post was originally built on. Same endpoint, same SDK, same code: only billing status decides whether human reviewers may read your customers' data. Nothing in the developer experience signals the boundary at the moment a developer crosses it. Practical consequences worth publishing: production must run on a billed project, and CI and staging keys must be billed too, because a lapsed billing account silently moves a deployment into the human-review regime. Google's marketing presents one unified 'Gemini API' product while the governing terms split it in two, which is a marketing-versus-terms discrepancy worth naming.

claim: Two qualifications to the API no-training default. First, FEEDBACK is the recurring carve-out: Anthropic states that submitting thumbs-up/down feedback puts that conversation in scope for training, and OpenAI states 'If you choose to provide feedback, the entire conversation associated with that feedback may be used to train our models.' Second, zero data retention is not self-serve: OpenAI states ZDR and Modified Abuse Monitoring are 'subject to prior approval by OpenAI and acceptance of additional requirements', and Anthropic's ZDR is 'subject to Anthropic's approval' and 'reviewed and applied on a per-organization basis'. Absent ZDR, both retain API data around 30 days for abuse monitoring.
source: Anthropic privacy centre; OpenAI API data controls documentation
note: The two things that turn a correct general answer into a wrong specific one. A developer clicking thumbs-up in a console is a real disclosure path, so feedback UI must be governed in any app handling sensitive data. And a buyer whose security questionnaire assumes ZDR is a config flag needs correcting EARLY because approval affects the project timeline. Also worth separating for readers: training and retention are different questions. Nobody trains on API data by default and nearly everybody retains it ~30 days, so 'do not keep our data' is the harder and slower ask.

claim: The three major cloud resellers carry explicit no-training commitments. AWS Bedrock FAQ: 'No, AWS and the third-party model providers will not use any inputs to or outputs from Amazon Bedrock to train Amazon Nova, Amazon Titan, or any third-party models' and 'Users inputs and model outputs are not shared with any model providers.' Google Cloud Service Specific Terms section 18 Training Restriction (last modified 29 July 2026): 'Google will not use Customer Data to train or fine-tune any AI/ML models without Customer's prior permission or instruction.' Azure OpenAI: 'prompts and completions are not used to train, retrain, or improve the base models' and are 'NOT available to OpenAI or other providers of Models sold by Azure'.
source: AWS Bedrock FAQs; Google Cloud Service Specific Terms s.18; Microsoft Learn Azure AI Foundry data privacy
note: The practical route for a buyer who needs contractual comfort fast: the DPA and sub-processor terms are already signed under an existing enterprise agreement. Azure is uniquely AUDITABLE: Microsoft documents that the ContentLogging attribute reads false in the portal JSON view or via 'az cognitiveservices account show', which is a rare verifiable control rather than a promise. Anthropic's own consumer-terms announcement names Bedrock and Vertex as sitting on the commercial side of its consumer/commercial boundary. Note the Vertex docs page on data governance now redirects to a nav shell, so cite the Service Specific Terms clause, which is the stronger source anyway.

claim: Meta moved the WhatsApp Business Platform from conversation-based to per-message billing effective 1 July 2025. Meta's docs state: 'Effective July 1, 2025, Meta charges on a per-message basis', 'You are only charged when a template message is delivered', and 'All non-template messages are free'. Charging is on delivery, not send. There is NO free monthly tier and no 1,000 free conversations under the current model. Meta charges by three template categories only: marketing, utility and authentication ('Each template must be categorized as authentication, marketing, or utility'), plus a separate authentication-international rate. Access to the Cloud API itself is free.
source: developers.facebook.com/docs/whatsapp/pricing and the new-template-guidelines page; rate card stated effective 1 July 2026
note: CORRECTS MY OWN BRIEF, which listed 'service' as a fourth template CATEGORY. It is not: service refers to free-form non-template replies inside the customer service window, which are free. The retired 1,000-free-conversations allowance is the single most common error in published WhatsApp pricing content and belongs to the old model. The 24-hour customer service window survives but its role changed: it no longer defines the billable unit, it defines when free-form replies and free utility templates are permitted. Free entry point windows from Click-to-WhatsApp ads remain and run 72 hours of fully free messaging.

claim: Meta's per-message rates for a Pakistani recipient, USD per delivered message, read 11 September 2026: marketing $0.0473; utility $0.0100; authentication $0.0100; authentication-international $0.0750; service $0 (free). Volume tiers apply to utility and authentication only, stepping utility from $0.01 down to $0.0075 above 50M, and authentication from $0.01 to $0.0075 above 20M. Marketing has no volume tier. Meta does not publish or bill Pakistan in PKR; PK rates are offered in USD, EUR, GBP, INR, AED and SGD.
source: Meta's own rate API behind the official calculator at whatsappbusiness.com, market=PK, validated against Meta's published North America marketing rate
note: THE headline figure for the WhatsApp post and the reason it is worth writing. Pakistan marketing at $0.0473 is roughly 1.9x the US rate of $0.025 and about 4x India's $0.0118, so every article quoting the US rate understates Pakistani marketing cost by about half. Meta's docs also record 'Effective April 1, 2026, Pakistan, higher utility and authentication rates', so these are post-increase figures. The rate-card PDFs are JS-injected and developers.facebook.com returns 400 to curl; the figures came from Meta's live rate API, which is equally primary. DO NOT publish a third-party claim that utility or service messages become chargeable inside the CSW from 1 October 2026: Meta's pricing-updates page carries no such entry and it was checked directly.

claim: A Business Solution Provider's charge is separate from and additional to Meta's per-message rate, and takes different shapes. Twilio: no platform fee, a flat markup of $0.005 per message inbound or outbound on top of Meta ('Twilio's per-message fee for WhatsApp is $0.005'), pricing page current as of August 2026. 360dialog: a platform fee of EUR 49, 99 or 500 per number per month, with Meta fees passed through. Interakt: $55/mo Growth or $69/mo Advanced PLUS a marked-up per-message rate, publishing Pakistan marketing at $0.0532 Starter, $0.0525 Growth and $0.052 Advanced against Meta's $0.0473.
source: twilio.com/en-us/whatsapp/pricing; 360dialog pricing; interakt.shop/whatsapp-conversation-pricing
note: TIER 2 because BSP pricing pages change frequently and one of the four checked (Wati) could not be read at all, its rate card sitting behind a login. The publishable structural point is robust regardless of the exact numbers: the BSP fee is a separate layer from Meta's, it takes at least three different shapes (flat per-message, flat monthly, or monthly plus marked-up rates), and conflating the two is the main error in published content. Interakt's Pakistan rates VARYING BY PAID TIER is what proves it is a markup rather than pass-through, and its Enterprise tier sells 'No Markup Charges' as a feature. A business can also onboard directly with Meta: a BSP is optional, not mandatory. | SECOND PASS ADDED (two independent verification runs agreed on all four BSPs): Interakt's full Pakistan table is marketing 0.0532/0.0525/0.052 and utility 0.0139/0.0130/0.0122 across Starter/Growth/Advanced. Its Starter AUTHENTICATION figure of 0.00112 is ANOMALOUS, an order of magnitude below its own other tiers and below Meta's $0.01 floor, so it is almost certainly a typo on Interakt's page: do not publish it, or flag it as apparently erroneous. Twilio also carries fees beyond the headline $0.005, namely a $0.001 failed-message processing fee and a Messaging Engagement Suite add-on at $0.015/message with the first 1,000 free monthly, so 'Twilio is just $0.005' is itself a simplification. Twilio's Pakistan ROWS are Meta pass-through rather than Twilio's own fee, which is exactly the conflation to warn readers about. Structural point worth publishing: Twilio and 360dialog are transparently ADDITIVE to Meta's rate, while the two India-based providers do not pass Meta's rate through at cost.

claim: FinCEN issued a FINAL rule published 14 August 2026 that 'permanently removes the requirement for U.S. companies and U.S. persons to report beneficial ownership information to FinCEN under the Corporate Transparency Act.' FinCEN states 'U.S. companies are exempt from the Beneficial Ownership Information (BOI) reporting requirements' and 'Only certain foreign companies registered to do business in the U.S. must report BOI.' A reporting company is now only an entity 'formed under the law of a foreign country that have registered to do business in any U.S. State or Tribal jurisdiction.' FinCEN will also delete previously reported information by US persons from the database.
source: FinCEN news release 11 August 2026; Federal Register final rule published 14 August 2026, doc 2026-16576; fincen.gov/boi and fincen.gov/boi-faqs
note: CORRECTS MY OWN BRIEF, which cited the March 2025 INTERIM final rule as the operative authority. That interim rule reached the same practical outcome but has been superseded by a permanent final rule, so any content citing the interim rule must be refreshed. DIRECT ANSWER for a Pakistani founder: a Wyoming, New Mexico or Delaware LLC is formed under US state law and is therefore NOT a reporting company, so it does not file a BOI report today. The owner's Pakistani nationality is irrelevant: the test is where the ENTITY was formed, not who owns it. BOI would only bite if they formed a company OUTSIDE the US and then registered it to do business in a US state. This area is surrounded by stale 2024 and 2025 content, so state the rule date.

claim: Form 5472 instructions (Rev. 12/2024): 'A penalty of $25,000 will be assessed on any reporting corporation that fails to file Form 5472 when due and in the manner prescribed.' 'Filing a substantially incomplete Form 5472 constitutes a failure to file Form 5472.' If failure continues more than 90 days after IRS notification, 'an additional penalty of $25,000 will apply... with respect to each related party for which a failure occurs for each 30-day period'. IRC 6038A(d) frames the base penalty as '$25,000 for each taxable year'. A foreign-owned US disregarded entity files a PRO FORMA Form 1120 with Form 5472 attached, completing only 'the name and address of the foreign-owned U.S. DE and items B and E on the first page', writing 'Foreign-owned U.S. DE' across the top, and filing by fax to 855-887-7737 or by mail to Ogden UT. 'If you are a foreign-owned U.S. DE, you cannot file Form 5472 electronically.'
source: IRS Instructions for Form 5472, Rev. 12/2024; IRC 6038A(d); Instructions for Form 1120 (2025)
note: THE E-FILING PROHIBITION is the single most commonly misstated point in LLC-vendor content, and it is the practical trap: a founder who assumes they can e-file discovers otherwise near the deadline. Due date is the 15th day of the 4th month after year end, so 15 April for a calendar-year LLC, extendable to 15 October on Form 7004, and the instructions warn NOT to use the regular Form 7004 address. The continuation penalty is uncapped. Note also that a substantially incomplete form counts as a failure to file, so the $25,000 is not only a late-filing risk.

claim: A US-Pakistan income tax treaty exists and is in force. IRS Table 3, List of Tax Treaties, updated through 26 September 2025, states it 'lists the countries that have tax treaties in effect with the United States' and Pakistan's row reads: TIAS 4232, general effective date 1 January 1960, citation 1960-2 C.B. 646, T.D. 6431. Signed 1957. No protocols are listed.
source: IRS Table 3 List of Tax Treaties PDF; irs.gov United States Income Tax Treaties A to Z; irs.gov Pakistan tax treaty documents
note: CORRECTS A WIDESPREAD MISSTATEMENT: writing that there is no US-Pakistan tax treaty is wrong. The likely ORIGIN of that error is identified and is worth publishing: Treasury's own treaties page does not list Pakistan, because that page publishes texts of treaties signed after 1996 and this one was signed in 1957. IRS Table 3, which explicitly lists treaties in effect, is the controlling source. Caveat to publish alongside it: this is one of the oldest US treaties still operative, predating modern treaty design, so it lacks a limitation-on-benefits article and modern reduced withholding rates. Its existence is not the same as it being useful in a given case.

claim: Instructions for Form SS-4 (Rev. 12/2025): an international applicant may apply by phone on 267-941-1099 (not toll-free), by fax from outside the US to 304-707-9471 with processing 'generally within 4 business days', or by mail to the EIN International Operation in Cincinnati with processing 'approximately 4 weeks'. Where the responsible party has no SSN or ITIN: 'Enter foreign or N/A on line 7b if the responsible party doesn't have and is ineligible to obtain an SSN or ITIN.' The online EIN application is unavailable: IRS states 'Your principal place of business is outside the U.S. If so, apply by phone, fax or mail.' Separately, on ITINs, IRS states 'You need an ITIN if you have a federal tax purpose and you're not eligible for an SSN' and that an ITIN 'is issued by the IRS for federal tax purposes only'.
source: IRS Instructions for Form SS-4 Rev. 12/2025; IRS ITIN page last updated 28 October 2025; IRS apply-for-EIN-online page updated 19 August 2026
note: The EIN belongs to the ENTITY and the ITIN to the PERSON; they are not substitutes, which is the confusion to clear up. Filing the pro forma 1120 plus 5472 does not itself require the owner to hold an ITIN. CAVEAT recorded by the researching agent and worth honouring: IRS states the ITIN principle rather than enumerating LLC-owner scenarios, so applying it to a specific founder is a reading of the rule rather than IRS wording about LLCs. Publish the principle and the common trigger (a personal 1040-NR obligation or a treaty claim needing a taxpayer ID), not a blanket yes or no.

claim: Delaware: the Division of Corporations states the LLC annual tax is '$400.00' due 'on or before June 1st', late penalty 'a penalty of $200.00 plus 1.5% interest per month', and 'There is no requirement to file an Annual Report.' New Mexico: the Limited Liability Company Act, NMSA 1978 ch. 53 art. 19, contains no annual or biennial report obligation for LLCs, and section 53-19-63's exhaustive fee schedule contains no annual or biennial report fee, listing only filing fees such as $50 original articles of organization and $100 foreign LLC registration. Wyoming could not be verified: all wyo.gov hosts are unreachable at TCP level, DNS resolving correctly but connections timing out.
source: corp.delaware.gov alt-entity tax instructions; NMSA 1978 ch.53 art.19 statute PDF; direct TCP testing of wyo.gov hosts
note: Delaware's shape is the surprising one: a flat $400 tax but NO annual report, which is the reverse of what most founders expect. New Mexico verified from the STATUTE rather than the SOS website, whose relevant subpages 404, and confirmed two ways: the phrase 'annual report' appears zero times in the Act, and the exhaustive fee schedule has no such fee. Important qualification to publish: 'no annual report' is not 'no ongoing obligation', since 53-19-5 still requires a registered agent and registered office and 53-19-66.1 permits administrative revocation if that lapses. WYOMING MUST NOT BE STATED from this research: the unreachability independently reproduces the stored finding wyo-gov-unreachable-reconfirmed, and a third-party figure was deliberately not substituted.

claim: IRS states 'Most types of U.S. source income received by a foreign person are subject to U.S. tax of 30%' and 'A reduced rate, including exemption, may apply if an Internal Revenue Code Section provides for a lower rate, or there is a tax treaty between the foreign person's country of residence and the United States.' Form W-8BEN is the 'Certificate of Foreign Status of Beneficial Owner for United States Tax Withholding'. Governing sections are IRC 1441, 1442 and 1443, reported on Forms 1042 and 1042-S.
source: IRS NRA withholding page, last updated 14 March 2026
note: MUST BE PUBLISHED WITH ITS LIMIT, which the researching agent flagged explicitly. Whether an LLC distribution to a foreign owner is FDAP at all depends on the entity's classification and the character and source of the income. For a DISREGARDED single-member LLC there is no separate distribution to withhold on, because the owner is treated as earning the income directly. No primary source addresses the disregarded-LLC fact pattern directly, so do not let the 30% figure be over-extended into 'every transfer to your own account is taxed 30%', which is the misreading this finding exists to prevent.

claim: App Store Review Guidelines (Last Updated 8 June 2026) guideline 4.2.6: 'Apps created from a commercialized template or app generation service will be rejected unless they are submitted directly by the provider of the app's content. These services should not submit apps on behalf of their clients.' Guideline 4.2 Minimum Functionality: 'Your app should include features, content, and UI that elevate it beyond a repackaged website. If your app is not particularly useful, unique, or app-like, it doesn't belong on the App Store.' 4.2.2: 'Other than catalogs, apps shouldn't primarily be marketing materials, advertisements, web clippings, content aggregators, or a collection of links.'
source: developer.apple.com/app-store/review/guidelines/, Last Updated 8 June 2026
note: COMMERCIALLY LOAD-BEARING FOR THIS AGENCY, beyond its value as content. An agency submitting client apps from its OWN developer account is squarely within 4.2.6. Apple's stated remedies are that the client submits under their own account, or the agency ships a single aggregated picker binary. 4.2.2 is the separate trap for the common client request to turn a website into an app. The researching agent flagged the agency exposure as ITS OWN INFERENCE from the rule rather than Apple wording about agencies, which is the honest framing to publish.

claim: Neither Apple nor Google publishes an overall app rejection rate. Apple's only published rejection-frequency figure is on its App Review page: 'On average, over 40% of unresolved issues are related to guideline 2.1: App Completeness, which covers crashes, placeholder content, incomplete information, and more.' Apple publishes a review-time figure, 'On average, 90% of submissions are reviewed in less than 24 hours', but no median and no figure for a rejection-fix-resubmit cycle. Google publishes no typical or median review time, only that some accounts face 'review times of up to seven days or longer in exceptional cases'. Apple's former 'Common App Rejections' page now returns HTTP 404 and its historical top-reasons ranking is gone.
source: developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/; support.google.com Play console help
note: A GUARD AGAINST THE OBVIOUS MISQUOTE. Apple's 40% figure is a share OF UNRESOLVED ISSUES attributable to guideline 2.1, not a rejection rate, and it must not be rounded into '40% of apps are rejected'. Any claim about how long a rejection cycle costs has to be framed as agency experience rather than vendor data, because no vendor publishes it. Also note /app-store/review/ now 301-redirects to /distribute/app-review/, so cite the new URL. Google does not display last-updated dates on its support pages, so Play policies cannot be version-pinned the way Apple's dated guidelines can.

claim: Google Play requires that 'Developers with personal accounts created after November 13, 2023, must run a closed test for their app with a minimum of 12 testers who have been opted in continuously for at least 14 days.' Google adds: 'Testers who opt in, test for fewer than 14 days, and then opt out do not count toward the requirement. If a tester opts out and opts back in later, the 14 days must be consecutive.' Production and Pre-registration remain disabled until the requirement is met. The requirement is stated for personal accounts.
source: support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/14151465
note: THE TESTER COUNT HAS CHANGED: it is now 12, reduced from the 20 at launch. Do not repeat the old number, which is what most published content still carries. The planning consequence for an agency is real: the rule is stated for PERSONAL accounts, so registering a client as an organization is the route that avoids the 14-day gate. The researching agent flagged that Google states the rule for personal accounts without explicitly stating the converse, so 'organization accounts bypass it' is an inference and should be published as such rather than as a Google statement.

claim: Apple guideline 5.1.1(v): 'If your app supports account creation, you must also offer account deletion within the app.' Google Play's User Data policy requires developers to 'Allow account deletion. This must be available both in-app and on an external web resource', and states 'Account freezing is not a valid substitute.' Separately on public identity: Apple's EU Digital Services Act trader requirements state 'Even if you don't distribute apps in the EU, you'll still need to declare a trader status', with individuals required to publish an address or P.O. Box, phone number and email on the product page, while organizations show a D-U-N-S-derived address. Google Play requires a legal name and address and a D-U-N-S number for organizations, and states 'Verified information will be shown on Google Play'.
source: Apple App Store Review Guidelines 5.1.1; Google Play User Data policy answer/10144311; Apple App Store Connect EU DSA trader requirements help
note: TWO PRACTICAL POINTS FOR CLIENT WORK. First, Play is STRICTER than Apple on account deletion: Apple requires an in-app path, Play requires in-app AND a web-accessible one, so building only the Apple requirement fails Play. Second, and this matters for individual developers in Pakistan: an individual-account developer's address becomes PUBLIC on both stores, and the EU DSA declaration is required even if you never distribute in the EU. An organization account with a D-U-N-S number is the privacy-preserving route, which the researching agent flagged as its own inference rather than vendor wording.

claim: Apple Developer Program enrolment is '99 USD per membership year', with a fee waiver available for nonprofits, accredited educational institutions and government entities. Google Play: 'There is a US$25 one-time registration fee', and 'Prepaid cards are not accepted.'
source: developer.apple.com/programs/enroll/; support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/6112435
note: Small but frequently misstated, and the recurring-versus-one-time distinction is the part that matters to a client budgeting for a two-platform launch: Apple recurs annually, Google does not. The Google note that prepaid cards are not accepted is a real practical obstacle for Pakistani developers, who commonly use them.

claim: The MIT NANDA report 'The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025' (v0.1, July 2025) uses the 95% figure exactly twice in 26 pages. The executive summary reads: 'this report uncovers a surprising result in that 95% of organizations are getting zero return' and 'Just 5% of integrated AI pilots are extracting millions in value, while the vast majority remain stuck with no measurable P&L impact.' Page 6 reads: 'The 95% failure rate for enterprise AI solutions represents the clearest manifestation of the GenAI Divide.' The report's own funnel, in the same executive summary, states: 'Sixty percent of organizations evaluated such tools, but only 20 percent reached pilot stage and just 5 percent reached production.'
source: Primary PDF, 26 pages, 923,623 bytes, sha256 dd5c5f53b9b01370..., retrieved from a mirror and extracted with pdftotext -layout; local copy at research/raw/nanda-genai-divide.txt
note: THE CORRECTION THAT MAKES THE POST. The circulated claim '95% of AI pilots fail' is NOT what the report says. It says 95% of ORGANIZATIONS get zero return, and its own funnel shows 20% reached pilot stage while 5% reached production, so of organisations that actually piloted, 5/20 = roughly 25% reached production. The 95% counts every organisation that never piloted anything as a failure. SUPERSEDES the earlier blocker mit-nanda-report-url-now-redirects: the primary document IS retrievable from mirrors even though the MIT URL now 302-redirects to a group overview page. Verified independently: both 95% occurrences located by grep, the funnel sentence read in context, byte size and page count match.

claim: The same report states, two lines after its '95% failure rate' sentence: 'Generic LLM chatbots appear to show high pilot-to-implementation rates (~83%).' Its executive summary also states 'Over 80 percent of organizations have explored or piloted them, and nearly 40 percent report deployment.'
source: Primary PDF lines 224-230 and 49-51 of the extracted text
note: A document reporting an 83% pilot-to-implementation rate for generic LLM chatbots was reported worldwide as proof that AI does not work. The 83% sits on the SAME PAGE as the '95% failure rate' sentence. This is the single most quotable fact for the post, because it is internal to the document rather than an outside critique, and it cannot be argued with.

claim: The report's notes page states its evidence base: 'a systematic review of over 300 publicly disclosed AI initiatives, structured interviews with representatives from 52 organizations, and survey responses from 153 senior leaders collected across four major industry conferences.' Its own limitations state: 'These percentages reflect our interview sample of 52 organizations and may not represent broader market patterns'; 'Our sample may not fully represent all enterprise segments or geographic regions'; 'Selection bias possible in organizations willing to participate in AI research'; 'Six-month observation period may be insufficient to fully assess successful implementation'; and 'These figures are directionally accurate based on individual interviews rather than official company reporting.'
source: Primary PDF notes page and Appendix 8.2, lines 21-23, 197, 804-805, 1010-1024
note: The sampling frame is conference attendees, which is a convenience sample and cannot support a population-level claim about organisations generally. Return is SELF-REPORTED rather than read from financial statements: the report's own success definition turns on what 'users or executives have remarked'. The authors disclose all of this themselves, which is to their credit and is also why the headline should never have been reported as a finding about the world. Note the filename is literally v0.1.

claim: The report's conclusion states: 'Systems like NANDA, MCP, and A2A represent early infrastructure for this web'. Its acknowledgments describe NANDA as a project that 'builds on Anthropic's Model Context Protocol (MCP) and the Google/Linux Foundation A2A to create infrastructure for distributed agent intelligence at scale.' The authors are affiliated with Project NANDA, and the report's sole named reviewer, Pradyumna Chari, is also a co-author. The report states: 'The views expressed in this report are solely those of the authors and reviewers and do not reflect the positions of any affiliated employers.'
source: Primary PDF conclusion line 972, Appendix 8.1 acknowledgments, and title/notes pages
note: The structure is diagnose a crisis, name the cause, prescribe the cure, and the cure is the authors' own protocol. Also material: the report is NOT MIT Sloan, is disclaimed by its own authors as not representing MIT, and the only named reviewer is a co-author, so it was not reviewed in any meaningful sense. State these as facts from the document rather than as accusations. IMPORTANT FAIRNESS POINT to publish: the authors disclosed the limitations and the affiliation openly. The failure is mostly in how the number was REPORTED, including a Fortune account that inflated the sample.

The marketing copy names the plans without the percentages; the numbers sit lower in a comparison table. Same page footnotes 'Join 615K+ businesses' and cites 'Internal DoorDash data' for every claim, so treat DoorDash's own performance claims as VENDOR DATA while the posted rate card is a primary fact about its own pricing. | MERGED 525 -> duplicate id written concurrently by a parallel research agent. The Premier tier carries a 'Growth Guarantee' under which restaurants receivin

claim: Deloitte/Google 'Milliseconds Make Millions' (March 2020) is based on 37 brands and 30 million mobile user sessions over a 4-week period at the end of 2019, split retail 15 brands, luxury 10, travel 6, lead generation 6, across Europe and the US.
source: Deloitte/Google, Milliseconds Make Millions report PDF, p.13-14
note: Read from the primary PDF via pdftotext -layout, not from a summary. Commissioned by Google, executed by 55 and Deloitte. Design strength: no UX redesigns ran on any site during the study, so speed is isolated. Design limit: it is an observational correlation across sites, NOT a randomised experiment, so 'a 0.1s improvement CAUSES +8.4%' overstates it. Data is from late 2019 and now ~6 years old.

claim: In the Deloitte/Google study, a 0.1 second improvement across four mobile speed metrics was associated with, for retail, +8.4% conversion rate, +9.2% average order value and +5.2% page views per session; travel saw +10.1% conversion.
source: Deloitte/Google, Milliseconds Make Millions report PDF, retail and travel sections
note: Retail findings rest on 20.5m of the 30m sessions; travel on 2.1m; luxury on 7.4m. State it as 'associated with', not 'caused'. This is the strongest citable page-speed-to-revenue number and it supports investing in a fast mobile WEB checkout rather than an app.

claim: Baymard Institute's documented average online shopping cart abandonment rate is 70.22%, aggregated from 50 separate studies spanning 2006 to 2025.
source: Baymard Institute, cart abandonment rate statistics page, updated 22 September 2025
note: INDEPENDENT RESEARCH: Baymard publishes the full list of the 50 aggregated studies and their individual rates, which is why this is citable where most abandonment stats are not. Caveat to state: it is a meta-average over a 19-year span, not a single measurement, and the earliest input is MarketingSherpa 2006 at 59.80%. Use it as an order-of-magnitude fact about checkout friction, not a precise current benchmark.

claim: Cochrane review (Gurol-Urganci et al., 2013, CD007458.pub3) found moderate-quality evidence from 7 studies and 5,841 participants that mobile text message reminders improved healthcare appointment attendance vs no reminders, RR 1.14 (95% CI 1.03 to 1.26): attendance rose from 67.8% without reminders to 78.6% with them. Review included 8 RCTs, 6,615 participants.
source: Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews 2013 Issue 12, CD007458.pub3, LSHTM open-access copy
note: INDEPENDENT RESEARCH, peer-reviewed, read from the full PDF via pdftotext. Also found: text reminders performed SIMILARLY to phone call reminders, RR 0.99 (95% CI 0.95-1.02, 3 studies, 2,509 participants), which matters because it means the cheap automated channel matches the expensive staffed one. Content assessed up-to-date 28 Feb 2013, so it is a landmark but DATED review; pair it with the 2026 Al-Turbag meta-analysis. GRADE moderate, not high.

claim: Al-Turbag, Mooney and Corry (2026) systematic review and meta-analysis of appointment reminders found a pooled RR of 1.11 (95% CI 1.05-1.19), an 11% increase in hospital appointment attendance vs usual care, from 10 RCTs contributing 8,236 participants.
source: Journal of Hospital Management and Health Policy 2026;10:2, published 6 March 2026, doi 10.21037/jhmhp-25-51
note: INDEPENDENT RESEARCH, peer-reviewed, and the most recent evidence found (March 2026). CRITICAL NUANCE that must be published with the number: in subgroup analysis the SMS-only result was RR 1.14 (95% CI 0.99-1.31, 4 studies, 4,636 participants) which CROSSES 1 and is NOT statistically significant, while telephone reminders were significant at RR 1.11 (95% CI 1.04-1.19). Heterogeneity is high: I-squared 83% overall, 91% for the SMS subgroup. So the honest claim is 'reminders reliably help, and the size of the SMS-specific effect is uncertain', not 'SMS cuts no-shows by X%'. Authors note a lack of formal economic evaluations.

claim: The ubiquitous '53% of mobile site visits are abandoned if a page takes longer than 3 seconds to load' traces to Google/DoubleClick, 'The Need for Mobile Speed', published September 2016.
source: Google/DoubleClick 2016 via Marketing Dive and secondary restatements
note: DO NOT cite as current. Two problems. (1) AGE: it is from September 2016, roughly a decade old, on 2016 mobile networks and devices. (2) SCOPE: the underlying DoubleClick work measured publisher/ad-supported mobile sites and reported ad viewability, session length and bounce rate, so it is not a retail checkout conversion finding, yet it is nearly always repeated as one. The original DoubleClick post is no longer at a stable live Google URL, which is why this stays unverified rather than verified. Use the Deloitte 2020 study instead for any speed-to-revenue claim.

claim: National Restaurant Association, 2026 State of the Restaurant Industry: 'Consumer spending is expected to push industry sales to a projected $1.55T nationwide, with real (inflation-adjusted) gains of 1.3% projected.' Employment: 'Operators say they'll add approximately 100K jobs, bringing total industry employment to 15.8M.' On technology the report says operators 'are looking to invest in more technology that boosts efficiency and strengthens guest connections', focusing on digital ordering, automation and data analytics. Methodology as stated: the report 'is based on analysis and forecasts by National Restaurant Association economists and surveys of restaurant operators and consumers conducted throughout the year.'
source: National Restaurant Association, 2026 State of the Restaurant Industry
note: ASSOCIATION RESEARCH, the appropriate source for sector-level restaurant claims, though the association represents operators so treat outlook figures as industry forecasting. LIMITATION: the public landing page does not disclose sample size, field dates, or the off-premises/takeout share, and the full report is paywalled. Cite the sales and employment forecasts and the direction of technology investment; do NOT state an off-premises percentage from this source without the full report. The technology language is generic (digital ordering, automation, analytics) and notably does NOT single out native apps. | MERGED 525 -> duplicate id written concurrently by a parallel research agent. The other copy was status=unverified tier=2; its claim read: The National Restaurant Association's State of the Restaurant Industry 2026 report was released 11 February 2026 and is based on the Association's economists' analysis plus surveys of restaurant operators and consumers conducted through the year. It is free to

claim: ASTP/ONC Data Brief 77 (July 2025, 2024 data): 77% of US individuals were offered online access to their medical records and 65% were offered and accessed a portal at least once in the past year, up from 25% in 2014. 16% have no portal at all; 59% have multiple portals.
source: Richwine C, ASTP Data Brief No. 77, July 2025, based on HINTS 7
note: INDEPENDENT RESEARCH (US government, nationally representative). Methodology from p.10: NCI Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS 7), paper and web, fielded March-September 2024, two-stage stratified address sample, N=7,278 respondents, response rate 27.31%, weighted to national estimates. This is the gold-standard denominator for any patient-portal claim.

claim: ASTP/ONC Data Brief 77: among those offered portal access, 87% accessed it when encouraged to do so by their provider versus 57% when not encouraged, a 30 percentage point difference. 89% of those offered access were encouraged by a provider.
source: Richwine C, ASTP Data Brief No. 77, July 2025
note: The highest-leverage statistic found for the clinic argument: a 30-point swing produced by front-desk staff behaviour, not by buying software. Central to the thesis that the constraint is adoption and habit, not app availability. Cross-sectional association, so 'encouraged patients access more' is the safe phrasing rather than a proven causal effect.

claim: Barker and Richwine (JAMA Network Open 2023): of 43,922,929 Google Play installs across 48 studied health-record apps, 98.7% went to patient-portal apps tied to EHR developers, health systems or insurers, and only 1.3% to third-party apps. Among people with multiple portals, only 2% used a third-party app to consolidate them.
source: Barker W, Richwine C, JAMA Netw Open 2023;6(11):e2343312
note: INDEPENDENT RESEARCH, peer-reviewed. Cross-sectional: Google Play install/review data for 26 portal apps and 22 third-party apps (2019, 2021, 2022) plus HINTS 6 (n=6,252). The core evidence that a standalone clinic app fails: patients install the app their EHR gives them and essentially nothing else. Pairs with ONC DB77 showing 59% juggle multiple portals yet only 7% use an organising app, so the demand exists and standalone apps still do not capture it.

claim: Kammrath Betancor et al. (2025), 98,067 appointments over 20 months across two German ophthalmology centres, found online booking associated with LOWER no-shows in a private practice (1.8% vs 5.9%, p<0.0001) but HIGHER no-shows in a university hospital (14.3% vs 11.2%, p<0.0001).
source: Kammrath Betancor P et al., Front Digit Health 2025;7:1567397
note: INDEPENDENT RESEARCH, peer-reviewed. THE nuance finding: the same intervention helped in one setting and hurt in the other. Authors attribute the hospital result to triage-based scheduling where patients lacked real autonomy over slot choice. Mechanism is self-selection (a patient who picks a slot they can make, attends), not online booking per se. Vendor blogs quote the 1.8% vs 5.9% arm and omit the hospital arm of the same study: that omission is the tell. Retrospective observational, not randomised.

claim: Junod Perron et al. (2013) non-inferiority RCT of 6,450 patients in an academic primary care clinic found missed appointments of 11.7% with text reminders vs 10.2% with telephone reminders (p=0.07, not significant), at a six-month cost of EUR 230 for text versus EUR 8,910 for telephone.
source: Junod Perron N et al., BMC Health Serv Res 2013;13:125
note: INDEPENDENT RESEARCH, randomised. The cleanest business-case number in the clinic set: roughly a 39x cost difference for statistically equivalent attendance, because EUR 8,700 of the phone cost was administrative labour. Supports the honest framing that automated reminders are an efficiency and margin argument, not a clinical-superiority argument. 2013 Swiss data, so state the vintage and note SMS costs have fallen further.

claim: Dantas et al. (2018) systematic review of 105 studies published 1980-2016 reports an average no-show rate of 23% across medical specialties, and identifies long lead time between booking and appointment, plus prior no-show history, as primary determinants.
source: Dantas LF et al., Health Policy 2018;122(4):412-421
note: INDEPENDENT RESEARCH, peer-reviewed systematic review. Tier 2 not 1 because the full text is paywalled: the 23% headline and 105-study count were confirmed via abstract and multiple independent citations, but the methods section was not read at source. The lead-time determinant is the under-used insight: it implies shortening booking-to-appointment gap beats adding reminders, and is exactly what real-time self-scheduling does.

claim: MGMA Stat poll (29 July 2025, 244 applicable responses): 71% of medical practices report fewer than 25% of their patients use digital self-scheduling; only 3% report more than 75% usage.
source: MGMA Stat poll, 29 July 2025
note: INDUSTRY ASSOCIATION. A one-question poll of self-selected member respondents, so it indicates distribution rather than a precise national rate: tier 2. Useful as a reality check against any projection of majority online booking. Moved only 2 points from a November 2024 poll where 73% were in the lowest band. NOTE: the same MGMA page repeats a 'nearly nine in ten patients would choose a practice based on self-scheduling' claim sourced to a NextGen Healthcare marketing eBook with no disclosed sample: that one is rejected below.

claim: The widely repeated figure that missed appointments cost the US healthcare system USD 150 billion a year, often paired with 'USD 200 per missed 60-minute slot'.
source: SCI Solutions (a healthcare scheduling IT vendor), recirculated by HCI Innovation Group and others
note: NEVER USE. Traces to a vendor that sells scheduling software, i.e. the company producing the headline number for the problem its product solves. No published methodology, no peer review, no government source. Appears to be back-of-envelope arithmetic (roughly 30% no-show x USD 200 per slot) where both inputs are themselves unsourced. If the scale of missed appointments must be conveyed, use the figures quoted in the Cochrane review background instead (England NHS, early 2000s: GBP 185m GP, GBP 34m practice nurse, about GBP 575m hospital), stating country and vintage.

claim: Claims that text appointment reminders reduce no-shows by 38%, and that online self-scheduling reduces no-shows by 38% per an 'Accenture Digital Health Survey', plus vendor claims of 60-70% no-show reductions in primary care.
source: Klara and nextpatient.co vendor blogs
note: NEVER USE. Contradicted by the pooled peer-reviewed evidence, which puts reminders at RR 1.11-1.14, an 11-14% RELATIVE improvement in attendance, nowhere near 38%. The identical 38% figure is attached to two completely different interventions (SMS and online booking) across vendor blogs, which is the signature of a number laundered between marketing pages. The 'Accenture Digital Health Survey' attribution could not be located in any Accenture publication.

claim: The assertion that '77% of individuals used the patient portal to schedule appointments', attributed to ONC/HINTS 2024 data.
source: search-engine summary misattributing ASTP Data Brief 77
note: NEVER USE. All 11 pages of Data Brief 77 were read and this statistic is not in it. In DB77, 77% is the share of individuals OFFERED online access to medical records, a different thing entirely. Neither DB77 nor DB69 publishes an appointment-scheduling use figure at all (DB69 use activities are: view test results 90%, view clinical notes 70%, download health information 32%, transmit to third party 20%). A conflation of two statistics produced by an AI search summary, and a live example of why the fetch-and-read gate exists.

claim: A specialty-by-specialty no-show table circulating as Neurology 26%, OB/GYN 18%, Dermatology 30%, Sleep medicine 39%, and similar.
source: vendor blogs (Curogram, Dialog Health, SchedulingKit)
note: NEVER USE. Appears only on scheduling-vendor blogs, with no named study, no sample and no methodology, and every value is a round or near-round number. Use the Dantas 2018 23% cross-specialty average instead, which has 105 studies behind it.

claim: UK ONS, 'Artificial intelligence in UK businesses: 2023 to 2026', fieldwork June 2026: 'Most businesses report that the use of AI has not resulted in a change to their overall workforce headcount so far... Across all size bands, around half of businesses reported that AI had no impact on headcount, with particularly high shares among businesses with 10 to 249 employees.' Also: 'Improving business operations is the most common use of AI, reported by over 60% of larger businesses; however, this has not yet translated into widespread changes in overall workforce headcount.' Where reductions do occur they concentrate in one use: 'Around 6% of businesses using AI for operational improvements report a decrease in headcount, compared with a smaller proportion using AI for other purposes.' ONS cites the Bank of England's survey published January 2026 as consistent: 'for most firms, the use of AI has had no material impact on the number of employees over the past three years.'
source: ONS article, BICS, fieldwork June 2026, fetched with scrapling 11 Sep 2026
note: DIRECTLY CONTRADICTS the dominant framing in popular AI coverage, and it comes from a national statistics office rather than a vendor. Verified by reading the ONS page directly rather than accepting an agent summary. Adoption figures from the same release: use among businesses with 10+ employees rose from around 12% in late 2023 to around 35% by June 2026, with 28% of businesses with 0-9 employees against 49% of those with 250+. Also worth publishing: employee-level use outruns business-level adoption, 55% of employees report using AI for work or education against 35% of businesses reporting any AI technology, which is the shadow-adoption story.

claim: US Census Bureau Business Trends and Outlook Survey, data collection period ending 3 May 2026: the national AI use rate is 19.8%. By firm size, '37% of firms with at least 250 employees reported using AI in their business operations' and '32% of firms with 100 to 249 employees said they used AI', while 'Less than 20% of firms with four or fewer employees reported using AI.' Between December 2025 and May 2026 'AI use increased among firms with at least 20 employees but didn't change significantly among firms with fewer than 20 employees.' By sector, Information (39.7%) and Finance and Insurance (33.9%) were both above the national rate.
source: census.gov BTOS article, headline 'Large Firms With at Least 20 Employees Biggest AI Users', fetched with scrapling 11 Sep 2026
note: An official measurement of the thing every vendor asserts without evidence. Verified by reading the Census page directly. CRITICAL METHODOLOGY CAVEAT reported by the researching agent and NOT independently confirmed by me: Census is said to have rewritten the core AI question on 17 November 2025, from AI use 'in producing goods or services' to 'in any business function', producing a level shift rather than real growth. If that is right, the 2023-to-2026 series must not be presented as a continuous adoption curve. VERIFY THE QUESTION CHANGE against the Census questionnaire before publishing any time series from this source.

claim: No aggregate AI productivity gain has been confirmed in official statistics. A Bank of England Bank Underground post (6 August 2026) comparing ONS output-per-hour by industry reports that measured gains sit in AI-PRODUCING sectors rather than adopting ones, with computer programming and consultancy moving from a 0.01 to a 0.10 percentage point contribution, while finance and insurance, a large adopter, contributed nothing positive. Its regression of adoption against productivity change returns R-squared of about 0.10 and the author states the result is 'only suggestive of a correlation, not causation'. The OECD warns that the firm-level productivity premium among AI adopters is substantially selection: 'the positive link between firms' productivity and AI adoption appears to be explained, to a considerable extent, by the fact that some firms, which are already more digital and more competitive, are also more likely to adopt AI in the first place.'
source: Bank of England Bank Underground, 6 August 2026; OECD 'AI adoption by small and medium-sized enterprises', December 2025
note: TIER 2 because these two sources were reported by a research agent and I have NOT yet read either primary document myself, unlike the ONS and Census records which I verified directly. Fetch and quote both before publishing. If they hold up, this is the honest frame for any cost or ROI post: adoption is real and rising, measured employment effects are near zero, and the productivity case is unproven at aggregate level with the firm-level evidence contaminated by selection. That is a far more defensible position than either the boosterism or the doom, and nobody occupies it.

claim: National Restaurant Association State of the Restaurant Industry 2025: smartphone app development ranks 9th of 15 technology investment areas at 40% of operators (fullservice 31%, limited-service 48%), well below digital/location-based marketing at 65% (rank 1), loyalty and reward systems at 58% (rank 2), POS at 52% and contactless ordering/payment at 49%.
source: NRA State of the Restaurant Industry 2025, p.64
note: INDUSTRY ASSOCIATION, read from the full report PDF at p.64, not from a press summary. THE headline stat for the restaurant argument: operators themselves rank app development near the bottom, and the things they rank above it (being findable, and repeat custom) are exactly the web/GBP/loyalty stack. Tier 2 rather than 1 for a real methodological reason recorded separately in nra-methodology-gap. Copy fetched from kioskindustry.org mirror because the NRA's own full report is paywalled at USD 349; cite the NRA as author and verify against the official copy before publishing.

claim: The National Restaurant Association does not publish sample size, fielding dates, sampling frame or margin of error for the State of the Restaurant Industry operator survey. Its stated methodology is only that the report is 'based on analysis and forecasts by National Restaurant Association economists as well as ongoing surveys of restaurant operators and consumers'.
source: NRA State of the Restaurant Industry 2025, methodology statement (inside cover)
note: METHODOLOGICAL CAVEAT that must accompany every NRA figure published. The only N disclosed anywhere in the document belongs to a DIFFERENT product, the Restaurant Operations Data Abstract 2024, described as 'nearly 1,000 restaurant operators nationwide' (p.67): do NOT attribute that N to the SOTRI survey, which is a distinct instrument. This is why every NRA finding here is tier 2, not tier 1.

claim: NRA State of the Restaurant Industry 2025: 95% of takeout customers were satisfied with how easy it was to order and pay, and only 25% of takeout customers (22% delivery) put 'make it easier to order and pay' in their top three requested improvements, ranking it below food temperature (40%), wait time (39%), food quality (38%), variety (35%), customisation (33%) and order accuracy (33%).
source: NRA State of the Restaurant Industry 2025, pp.54-55
note: The 'nobody asked for this' evidence, and the most underused finding in the set. An app is sold as solving ordering friction, but diners report ordering is already easy (95% satisfied) and rank fixing it near the BOTTOM of what they want. What they want most (hot food, shorter waits, better food) is operational, not digital. Same methodology caveat as nra-methodology-gap.

claim: NRA State of the Restaurant Industry 2025: 83% of operators say technology gives a competitive advantage and 69% say it made them more efficient, but only 28% say technology investment improved profitability. Separately, the NRA's February 2026 release reports 42% of operators said their restaurant was not profitable in the prior year.
source: NRA SOTRI 2025 p.60; NRA press release 11 February 2026
note: The efficiency-versus-profit gap is the honest frame for the whole topic: restaurants adopt technology and mostly do not see it reach the bottom line. Paired with 42% unprofitable, it makes discretionary app capex a direct competitor with survival spending. The 2026 press release is primary and free; the p.60 figures come from the 2025 PDF.

claim: Chipotle reported digital sales of 38.3% of food and beverage revenue in Q2 2026 (up from 35.5% year over year, USD 1.3bn in the quarter), and Domino's FY2025 10-K states more than 85% of its US retail sales came from digital channels. McDonald's reported about 210 million 90-day active loyalty users across 70+ markets by end of 2025.
source: Chipotle Q2 2026 results release; Domino's FY2025 Form 10-K (SEC EDGAR)
note: Chipotle and Domino's are tier 1: SEC filing and company IR release. The McDonald's 210m figure is company IR but was corroborated only via secondary outlets after a fetch timeout, so verify before publishing it specifically. TWO CRITICAL FRAMINGS. (1) This is the STEELMAN for apps and must be presented as such: apps demonstrably work at national-chain scale (Domino's ~7,000 US stores, Chipotle ~3,800, McDonald's ~13,500) with national ad budgets and mature loyalty programmes. (2) 'Digital sales' INCLUDES third-party marketplaces and web ordering, so it is not an app-only number: never equate digital share with app share.

claim: DoorDash charges 0% commission on orders placed through DoorDash Storefront, the restaurant's own website ordering channel, with the restaurant paying payment-processing fees only, against 15-30% commission for orders through the DoorDash marketplace.
source: DoorDash published merchant pricing, corroborated by Restaurant Dive
note: The single cleanest data point in the restaurant set, and it needs no third-party study: the platform's OWN rate card prices its marketplace at 15-30% and the restaurant's own web storefront at 0%. That is the direct-ordering economic argument stated by the least-biased-possible witness, the company that loses money on it. Pairs with doordash-commission-tiers. Partnership Plans are limited to merchants with 75 or fewer US locations, which is exactly the independent-restaurant segment.

claim: The claim that complete Google Business Profiles are '70% more likely to attract location visits and 50% more likely to lead to purchases', universally attributed to Google.
source: Backlinko, Chatmeter and dozens of SEO blogs, all attributing to 'Google' with no link
note: NEVER USE. Google's own Business Profile help documentation was fetched and states only that 'businesses with complete and accurate info are more likely to show up in local search results', with NO percentage of any kind. Every citation chain dead-ends at an unlinked 'Google'. This matters because the stat is near-universal in local-SEO content and is the one most likely to be reached for when arguing the GBP case. Argue GBP from the NRA priority ranking instead, or from properly sampled BrightLocal survey data once verified.

claim: A cluster of restaurant-technology statistics including 'food near me open now searches surged 875%', 'over 75% of local searches convert into leads', 'restaurants get 7x higher views on GBP than their website', '67% of consumers prefer to order via the restaurant's own website/app' attributed to Toast, and food-and-drink app day-30 retention benchmarks.
source: SEO and restaurant-tech vendor blogs; app-retention figures replicated across aggregator sites
note: NEVER USE, all of them. None has a named study, sample or methodology. The app-retention cluster is the important case: roughly seven sources appear to corroborate each other but are one uncited claim replicated across SEO aggregator content farms, mutually citing an AppsFlyer report that could not be reached. Cross-source clustering means these count as ONE weak source, not seven. NOTE THE HONEST GAP: 'restaurant apps get deleted' is the most rhetorically useful claim for this thesis and is exactly the one with no citable primary source. Do not substitute a fabricated number: rest the argument on the NRA ranking, the DoorDash rate card and the chain-scale contrast, which are all fully verifiable.

claim: Restaurant app development cost ranges commonly quoted as USD 15,000-150,000 with annual maintenance at 15-20% of build cost.
source: app development agency blogs (Aalpha, EnactOn, TrangoTech, IMG Global)
note: NOT safe as fact. Every source located is an agency that sells app development, so the estimate is produced by the party quoting the price, and the ranges vary wildly across sources (USD 8,000 to 400,000) with no methodology or project sample behind any of them. This is the same failure mode as the rejected offshore rate tables already in this store. If a cost figure is needed, attribute it explicitly as 'development agencies advertise X' and name the agency, rather than stating a market rate.

claim: Frequently cited Starbucks figures of '35.8 million 90-day active US Rewards members' driving 'about 60% of US company-operated revenue', and 'Mobile Order and Pay is 30% of US transactions'.
source: secondary outlets; NOT found in the Starbucks Q3 FY2026 earnings release on SEC EDGAR
note: NOT safe as fact. The Q3 FY2026 earnings release was fetched on EDGAR and these metrics are not in it: Starbucks appears to have stopped breaking out Rewards membership in the earnings release. The 'Mobile Order and Pay 30%' figure traces to 2023 and is stale. Starbucks is the most commonly reached-for example of a restaurant app succeeding, so if it is used the number must first be located in a current 10-Q, 10-K or investor deck.

claim: Acemoglu and Restrepo, 'Automation and New Tasks', Journal of Economic Perspectives 33(2), 2019, pp.3-30, peer reviewed. The decomposition: 'Effect of automation on labor demand = Productivity effect + Displacement effect', and 'Automation therefore increases the size of the pie, but labor gets a smaller slice. There is no guarantee that the productivity effect is greater than the displacement effect.' The so-so technologies passage: 'contrary to a common presumption in popular debates, it is not the brilliant automation technologies that threaten employment and wages, but so-so technologies that generate small productivity improvements.' The mechanism: 'The productivity effect of automation is therefore proportional to cost-savings obtained from such substitution. The greater is the productivity of labor in tasks being automated relative to its wage and the smaller is the productivity of capital in these tasks relative to the rental rate of capital, the more limited the productivity gains from automation will be.' And on wages: 'When wages are high and labor is scarce, automation will generate a strong productivity effect and will tend to raise labor demand. When wages are low and labor is abundant, automation will bring modest productivity benefits and could end up reducing labor demand.'
source: Journal of Economic Perspectives 33(2) 2019, free full text at AEA and a PDF at MIT Shaping Work
note: THE SPINE of the automate-or-hire post, and it is peer reviewed in a journal written for non-specialists, so it can be cited AND handed to a reader. The decision rule it implies, stated for a business owner: automation pays when your people are not especially good at the task relative to what you pay them AND the machine is genuinely good relative to what it costs. It fails when you automate something your staff do well and cheaply using a mediocre tool. The wage-scarcity result is the non-obvious one: the same tool is a good buy for a firm facing a hiring shortage and a bad buy for a firm with cheap available labour. NOTE the JEP paper uses automated customer service as its example, not self-checkout; Acemoglu uses self-checkout in interviews and popular writing, so cite MIT Sloan or Brookings if that example is wanted.

claim: Brynjolfsson, Li and Raymond, 'Generative AI at Work', Quarterly Journal of Economics 140(2), 2025, pp.889-942, peer reviewed. Study of 5,179 customer support agents at a software firm, identified from a staggered rollout (quasi-experimental difference in differences, not a true RCT). Access to a generative AI assistant increased issues resolved per hour by 14% on average, by 34% for novice and low-skilled workers, and had minimal near-zero effect for experienced and highly skilled workers. Mechanism: the AI disseminates the tacit best practices of the firm's best agents to everyone else. Corroborated by Noy and Zhang, Science 381(6654), 2023, a true RCT of 453 college-educated professionals, which found time taken down 40% and output quality up 18% on writing tasks, with inequality between workers falling because low-ability workers gained most.
source: QJE 140(2) 2025 (earlier NBER w31161); Science 381(6654) 2023, DOI 10.1126/science.adh2586
note: THE RESULT THAT FLIPS THE USUAL PITCH, and the single most decision-relevant finding for a small business. The strongest available evidence says the tool is worth most where staff are NEW. If your team is experienced, the measured return is close to zero. So the honest framing is that AI is an onboarding and training technology rather than a headcount-reduction one, which also happens to be what the official employment statistics show. Caveat to publish with Noy and Zhang: short self-contained artificial writing tasks by individuals, not sustained real work inside a firm.

claim: Brynjolfsson, Rock and Syverson, 'The Productivity J-Curve: How Intangibles Complement General Purpose Technologies', American Economic Journal: Macroeconomics 13(1), 2021, pp.333-372, peer reviewed. Adopting a general purpose technology requires large complementary investments in process redesign, co-invention and human capital which are costly immediately and invisible in the accounts, so measured productivity falls before it rises. Adjusting for intangibles related to computer hardware and software yields a TFP level 15.9% higher than official measures by end-2017. Related: Brynjolfsson, Hitt and Yang, 'Intangible Assets: Computers and Organizational Capital', Brookings Papers on Economic Activity 2002(1), studying 1,216 large firms 1987-97, found 'Each dollar invested in computers is associated with an increase in firm market valuation of over $10... compared with an increase of just over $1 per dollar of investment in other tangible assets', and that 'the combination of computers and organizational structures creates more value than the simple sum of their separate contributions.'
source: AEJ Macroeconomics 13(1) 2021; Brookings Papers on Economic Activity 2002(1)
note: REFRAMES THE BUYING QUESTION from 'will this tool pay for itself' to 'can I survive the dip, and do I have the management slack to make the complementary investment that turns the dip into a return'. A small firm with no spare management capacity is structurally worse placed to climb out of the J-curve, which is a defensible reason for caution rather than a failure of nerve. HONEST CAVEAT that must be published with the $10 figure: the sample is Fortune 1000 firms and the authors state their results do not necessarily apply to other periods or other types of firm. The $10 is not a return on the computer, it is a signal of unmeasured intangible capital the investment correlates with.

claim: Dell'Acqua et al., 'Navigating the Jagged Technological Frontier', Organization Science 37(2), 2026, peer reviewed, earlier HBS working paper 24-013. Pre-registered field experiment with 758 BCG consultants across 18 realistic consulting tasks using GPT-4. Inside the frontier: 12.2% more tasks completed, about 25% faster, quality up over 30%. Outside it, on a task deliberately chosen to sit beyond the model's capability, consultants with AI were 19 percentage points LESS likely to produce a correct solution than consultants with none. The 'jagged technological frontier' is the irregular boundary between tasks the model does well and badly, where the two are nearly indistinguishable in apparent difficulty and the system gives no signal it has crossed over.
source: Organization Science 37(2) 2026; SSRN 4573321
note: TIER 2 SOLELY BECAUSE OF A DISCLOSED CONFLICT, which must be stated wherever this is cited: the experiment was run in collaboration with Boston Consulting Group, on BCG's own consultants, with BCG-affiliated co-authors, and BCG sells AI consulting. Peer review in Organization Science mitigates but does not remove it. USE THE PUBLISHED FIGURES: over 30% quality and about 25% faster, not the widely circulated 40% and 25.1% which come from the 2023 working paper. The 19-point result is the empirical counterpart to so-so automation and the more useful half: the danger is not that the tool is bad, it is that you cannot tell from the output which side of the line you are on, and the paper notes AI made wrong answers MORE persuasive and coherent.

claim: Acemoglu, 'The Simple Macroeconomics of AI', NBER Working Paper 32487, May 2024, later published in Economic Policy 40(121), 2025. Baseline estimate is a total factor productivity gain of 0.71% over ten years, roughly 0.07% a year, and less than 0.55% adjusting for hard-to-learn tasks; GDP gain 1.1% over ten years, or 0.92% hard-task-adjusted. Method is Hulten's theorem: aggregate TFP gain equals the share of GDP in affected tasks (4.6%) times the average task-level cost saving (27% labour cost saving, converted using an AI-exposure-adjusted labour share of 0.57). These are roughly an order of magnitude below Goldman Sachs (7% global GDP, 1.5% annual US productivity growth) and McKinsey Global Institute (1.5 to 3.4 percentage points of added annual GDP growth).
source: NBER w32487, free PDF at MIT economics; journal version Economic Policy 40(121) 2025
note: CORRECTS A FIGURE I HELD WRONG: the paper's headline is 0.71%, not the 0.66% that circulates online. PUBLISH THE PUSHBACK ALONGSIDE IT, because this is genuinely contested rather than settled. Goldman Sachs responded that the 4.6% automatable-task share is too low, using about 25% instead, and that the Hulten framework ignores gains from labour reallocation and new task creation. Maxwell Tabarrok argues the Hulten small-shock approximation is invalid precisely for a general purpose technology. Chad Jones models AI as potentially changing the growth regime through automated idea production, a channel this accounting cannot capture by construction. The honest framing: Acemoglu's number is a lower bound conditional on AI being a normal task-automating technology, and the critics assume it is not. Nobody has settled it empirically.

claim: Peng, Kalliamvakou, Cihon and Demirer, 'The Impact of AI on Developer Productivity: Evidence from GitHub Copilot', arXiv:2302.06590, February 2023. NOT peer reviewed and no journal version located. An RCT of 95 programmers recruited through Upwork, asked to implement an HTTP server in JavaScript, found the treated group 55.8% faster (71.17 against 160.89 minutes, p=0.0017). The 95% confidence interval on that speed-up is [21%, 89%]. The difference in success rate had a confidence interval spanning zero, [-0.11, 0.25], meaning no detectable effect on whether the task was completed correctly.
source: arXiv 2302.06590, title page affiliations read directly
note: TIER 3, AND THE REASON MATTERS. Three of the four authors work for the company selling the product: Sida Peng at Microsoft Research (corresponding author), Eirini Kalliamvakou and Peter Cihon at GitHub Inc. This is a vendor study with an academic co-author, not independent research. The 55.8% figure is quoted constantly without its confidence interval of [21%, 89%], which makes the point estimate nearly meaningless on its own: the honest statement is 'somewhere between a fifth and nine-tenths faster'. Also usually dropped: no detectable effect on whether the code was CORRECT.
