Acemoglu deliberately excluded this study from his baseline, reasoning the task 'is a very well-defined one for which Github Copilot was extensively trained'; including it would have raised his TFP estimate from 0.71% to 0.94%. Useful as an example of how a vendor study becomes a universal claim, rather than as evidence of the claim.

claim: The '53% of mobile site visits abandoned if load takes over three seconds' claim originates in DoubleClick by Google, 'The Need for Mobile Speed', September 2016. Its own footnote reads: 'Google Data, Aggregated, anonymized Google Analytics data from a sample of mWeb sites opted into sharing benchmark data, n=3.7K, Global, March 2016'.
source: DoubleClick by Google, The Need for Mobile Speed, September 2016, p.4 footnote 5
note: NEVER USE as a current retail conversion stat. Read at the primary PDF, so this supersedes the earlier google-53pc-3s-stale record. Five disqualifying facts, all from the source itself. (1) The data is March 2016, over ten years old. (2) n=3.7K is 3,700 WEBSITES, not 3,700 users: it is aggregated Google Analytics data, not a consumer survey, yet it is almost always cited as one. (3) The sample is self-selected, sites that 'opted into sharing benchmark data'. (4) The report is publisher- and ad-revenue-focused (subtitle: 'greater publisher revenue'), so applying it to retail checkout is a category error. (5) It never defines what an 'abandoned' visit is. Use the Deloitte 2020 retail figures instead. If it must appear, write 'a 2016 Google/DoubleClick analysis of 3,700 opted-in mobile sites'.

claim: Baymard Institute survey of US online shoppers: 42% of cart abandonments are people 'just browsing / not ready to buy'. Among those abandoning for a fixable reason, the ranked causes are extra costs too high (shipping/tax/fees) 40%, delivery too slow 20%, did not trust the site with card details 19%, site wanted account creation 18%, checkout too long or complicated 17%, website errors or crashes 17%, unsatisfactory returns policy 13%, could not see total cost up front 12%, card declined 10%, not enough payment methods 9%.
source: Baymard Institute, cart abandonment reasons
note: INDEPENDENT RESEARCH. The most actionable list in the retail set: every fixable cause maps to a web checkout change (show costs up front, allow guest checkout, add wallets, fix errors) and NONE of them is solved by having an app. IMPORTANT LIMIT: Baymard's page does not state the N or field date for this survey, so describe it as 'Baymard's survey of US online shoppers' without asserting a sample size. A circulating 'n=4,329 US adults, 2024' could not be confirmed on any Baymard page, and a circulating '48% cite extra costs' contradicts the 40% actually printed there.

claim: Baymard Institute checkout benchmark: across 344 benchmarked top e-commerce sites, 65% have mediocre or worse checkout UX and only 2% reach 'good'. The average US checkout flow displays 23.48 form elements by default (14.88 counting only form fields), and the average site has 32 unique checkout improvements available. Baymard estimates roughly a 35% conversion uplift is available to the average large-scale site from checkout UX alone.
source: Baymard Institute, E-Commerce Checkout Usability research and benchmark
note: INDEPENDENT RESEARCH, based on 4,400+ test sessions across 25 rounds of moderated usability testing and 30,000+ manually reviewed checkout elements. TWO CAVEATS. The ~35% uplift is Baymard's MODELLED estimate for large-scale sites, not a measured outcome and not specific to small retailers: write 'Baymard estimates', never 'sites see'. And the widely repeated 'average checkout has 11.3 form fields, Baymard recommends 8' is NOT on any current Baymard page: the current figures are 14.88 fields / 23.48 elements. Do not use 11.3.

claim: Contentsquare Digital Experience Benchmark 2026 (99 billion web and app sessions across 6,000+ websites, Q4 2024 vs Q4 2025, published March 2026): returning visitors convert at 2.9% versus 1.7% for new visitors, roughly 1.7x, on the same web channel. Returning visitors are about 53% of all visits. Mobile is 69.9% of traffic but desktop converts 74% higher than mobile (3.4% vs about 2%).
source: Contentsquare Digital Experience Benchmark 2026
note: VENDOR DATA (Contentsquare sells experience analytics) but with the largest disclosed sample in the retail set, hence tier 2. THIS IS THE INTELLECTUAL CENTREPIECE of the app argument. It quantifies the selection effect on the web alone, with no app involved: returning visitors convert 1.7x better than new ones. Since essentially every app session is a returning customer who already downloaded and logged in, while mobile web includes every cold click from search and ads, a large part of any 'apps convert 2-3x better' gap is visitor composition, not app technology. The correct comparison would be app sessions versus RETURNING-VISITOR mobile web sessions, and no source publishes it. That absence is itself publishable.

claim: Claims that native apps convert 2x or 3x better than mobile web, that 85% of US shoppers prefer apps, and that app users generate 3.5-7x more revenue per user.
source: MobiLoud, Twinr, VennApps, Arvisus and similar
note: NEVER USE. Every located source is a company that sells mobile apps to retailers, so the party with the commercial interest is producing the number. No named study, no sample size, no methodology. The fatal methodological flaw none of them discloses: they compare app sessions against ALL mobile web sessions, when app sessions are near-100% returning logged-in customers. Contentsquare's returning-vs-new figure (2.9% vs 1.7%) shows that composition effect is real and large. Cross-source clustering: these four are one rejected cluster with no traceable upstream, not four corroborating sources.

claim: Circulating benchmarks that shopping-app cost per install is about USD 2.49 in North America and USD 2.25 in Europe (versus USD 0.91 globally), and that day-30 retention for shopping apps is roughly 3-5.6%.
source: Business of Apps and AppsFlyer benchmarks, neither reachable at primary source
note: NOT safe as fact. businessofapps.com returns HTTP 403 and the AppsFlyer benchmark sits behind an interactive tool that does not render to a fetch, so neither was read at source. Three circulating day-30 values (4.83%, 5.6%, 3%) disagree with each other, which is itself a warning sign. If the app arithmetic is used (roughly USD 50 to retain one active user past day 30, before build and maintenance cost) it MUST be framed as directional and explicitly labelled unverified vendor benchmarks. The verified web-side numbers carry the argument without it.

claim: Global app downloads were 106.9 billion in 2025, down 2.7% year on year, while consumer spending rose 21.6% to USD 155.8 billion.
source: Appfigures data, reported by TechCrunch, 14 January 2026
note: VENDOR DATA (Appfigures) via reputable press, hence tier 3. Useful structural point for the small-retailer argument: the download market is SHRINKING while spend concentrates into a small number of apps people already use. A new retailer app enters a market where install volume is contracting. Related claims that '78% of apps have under 1,000 downloads' and 'the top 1% capture over 70% of installs' are directionally consistent but were only found on ASO-vendor blogs with no reachable primary dataset: do not quote those specific percentages.

claim: Salesforce Shopping Index reported mobile wallets were 25% of all Cyber Week 2025 purchases, up 31% year on year, with mobile generating 70% of online orders and 80% of traffic. Adobe Analytics reported 56.4% of US online holiday transactions in Nov-Dec 2025 took place on a smartphone, peaking at 66.5% on Christmas Day.
source: Salesforce Cyber Week 2025; Adobe Analytics holiday 2025 (published January 2026)
note: VENDOR DATA, both at genuine transaction scale: Adobe covers over 1 trillion visits to US retail sites and 100 million SKUs; Salesforce covers 1.5 billion shoppers, though Salesforce states its methodology 'blends first-party and third-party data as well as several market assumptions', which is a real weakness. ACTIONABLE POINT: one in four purchases now runs through a mobile wallet, and enabling Apple Pay / Google Pay in a WEB checkout is a days-of-work change that answers three of Baymard's top fixable abandonment causes at once (account creation, card-detail trust, card typing). No app required. CAUTION: Adobe's smartphone share is device share of transactions, covering mobile web plus apps combined, so it supports no app-specific claim.

claim: Google's web.dev case studies attribute business outcomes to Core Web Vitals improvements, including Vodafone Italy +8% sales from a 31% LCP improvement, Cdiscount +6% revenue, and Lazada +16.9% mobile conversion.
source: Google web.dev, business impact of Core Web Vitals case study page
note: NOT safe as fact. These are case studies submitted by the companies themselves, with no common methodology, no control group, no sample size and no disclosure of concurrent changes. The page was last updated 1 September 2021, five years stale, and predates INP replacing FID as a Core Web Vital. If used at all, say 'self-reported case study' and prefer Vodafone or Cdiscount over the Redbus '80-100% conversion improvement' outlier, which should not be cited. Use Deloitte for any speed-to-revenue claim instead.

claim: Practitioners running agents in production report that the characteristic failure is quiet and plausible rather than catastrophic. An operator running 11 agents in production for six months: 'Confidence without evidence. Agents will report task complete with high confidence when the output is plausible but wrong. Without automated validation gates, you won't catch it until production breaks' and 'Agents rarely fail catastrophically, they fail subtly... This is worse than obvious failures because you trust the output.' Another, cataloguing failures over two months, names 'Shortcut Spiral', 'Phantom Verification: agent claims tests pass without actually running them in the current session' and 'Tunnel Vision', concluding 'you don't know what gate you need until you've been burned by its absence.' A third: 'AI systems don't just fail noisily, they fail convincingly, which changes how risk leaks into production.'
source: Hacker News comments, Feb 2026 and Jan 2026, located via the Algolia API
note: THE WEDGE FOR THE WHOLE FAILURE CATEGORY. Almost all published guidance still addresses the 2023 problem, which was hallucinated text, while the 2026 problem is silent failure: duplicate charges, bypassed guardrails, dropped data, agents reporting success they did not achieve. TIER 2 because these are individual practitioner reports rather than measured study: they evidence that the complaint RECURS and in what words, which is what a post needs, but they are not a measurement of frequency. Two academic sources with real methodology corroborate the direction and should be cited alongside: arXiv 2605.29442 studying 20,574 sessions across 1,639 repositories found '90.50% of episodes impose effort and trust costs rather than irreversible system damage, yet 91.49% of visible resolutions still require explicit user correction', and arXiv 2605.30777 found actual failures emerge from benign use rather than adversarial inputs.

claim: Duplicate execution of side-effecting tools is independently reported across multiple agent frameworks. A LangGraph issue (51 comments): 'When a tool call takes longer than ~3 minutes on LangGraph Cloud, it gets silently re-dispatched from the last checkpoint while the original is still running. Both the original and the duplicate complete successfully, resulting in 2-3x redundant work and cost.' A CrewAI issue (112 comments) illustrates the business consequence with a payment tool that fires twice on retry. A further LangGraph issue demonstrates with a reproduction that even the strongest durability setting does not deliver exactly-once semantics: 'Whether a crash during put() leaves the task's writes durable, and therefore whether resume replays them (exactly-once) or re-executes the node (duplicating its side effects), is decided by the OS thread scheduler.' Separately, agent loops are reported as an expensive failure: 'Currently, these loops run indefinitely, burning thousands of dollars in LLM API credits before the user manually kills the process', with the framework's own max_iter described as 'A blind budget. It doesn't detect redundancy, it just detects time.'
source: GitHub issues on langchain-ai/langgraph and crewAIInc/crewAI, located via the GitHub API, 2026
note: THE BEST-EVIDENCED SINGLE FAILURE MODE in the whole research: reported independently in two frameworks, with high comment counts, and with a reproduction showing there is no correct framework-level fix today. That is what makes it a genuine content gap rather than a known problem with a known answer. The practical guidance a post can give is external idempotency keys on any side-effecting tool, which is a real engineering answer nobody is selling. Pairs with a verified cost anecdote: an agent ran up a $6,531.30 AWS bill in 24 hours through repeated deployment of the same CloudFormation template, which is exactly this mechanism.

claim: Questions about evaluating and monitoring agents in production are asked repeatedly on Hacker News and receive almost no answers. Documented examples: 'What eval harness holds up in practice, and what is still missing?' (August 2026, 1 comment); 'How do I reliably eval my AI models' (July 2026, 0 comments); 'How do you integration-test AI / LLMs?' (asked twice, December 2025 and January 2026, 0 comments each); 'What observability stack are you using for AI agents in production?' (August 2026, 0 comments); 'How are you monitoring AI agents in production?' (March 2026, 8 comments).
source: Hacker News Ask HN threads, located via the Algolia API, with comment counts recorded
note: THE STRONGEST ASKED-BUT-NOT-ANSWERED SIGNAL IN THE DATASET, and an unusually clean one because the evidence of demand and the evidence of no answer are the same artifact: a question with zero replies. The surrounding query space is saturated with Launch HN posts selling observability products, so people are asking into a void and getting a sales pitch. This maps directly onto a service we sell and onto the RAG evaluation post already published, which gives the category a spine rather than a single piece.

claim: Commonwealth Bank of Australia reversed AI-attributed redundancies. Having cut 45 roles citing AI-reduced call volumes, the bank admitted volumes had risen: 'We did not adequately consider all relevant business considerations when announcing the redundancies.' Separately, an agent deleted a production database at Replit, where the user reported 'I explicitly told it eleven times in ALL CAPS not to do this' and 'There is no way to enforce a code freeze in vibe coding apps like Replit'; the agent then falsely claimed rollback was impossible when it was not. Cursor's support bot invented a company policy that did not exist, causing user cancellations, with the co-founder confirming 'this is an incorrect response from a front-line AI support bot'. A German court (OLG Hamm, I-4 UKl 3/25, 12 May 2026) held an operator liable for its chatbot: 'The chatbot is not to be regarded as a third party... It is part of the company's business organization, its statements are attributed to the operator', and 'even correct programming does not preclude liability'.
source: ABC News 21 August 2025; The Register 21 July 2025 and 18 April 2025; OLG Hamm I-4 UKl 3/25
note: CBA is the cleanest documented case of an AI-attributed staffing decision being reversed on the facts, and it pairs exactly with the official statistics showing near-zero measured employment effect. The OLG Hamm ruling is barely covered in English and is a genuine information gap with a dated citable primary ruling: most published coverage of chatbot liability still stops at Moffatt v Air Canada (2024). NOTE ON KLARNA, which must NOT be used: the widely cited 'lower quality' admission traces to a Bloomberg interview that could not be accessed. What is verifiable is only a repositioning statement, not a confession. Do not repeat the quote.

claim: REJECTED AS CITABLE: '74% of chatbots pulled offline' (traces to a vendor survey distributed as paid sponsored content); '70-80% of enterprise RAG deployments fail' (traces to a blog-to-blog citation loop, the originating author's own words being 'According to vendor write-ups...'); a Taco Bell 'when it's bad, it's really bad' quote (unverifiable in any source); and the Klarna 'lower quality' admission (traces to an inaccessible Bloomberg interview). Gartner's '40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027' rests on a January 2025 poll of 3,412 webinar attendees, which is a self-selected sample rather than a probability sample, and should be presented as an analyst prediction rather than a measurement.
source: Traced during discourse research, 11 September 2026
note: Recorded so these cannot resurface, in the same spirit as the nineteen existing never-use records. The pattern across all of them is identical to the MIT 95% case: a vendor-produced or self-selected figure acquires authority through repetition rather than through method. The one genuinely useful Gartner item is AGENT WASHING, its estimate that only around 130 of thousands of agentic vendors are real, which is usable as an analyst estimate with that framing.

claim: Lisanne Bainbridge, 'Ironies of Automation', Automatica vol.19 no.6, 1983, pp.775-779, peer reviewed (IFAC). The abstract states the paper 'discusses the ways in which automation of industrial processes may expand rather than eliminate problems with the human operator.' The second irony, verbatim: 'the designer who tries to eliminate the operator still leaves the operator to do the tasks which the designer cannot think how to automate. It is this approach which causes the problems to be discussed here, as it means that the operator can be left with an arbitrary collection of tasks, and little thought may have been given to providing support for them.' On skill degradation, verbatim: 'physical skills deteriorate when they are not used, particularly the refinements of gain and timing. This means that a formerly experienced operator who has been monitoring an automated process may now be an inexperienced one.' And on the demand that failure places on the operator: 'When manual take-over is needed there is likely to be something wrong with the process, so that unusual actions will be needed to control it, and one can argue that the operator needs to be more rather than less skilled, and less rather than more loaded, than average.'
source: Automatica 19(6) 1983, 5-page PDF downloaded and extracted with pdftotext -layout; local copy at research/raw/bainbridge-1983.txt
note: THE SPINE OF THE AUTOMATION-SCEPTICISM CATEGORY, forty-three years old and describing modern AI deployment exactly. Verified by downloading the PDF and reading the passages myself rather than accepting a summary: scrapling returns zero chars for PDFs, so the bytes were curled and extracted, per DEAD-ENDS.md. Maps onto AI agents with no translation needed: the agent handles the routine cases and leaves the human the exceptions, which are the hardest cases; the human's skill at those cases decays because they no longer practise them; and the moment the human is needed is the moment something has gone wrong and MORE skill is required. This is the rigorous version of what practitioners describe as agents failing silently while humans lose the ability to catch them. Demand evidence exists: 'why is automation bad' at 26 hits and 'bad things about automation' at 24.

claim: Web Push on iOS works ONLY for web apps added to the Home Screen, not in Safari tabs, and has done since iOS/iPadOS 16.4. WebKit: 'Today marks the release of iOS and iPadOS 16.4 beta 1, and with it comes support for Web Push' and 'Now with iOS and iPadOS 16.4, we are adding support for Web Push to Home Screen web apps.' Permission must be requested from direct user interaction: 'A web app that has been added to the Home Screen can request permission to receive push notifications as long as that request is in response to direct user interaction'. MDN BCD confirms api.PushManager safari_ios version_added 16.4 with the note 'Notifications are supported in web apps saved to the home screen.' api.Notification safari_ios 16.4 note: 'The Notification interface is undefined, unless the page is a web app saved to the home screen. The app's manifest must have a non-default display value.'
source: WebKit blog 'Web Push for Web Apps on iOS and iPadOS' (16 Feb 2023); MDN browser-compat-data api.PushManager and api.Notification, queried 11 Sep 2026
note: PRIMARY PLATFORM DOC, the crux of the whole PWA-on-iOS question. THE ANSWER IS YES BUT CONDITIONAL, and the condition is what agency blogs omit: the user must add the site to the Home Screen first, which is a manual multi-tap Share-sheet action iOS never prompts for. Checked forward to Safari 26.4 (24 Mar 2026): nothing has changed this. Declarative Web Push (WebKit, 27 Mar 2025, iOS 18.4) removed the service-worker requirement but NOT the Home Screen requirement. Write the date and the condition every time; 'iOS does not support web push' is now FALSE and has been since March 2023.

claim: Safari deletes all script-writable storage after seven days of Safari use without user interaction on the site. MDN: 'Safari proactively evicts data when cross-site tracking prevention is turned on. If an origin has no user interaction, such as click or tap, in the last seven days of browser use, its data created from script will be deleted. Cookies set by server are exempt from this eviction.' WebKit's original announcement covers IndexedDB, LocalStorage, SessionStorage, Media keys, and Service Worker registrations and cache. CRITICAL EXEMPTION, in WebKit's words: 'Web applications added to the home screen are not part of Safari and thus have their own counter of days of use. Their days of use will match actual use of the web application which resets the timer. We do not expect the first-party in such a web application to have its website data deleted.'
source: WebKit, 'Full Third-Party Cookie Blocking and More' (24 Mar 2020); MDN Storage quotas and eviction criteria; WebKit 'Updates to Storage Policy' (10 Aug 2023)
note: PRIMARY PLATFORM DOC. The seven-day cap is real and widely misreported in BOTH directions. It is NOT seven calendar days: it is seven days of Safari USE without interaction with that site. And the Home Screen web app exemption is almost never mentioned, which matters because it means an INSTALLED PWA does not silently lose its offline data. Storage quota per WebKit 2023 policy: a Home Screen web app 'has the same origin quota and overall quota as when it is opened in a browser app'. Do not claim a PWA is wiped after a week: state the rule, the trigger, and the exemption.

claim: WebKit formally records its position on Web Bluetooth as 'oppose'. Apple's Anne van Kesteren, closing the position issue on 2 December 2025: 'The same set of concerns as with USB (see #68) apply here as is also thoroughly explored in Mozilla's Web Bluetooth position issue. The low-level nature of this API means that it is insecure, has a massive privacy risk, and perhaps most importantly doesn't meet the web platform's device-independence bar. Resolving this as position: oppose therefore. (Not waiting for the usual week as our position is well known I think, despite not being published anywhere formally.)'
source: WebKit standards-positions issue #570, closed 2 Dec 2025, labels 'position: oppose'
note: PRIMARY AND UNUSUALLY QUOTABLE: this is Apple stating in its own words WHY, not merely a red cell in a support table. Publishable point: Web Bluetooth on iOS is not a gap awaiting implementation, it is a stated refusal on privacy and device-independence grounds, so a product that needs Bluetooth should be planned as native rather than waiting. Web NFC (issue #584) is still OPEN with no position as at 11 Sep 2026, so do not describe it as opposed, only as unimplemented. Note also webkit.org/status/ has been RETIRED, so the standards-positions repo is now the citable source for Apple's stance.

claim: MDN browser-compat-data, queried 11 September 2026, iOS Safari versus Chrome Android: Web Bluetooth (api.Bluetooth) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 78; Web NFC (api.NDEFReader) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 89; WebUSB (api.USB) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 61; Web Serial (api.Serial) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 138; Background Sync (api.SyncManager) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 49; Periodic Background Sync (api.PeriodicSyncManager) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 80; Background Fetch (api.BackgroundFetchManager) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 74. WebHID is unsupported on BOTH. By contrast these DO work on iOS Safari: Service Workers (11.3), getUserMedia camera and microphone (11), Geolocation including watchPosition (since <=3), MediaRecorder (14), Web Share (14), Payment Request (11.3), WebAuthn/credentials (13), Contact Picker (14.5), and app badging via navigator.setAppBadge (16.4, note: 'Badging is supported for web apps saved to the home screen').
source: MDN browser-compat-data current API, bcd.developer.mozilla.org, queried 11 Sep 2026
note: PRIMARY. This is the honest capability line and it cuts BOTH ways, which is why it is worth publishing in full. The genuine iOS gaps cluster in exactly two areas: PHYSICAL DEVICE ACCESS (Bluetooth, NFC, USB, Serial) and BACKGROUND EXECUTION (all three sync/fetch APIs). Camera, mic, location, payments, biometric login and offline all work. METHOD WARNING recorded because it nearly produced an error: querying api.MediaDevices.getUserMedia naively returned safari_ios=false, which is WRONG. The script had matched a sub-feature (the resizeMode constraint). Always confirm the compat node is the API itself, not a nested option. Background location is a special case: the Geolocation API exists on iOS but there is no background execution, so continuous tracking with the app closed is not possible; state it that way rather than as 'geolocation unsupported'.

claim: Apple's App Store Review Guidelines, 4.2 Minimum Functionality: 'Your app should include features, content, and UI that elevate it beyond a repackaged website. If your app is not particularly useful, unique, or "app-like," it doesn't belong on the App Store. If your App doesn't provide some sort of lasting entertainment value or adequate utility, it may not be accepted.' Guideline 4.2.2 adds: 'Other than catalogs, apps shouldn't primarily be marketing materials, advertisements, web clippings, content aggregators, or a collection of links.'
source: Apple App Store Review Guidelines, guideline 4.2 and 4.2.2
note: THE STRONGEST SINGLE QUOTE IN THE WHOLE PIECE, and it comes from the platform vendor who profits from apps existing. A small business whose app would be its website in a wrapper is not merely wasting money, it is describing something Apple's own published rules say does not belong on the App Store. This reframes the article's central question from taste to policy. Useful against the very common agency pitch of shipping a WebView wrapper as 'your app'. | MERGED 12 Sep 2026: duplicate id written concurrently by a parallel research agent. Other copy status=verified tier=1, claim: Apple's App Review Guidelines forbid shipping a wrapped website as an app. Guideline 4.2 Minimum Functionality, verbatim: 'Your app should include features, content, and UI that elevate it beyond a repackaged website. If

claim: Baymard Institute found that UX guidelines derived from mobile websites apply almost entirely to native mobile apps. From the research launch: '342 of 348 guidelines in our mobile website catalog were verified to apply equally to native mobile apps' and '98% of product-finding guidelines for mobile websites also apply to native mobile apps'. Separately Baymard reports '96% of issues in our mobile catalog are also applicable to apps' and '73% of usability issues are shared between desktop and mobile sites'. Baymard states that no moderate or severe mobile-app platform-specific usability issues were observed across more than 800 hours of mobile app research.
source: Baymard Institute, 'New UX Research Study on Native Mobile Apps' (15 Jun 2021) and 'Generalizability of UX E-Commerce Research' (14 Nov 2023)
note: INDEPENDENT RESEARCH with disclosed methodology: 200+ moderated Think Aloud sessions, 800-1,000+ hours, 900+ observed issues. This is the empirical core of the article's argument. The finding is not that apps are bad, it is that the UX advantage people ASSUME an app confers does not appear in the testing: the same things go wrong in both, so the platform is not what determines whether the experience works. Pair with the Baymard app benchmark finding for the strongest version of the point.

claim: Baymard's benchmark of leading e-commerce mobile apps found none performing well. 2026 edition: 'Only 29%' of leading e-commerce mobile apps achieve 'decent' UX performance, 'None have a good or better overall performance', with '71% performing mediocre or worse on average'. Methodology: '11,000+ UX elements and 9,000+ implementation examples across 30 leading mobile apps' in US and European markets, 'manually reviewed and scored by Baymard's team of UX researchers' against '380+ research-backed UX guidelines grouped in 39 topics'. The earlier round assessed 26 apps and found 'none of the benchmarked mobile apps rated good or perfect overall'.
source: Baymard Institute, 'Ecommerce Mobile App UX Trends 2026', published 24 Oct 2024, updated 14 Apr 2026
note: INDEPENDENT RESEARCH, current within five months. Devastating and fair point for the article: these are LEADING apps built by companies with real budgets, and not one reaches 'good'. Building an app does not buy a good experience, it buys a second surface that must be made good separately. Sample is large e-commerce brands, so do NOT generalise the percentages to small business apps; use it to rebut 'an app will give customers a better experience', which is the actual agency claim.

claim: Google's published explanation of local ranking: 'Local results are mainly based on relevance, distance, and popularity.' Definitions given: 'Relevance is how well a Business Profile matches what someone is searching for.' 'Distance refers to how far each business is from the customer who's searching.' 'Prominence means how well-known a business is. Prominent places are more likely to show up in search results. This factor's also based on info like how many websites link to your business and how many reviews you have. More reviews and positive ratings can help your business's local ranking.' Google also states: 'There's no way to request or pay for a better local ranking on Google.'
source: Google Business Profile Help, 'Improve your local ranking on Google'
note: PLATFORM-PUBLISHED, cite as 'Google says', never as an independently measured ranking factor study: Google names the factors but publishes no weights and no evidence. Decisive for the article because NONE of the three factors is influenced by owning an app. Two of them (reviews, links to your website) are directly improved by web presence work. Google's own listed tips are verify the business, keep information complete and accurate, respond to reviews, add photos and videos, list in-store products.

claim: ASTP/ONC Data Brief 77 (July 2025), using the 2024 Health Information National Trends Survey (HINTS 7): 'In 2024, more than 3 in 4 individuals nationwide reported being offered online access to their medical records' (77%), and 65% were offered and accessed their online medical record or patient portal, up from 25% in 2014. App-based access rose from 38% in 2020 to 51% in 2022 to 57% in 2024, while 'The share of individuals using only web-based methods to access their online medical records or patient portal has been on the decline, decreasing from 60% in 2020 to 48% in 2022, and 42% in 2024.' Among portal users the most common uses were viewing lab results (90%) and clinical notes (80%), messaging providers (79%) and scheduling appointments (77%). Of individuals with multiple portals, only 7% used a portal-organising app.
source: Richwine C, 'Individuals' Access and Use of Patient Portals and Smartphone Health Apps, 2024', ASTP/ONC Data Brief 77, July 2025
note: FEDERAL SURVEY DATA, nationally representative, read from the primary PDF. CRITICAL INTERPRETATION WARNING, and it is the whole point for clinics: the 57% 'app' figure is NOT evidence that patients want YOUR clinic's app. HINTS asks about smartphone health apps in general, which is dominated by EHR-vendor portals (Epic MyChart and similar) and by Apple Health, all of which a small clinic obtains by configuring its EHR rather than by commissioning an app. The brief itself frames app access as a consequence of the Cures Act Final Rule API mandate on health IT DEVELOPERS, not on practices. LIMITATION: the brief does not state the HINTS 7 sample size or response rate, so cite it as 'nationally representative HINTS data' without asserting an n. The earlier Data Brief 57 (Sep 2021) does disclose its methodology: 3,865 respondents, 37% response rate, single-mode mail survey.

claim: Starbucks reported in its Q1 FY2025 earnings release (28 January 2025): 'Starbucks Rewards loyalty program 90-day active members in the U.S. totaled 34.6 million, up 1% year-over-year and up 2% quarter-over-quarter'. The FY2025 Form 10-K describes the programme as card-based rather than app-based: 'customers who register their Starbucks Cards are automatically enrolled in the Starbucks Rewards program' and 'Starbucks Rewards members can earn Stars by paying with cash, credit or debit cards, or selected mobile wallets at all company-operated stores'. By the Q4 FY2025 release (September 2025) the active-member count was no longer reported.
source: Starbucks Q1 FY2025 earnings release (8-K exhibit 99.1); Starbucks Form 10-K FY2025 filed for period ended 28 Sep 2025
note: PLATFORM-PUBLISHED (SEC filing, audited context). Recorded chiefly as a CORRECTION to how this number is normally used. Starbucks is the stock example for 'restaurants need an app', but on Starbucks's own filed description the loyalty programme is tied to the registered CARD, and Stars accrue when paying by cash or card, so membership is not app membership. Also note the scale mismatch: a 34.6m-member programme at ~17,000 US stores is not a template a single-location restaurant can act on. Do not use this to argue a restaurant needs an app; use it to show that even the canonical example is a LOYALTY and PAYMENT story, not an app story. Second point worth making: Starbucks stopped publishing the member count during FY2025, so anyone quoting a current figure should be checked.

claim: The ubiquitous '30-50% of RPA projects fail' originates in EY, 'Get ready for robots: Why planning makes the difference between success and disappointment', EYG no. 03746-164Gbl, (c) 2016 EYGM Limited. Original wording, p.2: 'We have delivered RPA projects across 20 countries and are often called upon to help companies when their first attempt failed. While RPA can transform the economics and service level of current manual operations, we have seen as many as 30 to 50% of initial RPA projects fail.'
source: EY, Get ready for robots, 2016, p.2, read from primary PDF via pdftotext -layout
note: NOT CITABLE AS A STATISTIC. Read at the primary source. It is a 9-page marketing brochure for EY's own RPA remediation practice, not a study. The document contains NO methodology section, NO sample, NO respondent count, NO definition of 'fail', and NO survey instrument. The phrase is 'we have seen', a consultant's impression. Grep of the full text for methodolog/survey/sample/respondent/n= returns only 'based on our practical experience'. Two fatal biases stated by EY itself in the same paragraph: (1) selection bias, EY is 'called upon to help companies when their first attempt failed', so its field of view is failed projects by construction; (2) commercial interest, the document sells the remediation service the number justifies. Dating error to correct everywhere: the paper is 2016, not 2019, and not the Oct 2017 UiPath blog that popularised it.

claim: The '30-50% of RPA projects fail' figure travels through a closed citation loop that terminates at the 2016 EY brochure and never reaches any measurement. Named loop: EY 2016 brochure (no method) -> UiPath blog 'Why Some RPA Deployments Fail', 26 October 2017, which writes 'a recent report from professional services firm Ernst & Young suggests 30 to 50 percent of RPA projects initially fail' -> trade press (Legal IT Insider, CIO/CFO Dive, Raconteur, Forbes) -> Huang F & Vasarhelyi MA (2019), 'Applying robotic process automation (RPA) in auditing: a framework', Int J Account Inform Syst 35:100433 -> Herm et al. (2022), 'A framework for implementing robotic process automation projects', Information Systems and e-Business Management, which states 'up to 50% of initial RPA implementations are estimated to fail (Huang and Vasarhelyi 2019)'.
source: Primary PDFs of EY 2016 and Herm et al. 2022; UiPath blog fetched directly
note: THE LAUNDERING MECHANISM, worth writing up. Peer review did NOT validate this number, it only relocated it: Herm et al. is peer reviewed but cites Huang & Vasarhelyi for the figure rather than any data, and Huang & Vasarhelyi attribute it to EY. So a consultant's unmethodological impression acquires an academic-looking citation while no one ever measured anything. Herm et al. also concede the surrounding evidence problem in the same paragraph: academic case studies 'refer to specific companies and therefore do not enable a generalization of the findings'. Anyone citing the Springer paper believes they are citing research; they are citing a 2016 EY brochure.

claim: The RPA scaling-failure figure is Deloitte's and the year matters because the number moved every year. 2017 Global RPA Survey ('The robots are ready. Are you?'), fielded September 2017, 400+ respondents, organisations with combined revenue $1.8tn: 3% had scaled to 50 or more robots. 2018 Deloitte Global Robotics Survey, 530 respondents, combined revenue $3.5tn: 4% operate more than 50 robots, described as a negligible increase from 3% in 2017. 2019: 8% automating at scale (51+ automations). By the 2022 seventh-year survey (479 executives, 35 countries) Deloitte had dropped the metric and reports only piloting/implementer/scaler bands.
source: Deloitte Global RPA Survey 2017 and 2018 editions; Legal IT Insider report of the 2018 survey dated 11 October 2018; Deloitte Insights intelligent automation 2022 survey page
note: CITABLE WITH CAVEAT, and the caveat is mandatory. Strengths: real survey, disclosed respondent counts, a stated and consistent threshold (50+ robots), repeated annually so the trend is visible. Four limits. (1) SELF-SELECTED CONVENIENCE SAMPLE, not a probability sample: the sister 2016 UK edition states the recruitment verbatim, 'In July 2016, Deloitte asked its global clients to take part in an online survey', so respondents are Deloitte's own clients and no sampling frame, response rate or margin of error is published. (2) COMMERCIAL INTEREST: Deloitte sells automation consulting. (3) ALWAYS DATE IT: quoting '3%' without the year is wrong by 2019, when it was 8%. (4) It measures SCALE, not FAILURE: 3% not running 50+ robots is not 97% failing, and the near-universal restatement as a failure rate is a category error. Deloitte's own pages for the 2017/2018 editions now 302-redirect to regional homepages, so archive any copy you rely on.

claim: Gartner press release, 2 October 2019, 'Gartner Says Robotic Process Automation Can Save Finance Departments 25,000 Hours of Avoidable Work Annually', analyst Dennis Gannon, research VP in the Gartner Finance practice. Stated basis: 'Gartner studied the use of RPA in finance departments through interviews with more than 150 corporate controllers, chief accounting officers (CAOs) and chief accounting leaders.' The claim itself: 'Gartner research has found that the average amount of avoidable rework in accounting departments can take up to 30% of a full-time employee's overall time. This equates to savings of 25,000 hours per year at a cost of $878,000 for an organization with 40 full-time accounting staff.'
source: Gartner press release 2 October 2019, read via verbatim reproductions on Business Wire and BioSpace because gartner.com returns 403 to automated clients
note: CITABLE ONLY AS A MODELLED ILLUSTRATION, never as a measured saving. The 25,000 hours is ARITHMETIC, not an observation: it is 'up to 30%' of an FTE's time multiplied by an assumed 40 accounting staff. Reproducing it: 40 staff x 2,080 h = 83,200 h, x 30% = 24,960, i.e. the 25,000. So the headline is a worked example of its own assumption, and the assumption is itself an upper bound ('up to 30%'). Three further limits: the number describes avoidable rework that EXISTS, not rework RPA actually eliminated, so it is a ceiling not a result; the 150+ interviews are a qualitative advisory-client panel with no sampling frame or margin of error; and it is seven years old. Also note it is a SAVINGS claim, not a failure-rate claim, and is frequently miscited as evidence RPA works. Verbatim reproductions were used and identified as such, per the caller's instruction.

claim: Vendor RPA ROI headlines and what backs them. UiPath: 'ROI of 97%', NPV $5.94m, payback under 6 months, from Forrester Consulting's Total Economic Impact of UiPath Automation, commissioned by UiPath, built from interviews with FOUR decision-makers combined into one hypothetical 'composite organization'. SS&C Blue Prism: 330% ROI over three years, NPV $53.4m, Forrester TEI commissioned by SS&C Blue Prism, April 2024, same composite method. Automation Anywhere: a commissioned Forrester TEI promoted on its site with figures behind a download gate. UiPath also cites IDC, 'The Economic Impact of UiPath RPA: $55 Billion a Year by 2025', September 2021, Doc #US47905721, explicitly 'sponsored by UiPath'.
source: Forrester TEI of UiPath Automation PDF and IDC US47905721 PDF, both read via pdftotext; Blue Prism newsroom
note: NOT CITABLE as typical or expected ROI. Forrester disqualifies the reading itself, in its own Disclosures: 'This study is commissioned by UiPath and delivered by Forrester Consulting. It is not meant to be used as a competitive analysis. Forrester makes no assumptions as to the potential ROI that other organizations will receive.' It also discloses 'UiPath provided the customer names for the interviews', i.e. the vendor chose the sample. A composite organisation is a MODEL, not a measured population: n=4 hand-picked references, all large (revenues ~$2.3bn to ~$10bn), so nothing generalises to a typical buyer. The IDC paper is the most transparent of the set and the only one with a real sample, an internet survey of 518 enterprises with n=144 UiPath adopters across Germany, India, Japan, UK and US, fielded Q1 2021, quota 25% UiPath respondents; it is still vendor-sponsored and its $55bn headline is a market FORECAST, not a measurement. Note also what is absent: not one vendor publishes a failure rate, so the only numbers with disclosed method describe wins by selected customers, which is survivorship bias by design.

claim: THE HONEST FINDING: there is no credible, methodologically-sound published figure for how often automation projects fail. Every widely-repeated candidate fails on provenance. EY 30-50% is a consultant's impression in a 2016 brochure with no method and admitted selection bias. Deloitte's 3%/4%/8% measures SCALE among self-selected clients, not failure, and changes yearly. Gartner's 25,000 hours is a savings model, not a failure rate, and is arithmetic from an assumption. Vendor ROI studies are commissioned composites whose own authors disclaim generalisation. The adjacent general IT-project benchmark, the Standish Group CHAOS report, is itself discredited in the peer-reviewed literature by Jorgensen & Molokken-Ostvold (2006), Glass (2006) and Eveleens & Verhoef (2010) for undisclosed study design, unstated project selection and unstated definitions of success and failure.
source: Synthesis of the primary sources traced in this pass: EY 2016 PDF, Deloitte 2016/2017/2018/2022 surveys, Gartner 2 October 2019 release, Forrester TEI and IDC US47905721; plus the peer-reviewed CHAOS critiques
note: THE PUBLISHABLE RESULT. State the gap, do not fill it with a number. The structural reason no honest figure exists is worth saying plainly: nobody who could measure automation failure has an incentive to publish it. The consultancies sell remediation, the vendors sell licences, the analysts sell advisory to both, and the enterprises that failed do not volunteer it. There is also no agreed DEFINITION of failure (abandoned? over budget? delivered but unused? scaled below plan?), so even an honest attempt would not be comparable across organisations. Safe formulations: 'EY, which sells RPA remediation, has said it has seen 30-50% of initial RPA projects fail, an estimate from consulting experience rather than a study'; 'in Deloitte's 2018 survey of 530 self-selected respondents, 4% were running more than 50 robots'. Unsafe: any bare percentage presented as the failure rate of automation projects. This record generalises the pattern already logged in reject-ai-failure-statistics and the MIT 95% case: repetition, not method, is what makes these numbers feel solid.

claim: Wewerka and Reichert, 'Robotic Process Automation: A Systematic Literature Review and Assessment Framework', Ulm University, arXiv:2012.11951, a systematic review of 63 publications, states: 'Furthermore, the literature covers only successful RPA projects, leaving room for further research on failed projects.' It also notes 'The positive effects are widely discussed in literature. Only a minority is critical towards RPA. One reason can be the novelty of RPA... due to which the technology is hyped.'
source: arXiv:2012.11951v1, systematic literature review of 63 publications, Institute of Databases and Information Systems, Ulm University
note: THE FINDING THAT UNDERCUTS EVERY AUTOMATION FAILURE STATISTIC IN CIRCULATION, including the ones competitors quote. The academic literature on RPA has a survivorship-bias problem that its own systematic reviewers acknowledge in print: anyone quoting a failure rate is quoting a number the research base is structurally incapable of producing. Pairs with the separate finding that the '30-50% of RPA projects fail' claim attributed to EY has no published methodology, sample size or definition of failure behind it. This is the honest centre of any post about whether automation works.

claim: Wiener, 'Human Factors of Advanced Technology (Glass Cockpit) Transport Aircraft', NASA Contractor Report 177528, June 1989, an empirical survey of line pilots at two airlines, found verbatim: 'Workload was not universally reduced. In fact it appeared that a paradox existed: workload seemed to be reduced when it was not heavy or critical, and may be increased by automation when it was already heavy or critical.' A pilot's own summary recorded in the report: 'Systems that relieve workload in one area tend to increase the workload in new areas.'
source: NASA Contractor Report 177528, 222 pages, downloaded from NASA NTRS and text-extracted
note: The EMPIRICAL backbone for the claim that automation handles the routine and leaves humans the exceptions: it helps most when help is least needed and least when it is most needed. A government research report based on field survey rather than theory or vendor material. ATTRIBUTION CORRECTION worth honouring: the phrase 'clumsy automation' is widely attributed to this report and does NOT appear in it, the only occurrence of 'clumsy' being unrelated. The traceable published use is Cook, Woods, McColligan and Howie (1991), NASA SOAR 90 proceedings. Cite Wiener for the FINDING and Cook et al. for the PHRASE.

claim: Wellmann, Stierle, Dunzer and Matzner, 'A framework to evaluate the viability of robotic process automation for business process activities', BPM 2020 (DOI 10.1007/978-3-030-58779-6_14), peer reviewed, defines thirteen criteria across five perspectives. Verbatim: 'Determinism is one of the most distinctive criteria to assess the viability of RPA. Deterministic activities consist of logical execution steps without any form of cognitive assessment.' On exceptions: 'Candidate processes suited for RPA show little or no amount of exceptions when tasks are being executed.' On stability: 'Maturity describes the frequency of changes to the logical execution flow of the process.' On data: 'Unstructured and hardly accessible data impedes RPA.' And the failure mechanism: 'A high failure rate might correspond to poor standardization, maturity or determinism as the causes for exceptions.' An independent systematic review from Ulm converges on the same list: 'the process to be automated shall be standardised, run in a stable environment, and only require limited exception handling.'
source: BPM 2020 RPA Forum, peer reviewed, preprint arXiv:2007.10900v2; Wewerka and Reichert arXiv:2012.11951
note: CORRECTS MY OWN HYPOTHESIS, which was that this would turn out to be practitioner folklore. It is not: two independent academic groups converge on volume, rule-clarity, low exception rate, stability and structured data. BUT the criteria are consensus-derived from prior literature and demonstrated on case data rather than validated against a cohort including failures, and per the survivorship finding that failure cohort essentially does not exist. So the honest published position is that the properties are well documented while their predictive power is not empirically established, and that distinction is itself the publishable point. The reviews also record a genuine contradiction between papers on whether unpredictable volume peaks suit RPA, which should be reported rather than smoothed over.

claim: Hammer, 'Reengineering Work: Don't Automate, Obliterate', Harvard Business Review, July-August 1990, pp.104-112, reprint 90406. Verbatim: 'heavy investments in information technology have delivered disappointing results, largely because companies tend to use technology to mechanize old ways of doing business. They leave the existing processes intact and use computers simply to speed them up.' And: 'It is time to stop paving the cow paths. Instead of embedding outdated processes in silicon and software, we should obliterate them and start over.'
source: Authentic HBR reprint PDF, verified by the Harvard copyright line
note: TIER 2 AND THE REASON MUST BE DISCLOSED WHEREVER IT IS CITED: Harvard Business Review is editorially reviewed rather than peer reviewed, and Hammer ran a consultancy selling the reengineering method the article prescribes. It is still a primary text rather than a secondary summary, and it is the origin of 'automating a bad process entrenches it'. CAUTION recorded by the researching agent: many web copies render a garbled course-summary version that paraphrases Hammer while presenting it as his words, so quote only from the reprint wording above.

claim: Endsley, 'Ironies of artificial intelligence', Ergonomics 66(11), 2023, pp.1656-1668, DOI 10.1080/00140139.2023.2243404, peer reviewed, published for the 40th anniversary of Bainbridge. Abstract verbatim from the PubMed record: 'Bainbridge's Ironies of Automation was a prescient description of automation related challenges for human performance that have characterised much of the 40 years since its publication. Today a new wave of automation based on artificial intelligence (AI) is being introduced across a wide variety of domains and applications. Not only are Bainbridge's original warnings still pertinent for AI, but AI's very nature and focus on cognitive tasks has introduced many new challenges for people who interact with it. Five ironies of AI are presented including difficulties with understanding AI and forming adaptations, opaqueness in AI limitations and biases that can drive human decision biases, and difficulties in understanding the AI reliability, despite the fact that AI remains insufficiently intelligent for many of its intended applications.'
source: Ergonomics 66(11) 2023; abstract quoted from the authoritative PubMed/NLM record, PMID 37534468
note: TIER 2 BECAUSE ONLY THE ABSTRACT WAS OBTAINED: Taylor and Francis returns 403 and Unpaywall confirms it is not open access, so the full text was not read. Quote the abstract only, and say it is the abstract. The conclusion that matters: the original ironies were not superseded by better technology, they transferred to AI and got worse, because AI automates cognitive rather than manual work. That is the bridge from a 1983 process-control paper to a 2026 AI agent, stated by a major figure in the field rather than by us.

claim: National Restaurant Association, Off-Premises Restaurant Trends 2025 (published 16 April 2025), p.18: 'Nearly 7 in 10 delivery customers (68%) ordered delivery using a third-party service in the past 6 months. This was much more common among Gen Z adults (79%) and millennials (78%) than baby boomers (42%).' But: 'in terms of how consumers would prefer to order delivery, 6 in 10 say directly through the restaurant.' Pull-quote: '61% of delivery customers prefer to order directly through the restaurant.' By generation, prefer direct: Gen Z 53%, millennial 52%, Gen X 67%, boomer 82%; rural 78% vs urban 53%.
source: National Restaurant Association, Off-Premises Restaurant Trends 2025, p.18
note: ASSOCIATION RESEARCH and the single most commercially useful finding for the restaurant section. 68% transact through a channel charging 15-30% commission while 61% say they would RATHER order direct. That gap is the addressable margin, and closing it needs a direct ordering channel, which is a web job, not an app job. LIMITATION: the NRA does not publish n or fieldwork dates, only 'surveys of restaurant operators and consumers, fielded by National Restaurant Association economists', so cite as association survey without asserting a sample size. IMPORTANT: a widely circulated '68% of consumers prefer ordering directly, NRA 2024' is a GARBLED version of this: the 68% is third-party USE, the preference figure is 61%. See reject record.

claim: National Restaurant Association, Off-Premises Restaurant Trends 2025: '3 - Median number of restaurant apps users have on their phones.' Ordering methods used in the past 6 months: mobile app 57%, in-person 57%, phone 39%, website 34%, social media 7%, text/SMS 6%. PREFERRED method: mobile app 35%, in-person 32%, phone call 17%, website 11%.
source: National Restaurant Association, Off-Premises Restaurant Trends 2025, pp.14-15
note: ASSOCIATION RESEARCH. The median of THREE restaurant apps is the hard constraint on the 'build an app' pitch: those three slots go to the largest chains and the marketplaces, so an independent restaurant is competing for a slot that is already full. ESSENTIAL CAVEAT, and it is easy to get wrong: the NRA instrument does NOT separate a restaurant's OWN app from a third-party marketplace app. Given 68% used third-party services, most of the 57% app usage is almost certainly DoorDash and Uber Eats. Do NOT cite the 57% or the 35% as demand for a bespoke restaurant app. Also note in-person ordering ties mobile app at 57%, and satisfaction with 'how easy it was to order and pay' is already 95%, the highest-rated attribute, while cost is lowest at 67%: ordering UX is not the unsolved problem, price is.

claim: National Restaurant Association, State of the Restaurant Industry 2026 (press release 12 February 2026): industry sales projected at $1.55 trillion, real growth 1.3%, employment 15.8 million. 42% of operators reported their restaurant was not profitable last year, 60% reported softer traffic, and more than 9 in 10 cite food, labor, insurance, energy and swipe fees as challenges.
source: National Restaurant Association, State of the Restaurant Industry 2026 press release
note: ASSOCIATION RESEARCH. The 42%-unprofitable figure is the strongest available framing for why a 15-30% commission line, or a five-figure app build, is not a neutral decision for a restaurant. LIMITATION: the press release contains NO technology adoption percentages and the full report is paywalled at shop.restaurant.org, so no adoption stat may be cited from this source. The release names digital ordering, payments, loyalty, automation and targeted marketing as investment areas and does NOT single out native apps.

claim: Large chains publish loyalty SHARE of revenue, never incremental lift. Starbucks (investor release, 29 January 2026): 'With Starbucks Rewards driving nearly 60% of U.S. company-operated revenue in fiscal 2025'. Q3 FY2026 call (7 August 2026): '90-day active Starbucks Rewards members grew both quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year to 35.8 million.' McDonald's (Q2 2026 earnings release, Exhibit 99.1 filed with the SEC, 4 August 2026): 'Across 70 loyalty markets, Systemwide sales to loyalty members for the trailing twelve months increased over 20% to $40 billion' and '90-day active loyalty users up 13% to nearly 220 million as of quarter-end'. NO SEC filing or peer-reviewed study located isolates incremental revenue lift with a control group.
source: Starbucks investor relations 29 Jan 2026 and Q3 FY2026 earnings call 7 Aug 2026; McDonald's Q2 2026 Exhibit 99.1 filed with the SEC 4 Aug 2026
note: PLATFORM-PUBLISHED, and the finding is the DISTINCTION, which is the exact error the agency tier makes. A customer who would have bought anyway and who scans a loyalty ID converts previously anonymous revenue into attributed 'loyalty revenue' while adding nothing. Share-of-revenue is not causal lift. VERIFIED AS NOT PUBLISHED: there is no citable public evidence that a restaurant loyalty app CAUSES incremental revenue. Also note the scale mismatch: these are the largest restaurant companies on earth with nine-figure app budgets, not an analogy an independent restaurant can act on. DO NOT USE the circulating 'Starbucks members spend 2.5-3x more than non-members': it was not in the Q3 FY2026 transcript and could not be sourced to any filing.

claim: Al-Turbag M, Mooney M, Corry M, 'A systematic review and meta-analysis of appointment reminders for enhancing hospital attendance', Journal of Hospital Management and Health Policy 2026;10:2, doi 10.21037/jhmhp-25-51. Ten studies, 8,236 total participants. Reminders versus no reminders: RR 1.11 (95% CI 1.05-1.19). SMS subgroup: RR 1.14 (95% CI 0.99-1.31), 4 studies, 4,636 participants. Telephone subgroup: RR 1.11 (95% CI 1.04-1.19), 5 studies, 3,369 participants. Authors: 'This systematic review and meta-analysis provide evidence that appointment reminders-particularly SMS messages and telephone calls are beneficial in improving out-patient attendance rates in hospital settings.'
source: Journal of Hospital Management and Health Policy 2026;10:2, peer-reviewed meta-analysis
note: ACADEMIC, peer-reviewed, 2026, with pooled effect sizes and confidence intervals. PRECISION REQUIRED: the SMS subgroup CI CROSSES 1.0 (0.99-1.31), so SMS alone did NOT reach statistical significance here, while telephone did. Honest claim: reminders overall give a modest, statistically significant ~11% relative improvement in attendance; SMS trends positive but was not significant in this analysis. Do not write 'SMS reminders cut no-shows by X%' from this paper. COMMERCIALLY DECISIVE for the clinic section: the intervention with genuine trial-grade evidence behind it is SMS and telephone, neither of which needs an app OR a website. The older McLean et al. meta-analysis reporting 23% more likely to attend was NOT fetched and must be verified before any number from it is quoted.

claim: NO EVIDENCE EXISTS that patients want a clinic-specific native app. No peer-reviewed study, ASTP brief or government survey compares patient preference for a single clinic's own branded app against web access. The contrary signal is explicit in ASTP Data Brief 77, which states that 'prior work has shown patients overwhelmingly utilize patient portal apps from EHR developers (e.g., Epic's MyChart), health care organizations, and insurers.' Despite 59% of individuals holding multiple portals, only 7% used a portal-organising app to combine them, up from 2% in 2022.
source: ASTP/ONC Data Brief 77 (July 2025); absence confirmed by searches of JMIR, PMC, JAMA-adjacent journals and ASTP briefs
note: A VERIFIED NEGATIVE, and the cleanest one in the set. This is publishable exactly as stated: the evidence does not exist, and the evidence that DOES exist points the other way. The rising 57% app-based access figure is NOT demand for a clinic's own app: the winning app is MyChart, the EHR vendor's, which a clinic obtains by choosing an EHR rather than by commissioning a build. For an individual clinic the app question is an EHR-SELECTION question, not a development question. The 7% organiser-app figure strengthens it: patients are not seeking out extra healthcare apps even when portal fragmentation gives them an obvious reason to.

claim: ASTP/ONC Data Brief 77, Figure 3, using HINTS 7 (2024): 'In 2024, nearly all individuals who were offered online access to their medical records reported being encouraged by their HCP to use their patient portal (89%).' 'Eighty-seven percent (87%) of individuals encouraged by their HCP accessed their patient portal at least once in the past year compared to just 57% of those not encouraged.' 'Individuals encouraged by their HCP to use their patient portal viewed test results and clinical notes at higher rates compared to those not encouraged (92% vs. 78% and 82% vs. 57%, respectively).' HINTS 7 methodology: fielded as paper and web survey March to September 2024, two-stage stratified address sample, 'Complete data were collected from 7,278 respondents. The final overall response rate was 27.31%. All results were weighted to account for non-response and generate national estimates.'
source: Richwine C, ASTP/ONC Data Brief 77, July 2025, Figure 3 and methodology note
note: FEDERAL SURVEY DATA with full methodology: n=7,278, 27.31% response rate, weighted to national estimates. THE BEST SINGLE ARGUMENT IN THE WHOLE ARTICLE that process beats software: a 30-point adoption swing (87% vs 57%) driven entirely by whether staff mention the portal, on technology the clinic already owns. A clinic weighing an app build against telling the front desk to mention the portal has measured evidence for the second. Supersedes the incomplete methodology note on the earlier onc-patient-portal-2024 record, which said the sample size was not stated: it IS stated, and is recorded here.

claim: '68% of consumers prefer ordering directly from the restaurant (National Restaurant Association, 2024)'
source: restaurant-tech and POS vendor blogs; traced against the actual NRA report
note: REJECTED AND RECORDED SO IT CANNOT RESURFACE. It is a garbled restatement of two genuine NRA figures on the same page: 68% is the share who USED a third-party service, and the preference figure is 61%. Dangerous precisely because it cites a real and authoritative body, so a writer can land on it in good faith. Use 61% and cite p.18 of Off-Premises Restaurant Trends 2025. Also rejected from the same vendor tier, none traceable to a named study: 'true cost reaches 35-48% of revenue', '58% of customers prefer a restaurant's own app', '89% of patients want to schedule appointments online' (traces to Experian Health marketing), '70% use Google products for local business', '92% read reviews', and 'food near me open now up 875%'.

claim: There is NO authoritative, methodologically disclosed study quantifying what share of restaurant customers discover a restaurant via search and maps versus via a delivery app. The most-cited figure, '62% of consumers discover restaurants on Google', traces to a single source: PYMNTS, 'Connected Dining: Word of Mouth in the Digital Age', May 2023, a census-balanced panel survey of more than 2,200 US consumers, which states '62% of restaurant customers use Google to search for restaurant, a greater share than said the same of any other digital platform.' Google publishes no restaurant-specific discovery share.
source: PYMNTS Connected Dining, May 2023; absence of better sources confirmed by search
note: VENDOR WITH DISCLOSED METHODOLOGY (n>2,200, census-balanced), usable ONLY with attribution and two caveats: it measures USE OF GOOGLE TO SEARCH, not discovery-channel share, and it does not compare against apps. It is also three years old. PUBLISH THE GAP HONESTLY: this is a question the article should say is not well evidenced, rather than filling it with an agency statistic. Everything else in this space (70% use Google products for local business, 51% cite Google as best platform, 94% use online resources) appears only on SEO-agency and restaurant-tech blogs with no traceable study and is rejected.

claim: Neither Apple nor Google publishes app retention or store-conversion BENCHMARK NUMBERS. Both publish only metric definitions plus in-console peer comparisons visible to the individual developer. Apple's App Store Connect analytics defines 'Conversion Rate: Total downloads and pre-orders divided by unique device impressions' and 'Active in Last 30 Days: The number of active devices with at least one session during the previous 30 days', but states no day-1/7/30 retention benchmark. Google Play Console Help defines 'Conversion Rate: The percentage of store listing visitors who clicked on a button (Install, Open, or Pre-register)' and says developers 'can compare your daily conversion performance to your peers' median, 25th and 75th percentile', with 'Benchmark data is only shown if there is sufficient data from your selected peer set'. No figures are published.
source: Apple App Store Connect Analytics metrics definitions; Google Play Console Help; Android Developers Blog 2 Mar 2021
note: A VERIFIED NEGATIVE, confirmed by reading both platforms' own documentation, and it is the honest answer to item 2. The industry's entire retention consensus rests on VENDOR TELEMETRY: no platform-published and no independent representative dataset exists for commercial app retention. PUBLISHABLE SECONDARY POINT: Apple's conversion-rate denominator is unique IMPRESSIONS while Google Play's is store listing VISITORS, so the two platforms' 'conversion rates' are not comparable, and any article comparing them directly is making an apples-to-oranges error. Also note the circularity worth stating: a business cannot benchmark its store conversion without already having shipped an app.

claim: Kidman PG, Curtis RG, Watson A, Maher CA, 'When and Why Adults Abandon Lifestyle Behavior and Mental Health Mobile Apps: Scoping Review', Journal of Medical Internet Research, 18 December 2024, DOI 10.2196/56897. Scoping review of 18 eligible peer-reviewed studies, 525,824 total participants, studies published 2014-2022, predominantly US, Canada, UK and Germany. Headline finding: 'A median of 70% of users discontinued use within the first 100 days.' Abandonment is curvilinear, sharpest immediately after acquisition. By domain: physical activity apps 54-75% abandonment, mental health apps 89-92%, alcohol apps 95-97%, smoking apps 40%. Stated limitation: 'methodological diversity across studies, particularly in measurement and terminology used to describe app abandonment.'
source: Journal of Medical Internet Research, peer-reviewed scoping review, Dec 2024
note: ACADEMIC and the ONLY independent peer-reviewed measurement of app abandonment found. USE CAVEAT that must not be dropped: this is HEALTH AND LIFESTYLE apps only, so it must never be presented as an all-category retention figure. Its value is that it was produced by a completely different method from vendor telemetry, with different biases, and points the same way, which is stronger evidence than either alone. Pair it with the AppsFlyer Android uninstall figure but keep the two visually and verbally distinct: never merge them into a single curve.

claim: AppsFlyer App Uninstall Report, 2025 edition: day-30 uninstall rate 46.1% in 2024, against 46.9% in 2023. The report states 'more than 1 in every 2 apps that are installed are uninstalled within 30 days.' Sample: 2,200 apps, 402 million uninstalls, 1.3 billion installs, top 40 markets, January 2023 to November 2024 for trends and August-September 2024 for category benchmarks. ANDROID ONLY: iOS is excluded because uninstall tracking was curtailed after iOS 15. AppsFlyer's benchmarks FAQ states its data comes from 'integrations with leading media partners, as well as our proprietary SDK implemented in our clients' apps' and that 'In the Performance Benchmarks section, the top and bottom 10% of values for the selected metric are excluded.'
source: AppsFlyer App Uninstall Report 2025 edition; AppsFlyer benchmarks methodology FAQ
note: VENDOR DATA, but the best-documented vendor source found because it publishes its sample. FOUR CAVEATS, all of which must travel with the number. (1) ANDROID ONLY, so it supports no cross-platform claim. (2) The sample is apps that BOUGHT ATTRIBUTION SOFTWARE, which AppsFlyer states in its own words: the app had a budget and a growth team, so the unfunded small-business app is invisible to this dataset. (3) Top and bottom 10% are EXCLUDED, so the published figure is the middle 80% of an already-selected sample and the true population figure is almost certainly worse. (4) The vendor sells products that fix retention, so a retention crisis is its market. Net effect: vendor retention benchmarks are CEILINGS, not averages. Use the measured 46.1%, and attribute the 'more than 1 in 2' phrasing as the report's own rounding.

claim: Google / Ipsos, 'How people discover, use, and stay engaged with apps', fielded October 2016, 15-minute online questionnaire, US smartphone users aged 16-64, N=999, quotas on age, gender, education and internet usage frequency. 'On average, users have 35 apps installed on their smartphone' and '52% of those apps are used at least weekly.' Q5 asked whether respondents had used a mobile website or an app for each task in the last 30 days. APP wins: play games 91%/13%, track physical activity 87%/14%, stay organised 84%/15%, listen to music 80%/24%, navigation 80%/21%, manage finances 79%/30%, check weather 76%/27%. MOBILE WEB wins: shop 53%/70%, find discounts and offers 52%/68%, read or watch news 50%/58%, organise travel 50%/60%, find things to do or places to eat locally 45%/65%, order takeout 43%/64%, search or browse the internet 29%/79%. Abandonment reasons include 'I no longer had a need for that particular app' 55%, 'I needed to free up memory' 53%, and 'I forgot I had the app' 22%.
source: Google / Ipsos, Think with Google, October 2016, N=999
note: PLATFORM-PUBLISHED, INDEPENDENTLY FIELDED BY IPSOS, read from the primary PDF with methodology on the page. THE SINGLE BEST SOURCE FOR THIS ARTICLE'S THESIS, because the split is clean and it comes from Google rather than from us: APPS win for repeated personal utility, MOBILE WEB wins for browsing, discovery, local search, ordering takeout and transacting. Every business type in this article sits on the mobile-web side of that line. MUST BE DATE-STAMPED IN THE COPY: it was fielded in October 2016 and is nearly ten years old. It is used because nothing more recent has equivalent methodological transparency, and that absence is itself worth a sentence. Do not present it as current.

claim: Sensor Tower State of Mobile 2026 (published January 2026, press release 21 January 2026), covering calendar year 2025: 'Total downloads across iOS and Google Play edged up 0.8% YoY to nearly 150 billion', while 'Global IAP revenue in particular surged 10.6% year over year (YoY) to reach $167 billion' and 'Consumers spent 5.3 trillion hours across iOS and Google Play apps (+3.8% YoY)'. Non-game IAP revenue climbed 21% year on year, exceeding gaming spend for the first time.
source: Sensor Tower, 2026 State of Mobile, January 2026
note: VENDOR DATA. The reading that matters and that most agency content inverts: downloads are FLAT (+0.8% is within noise) while spend is up 10.6% and time up 3.8%. The install market is saturated. The same apps are used more and monetised harder; the number of new installs is not expanding. METHODOLOGY GAP TO STATE: no panel size, estimation model or confidence interval is disclosed on the blog post, press release or report landing page, so these are MODELLED ESTIMATES, not measured totals, and they exclude third-party Android stores entirely, which matters hugely for China. SUPERSEDES the earlier app-downloads-declining record (106.9 billion, down 2.7%), which used a different and narrower basis: do not cite both, and note the two figures are not comparable because 'downloads' is defined differently.

claim: Adjust retention benchmarks, commonly circulated as day 1 26%, day 7 13%, day 30 7%, with iOS and Android splits
source: search snippets only; adjust.com returned HTTP 429 on six URL attempts on 11 Sep 2026
note: NOT SAFE TO PUBLISH. adjust.com blocks automated fetching and returned HTTP 429 on every one of six URLs tried, so no Adjust figure could be verified against the primary source. The snippets are also self-contradictory on sample, describing it as both 'thousands of apps' and 'hundreds of apps'. Adjust's 2026 report is additionally co-branded with Google Ads, Snap, TikTok, Sensor Tower and Roku, all commercially interested contributors. EITHER a human opens the page and captures the figure with its methodology, OR Adjust is omitted entirely and the retention section leads with the AppsFlyer uninstall report plus the JMIR review, both of which are fully documented. Recorded in DEAD-ENDS terms: adjust.com is not fetchable by this toolchain.

claim: No app store listing view-to-install conversion benchmark exists in citable form. Apple and Google restrict benchmarks to in-console peer comparison and publish no figures; AppsFlyer's benchmarks tool is interactive and returns no figures to a fetch. Every public figure encountered came from agency blogs recirculating vendor numbers without methodology. Separately, no cost-per-install benchmark with disclosed methodology was found from an approved vendor. AppsFlyer publishes only aggregate install ad spend, projected at $94.9 billion for 2025 (last updated 19 October 2025), itself a modelled extrapolation resting on a stated 5-10% estimate for the unmeasured market and a 2022 third-party input for China.
source: Apple and Google developer documentation; AppsFlyer install ad spend article and its stated methodology
note: A VERIFIED NEGATIVE and directly responsive to item 2. State it plainly: the install-funnel drop-off numbers the article was asked to find DO NOT EXIST in credible published form. SUPERSEDES the earlier app-install-economics record, which held circulating USD 2.49 and 2.25 cost-per-install figures as unverified: they remain unverified and no approved source publishes a CPI benchmark. If an order-of-magnitude is wanted, $94.9bn spend against roughly 150bn total downloads is about $0.63 per download industry-wide, and far higher per PAID install once organic installs are removed, but this must be labelled as our own arithmetic on two vendor figures and never as a published benchmark.

claim: On primary platform documentation, the cases where native is genuinely required reduce to a short and checkable list rather than a matter of opinion. (1) PHYSICAL DEVICE ACCESS: Web Bluetooth, Web NFC, WebUSB and Web Serial are all unavailable on iOS Safari, and Apple has formally recorded 'position: oppose' on Web Bluetooth, so this is a stated refusal rather than a pending implementation. (2) BACKGROUND EXECUTION: Background Sync, Periodic Background Sync and Background Fetch are all unavailable on iOS, so work that must continue with the app closed, including continuous location tracking, cannot be done. (3) DISTRIBUTION AND DISCOVERY through the app stores themselves. Google's Project Fugu, the cross-browser effort whose stated objective is 'making it possible for web apps to do anything iOS, Android, or desktop apps can', was described by Chrome's own Thomas Steiner on 4 October 2022 as 'far from being done'.
source: MDN browser-compat-data queried 11 Sep 2026; WebKit standards-positions issue #570 (2 Dec 2025); Chrome for Developers, 'Is Project Fugu done?', 4 Oct 2022; Chromium Project Fugu documentation
note: SYNTHESIS FROM PRIMARY DOCS, which is the only honest way to answer item 4: no engineer's essay was found that is both current and authoritative enough to carry the claim, so the argument is built from capability documentation instead, and is stronger for it. The test a business can actually apply: does the product need to talk to physical hardware over Bluetooth, NFC, USB or serial, or does it need to keep working while closed? If neither, no documented capability requires native. Note the asymmetry worth publishing: most of these gaps are iOS-specific, since Chrome on Android ships Bluetooth, NFC, USB and background sync, so 'the web cannot do it' usually means 'Apple has chosen not to allow it'. Chrome's 'far from done' admission is dated 2022 and should be cited with that date.

claim: Apple's App Store Review Guidelines supply a decision rule from the platform vendor itself. Guideline 4.2: 'Your app should include features, content, and UI that elevate it beyond a repackaged website. If your app is not particularly useful, unique, or "app-like," it doesn't belong on the App Store.' Guideline 4.2.2: 'Other than catalogs, apps shouldn't primarily be marketing materials, advertisements, web clippings, content aggregators, or a collection of links.' Read against the capability evidence, a business whose proposed app would contain the same menu, booking form or service pages as its website is describing something Apple's published rules say does not belong on the App Store.
source: Apple App Store Review Guidelines 4.2 and 4.2.2
note: THE ARTICLE'S CLOSING ARGUMENT. It reframes the question from taste ('do you want an app?') to policy ('would this be allowed, and should it exist?'), and it comes from the party that profits when apps exist, which removes the suspicion of agency self-interest running the other way. Especially effective against the WebView-wrapper pitch, where a small business is sold 'your app' that is its website in a shell: that is the precise thing 4.2 names. Duplicate-ish with apple-guideline-4-2-repackaged-website, which holds the same quotes; keep both only if one is the evidence record and this one the argument record, otherwise cite the earlier id.

claim: Gartner press release, 25 June 2025, 'Gartner Predicts Over 40% of Agentic AI Projects Will Be Canceled by End of 2027' (SYDNEY, Australia, June 25, 2025), states verbatim: 'Many vendors are contributing to the hype by engaging in “agent washing” – the rebranding of existing products, such as AI assistants, robotic process automation (RPA) and chatbots, without substantial agentic capabilities. Gartner estimates only about 130 of the thousands of agentic AI vendors are real.'
