Headline prediction verbatim: 'Over 40% of agentic AI projects will be canceled by the end of 2027, due to escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls, according to Gartner, Inc.' Named analyst Anushree Verma, Senior Director Analyst. The only disclosed methodology in the release is a separate January 2025 Gartner poll of 3,412 webinar attendees on investment posture; NO methodology is published for the 130 figure or the 40% prediction.
source: Gartner press release 25 June 2025, read in full via Wayback Machine snapshot of gartner.com (gartner.com itself returns HTTP 403 to automated clients)
note: ARCHIVED PRIMARY, not a reproduction: wording confirmed character for character including the en dash in the agent washing sentence. Analyst estimate with NO published methodology for the 130 figure: no sample frame, no inclusion criteria, no definition of the 'thousands' denominator. Must be framed as a Gartner estimate, never as a measurement. Do not attribute the 40% prediction to Verma; it is a firm forecast. Do not use RCR Wireless's paraphrase as a Gartner quote.

claim: US default: a contractor, not the commissioning buyer, owns copyright in commissioned software absent a written assignment. 17 U.S.C. §101 defines a work made for hire as '(1) a work prepared by an employee within the scope of his or her employment' or '(2) a work specially ordered or commissioned for use as a contribution to a collective work, as a part of a motion picture or other audiovisual work, as a translation, as a supplementary work, as a compilation, as an instructional text, as a test, as answer material for a test, or as an atlas, if the parties expressly agree in a written instrument signed by them that the work shall be considered a work made for hire.' SOFTWARE IS NOT AMONG THE NINE CATEGORIES. US Copyright Office Circular 30 (rev. 08/2024) states four criteria and: 'If a work fails to satisfy any of these requirements, it is not a work made for hire.' Its questionnaire: 'question 3: Is there a written agreement between the commissioning party and the creator of the work? ... No? The work is not a work made for hire.'
source: 17 U.S.C. §101 (Cornell LII) and US Copyright Office Circular 30, 'Works Made for Hire', revised 08/2024, read in full from copyright.gov PDF
note: OFFICIAL PRIMARY, quoted verbatim from the statute and the Copyright Office's own circular. The load-bearing point for buyers: custom software is not one of the nine enumerated categories, so a 'work made for hire' clause alone can FAIL for software. The reliable instrument is a written ASSIGNMENT of copyright. CCNV v. Reid, 490 U.S. 730, decided 5 June 1989, supplies the employee-vs-contractor agency test.

claim: UK default: the contractor owns copyright in commissioned work. Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 s.11: '(1) The author of a work is the first owner of any copyright in it, subject to the following provisions. (2) Where a literary, dramatic, musical or artistic work, or a film, is made by an employee in the course of his employment, his employer is the first owner of any copyright in the work subject to any agreement to the contrary.' The Act contains NO commissioned-works provision. UK Intellectual Property Office guidance 'Ownership of copyright works' states verbatim: 'When you ask or commission another person or organisation to create a copyright work for you, the first legal owner of copyright is the person or organisation that created the work and not you the commissioner, unless you otherwise agree it in writing.'
source: CDPA 1988 s.11 (legislation.gov.uk) and UK Intellectual Property Office guidance 'Ownership of copyright works', published 19 August 2014
note: OFFICIAL PRIMARY, both the statute and the IPO's own guidance quoted verbatim. Software counts as a literary work under the CDPA. Same practical upshot as the US via a different route: without a written assignment the agency keeps the copyright, and the buyer may get only an implied licence. Robin Ray v Classic FM [1998] FSR 622 (Lightman J) is the leading authority on implied licence and the minimalist approach, but BAILII and CaseMine both returned 403, so the judgment text was NOT reached; corroborated only via CMS and secondary summaries.

claim: The Standish CHAOS figures should not be cited as evidence of software project failure rates. Eveleens and Verhoef (IEEE Software, Jan/Feb 2010, pp.30-36), using 5,457 forecasts of 1,211 real-world projects, find the Standish definitions 'are misleading, one-sided, pervert the estimation practice, and result in meaningless figures' and demonstrate that with the opposite institutional bias 'Landmark Graphics would improve its Standish success rate from 6 percent to 94 percent'. Standish chairman Jim Johnson told them all Standish data 'should be considered Standish opinion and the reader bears all risk in the use of this opinion', a disclaimer the authors say 'to our knowledge was never stated in the Chaos reports'. Jorgensen and Molokken (Information and Software Technology 48(4), 2006) could find no definition of the cost overrun measure at all: 'we were unable to find an explicit definition of the cost overrun measure applied in the CHAOS reports.' The 1994 sample was 365 surveys recruited by asking executives 'to share failure stories'. Peer-reviewed surveys of the same era show ~30-34% average overrun (Jenkins 1984 34%, Phan 1988 33%, Bergeron 1992 33%), against Standish's 189%.
source: Eveleens & Verhoef, 'The Rise and Fall of the Chaos Report Figures', IEEE Software 2010; Jorgensen & Molokken, 'How Large Are Software Cost Overruns? A Review of the 1994 CHAOS Report', Information and Software Technology 48(4), 2006. Both PDFs read in full.
note: PEER-REVIEWED, both read at primary source. NEVER-USE flag on the Standish figures (16% success, 189% overrun, '70% of IT projects fail'). Three independent evidence streams converge near 30% average overrun (Jorgensen's table, Flyvbjerg's 27%, Eveleens); Standish is the outlier and its method is undisclosed. Jorgensen's honest limitation should be reproduced: the paper does not PROVE the 189% is biased, because Standish will not release the data.

claim: Gartner, 12 July 2022 (STAMFORD, Conn.): 'Fifty-six percent of organizations said they had a high degree of purchase regret over their largest tech-related purchase in the last two years'. Methodology disclosed verbatim: 'In November and December 2021, Gartner surveyed 1,120 respondents in North America, Western Europe and Asia/Pacific', respondents 'required to be at a manager level or higher ... and directly involved in the evaluation or selection'. Hank Barnes, verbatim: 'The survey found that the organizations that indicated they had high regret for their purchase took, on average, 7 to 10 months longer to complete that purchase.' Also '67% of people involved in technology-buying decisions are not in IT'. Separately, Gartner 14 June 2023: 60% of technology buyers involved in renewal or expansion decisions 'regret nearly every purchase they make, a 6% increase from 2020', from a survey 'from February through March 2023 among 1,503 respondents from organizations with an annual revenue of at least $50 million'.
source: Gartner press releases 12 July 2022 and 14 June 2023, both read in full via Wayback Machine snapshots of gartner.com
note: ARCHIVED PRIMARY with disclosed methodology (analyst tier, not peer-reviewed; sampling frame and questionnaire not published). These are TWO DIFFERENT studies measuring different populations and must not be conflated. The '7 to 10 months longer' finding is the most useful: regret tracks a slow painful buying process, not just a bad product.

claim: Avelino, Passos, Hora and Valente, 'A Novel Approach for Estimating Truck Factors' (ICPC 2016), studied 133 popular GitHub systems (over 373K files, 41 MLOC, over 2 million commits) and found 'the majority of our target systems (65%) have TF <= 2'. In the body: 46 systems (34%) have TF = 1 (e.g. mbostock/d3, less/less.js) and 42 systems (31%) have TF = 2. Highest were torvalds/linux TF = 57, fzaninotto/Faker TF = 23, php/php-src TF = 18, git/git TF = 12, v8/v8 TF = 11, rails/rails TF = 9.
source: Avelino et al., ICPC 2016, PDF read in full from the authors' university page
note: PEER-REVIEWED, read at primary source. CORRECTION TRAP: search snippets and secondary write-ups state '46% have TF=1 and 28% have TF=2'. The paper says 34% and 31% (46 systems, not 46 percent). Use 34/31/65, never 46/28.

claim: Herbsleb and Mockus, 'An Empirical Study of Speed and Communication in Globally Distributed Software Development', IEEE TSE 29(6), June 2003, pp.481-494. Abstract verbatim: 'One key finding is that distributed work items appear to take about two and one-half times as long to complete as similar items where all the work is colocated.' Raw figures: single-site MRs about five days, 'MRs which involved more than one site took 12.7 days, more than 2.5 times as long, to complete. The difference is statistically significant (p < 0.001) using a t-test.' Department B replication: seven days vs 18 days. CRITICAL CAVEAT, verbatim from the paper: 'Surprisingly, given all other factors, distributed MRs do not have significantly longer intervals than single-site MRs. A replication of this model using data from Department B also did not show an effect for distributed versus same-site MR intervals, given all the other factors in the model.' The authors' mechanism: 'It appears that splitting work across sites slows the work down primarily because it requires the involvement of more people than comparable work accomplished all at one site.'
source: Herbsleb & Mockus, IEEE Transactions on Software Engineering 29(6), June 2003. Full PDF read directly.
note: PEER-REVIEWED, read at primary source and the regression caveat independently confirmed. NEVER cite the 2.5x figure without the caveat: under multiple regression the distributed variable was NOT significant. The paper does NOT support 'offshore teams are inherently 2.5x slower'; it supports 'distributing work pulls more people into each change, and headcount per change drives delay'. Sample: 2,227 modification requests, Lucent, July 1997 to July 1999. DATE THE DATA: pre-broadband, pre-modern-CI.

claim: NEVER-USE list. Every widely circulated offshore failure-rate and cost-savings percentage tested in Sept 2026 failed verification. (1) '60% of outsourced projects fail because of poor cultural compatibility': no named source, no hyperlink, agency blogs citing each other. (2) '59% of companies report dissatisfaction with offshore outcomes, Deloitte 2024 Global Outsourcing Survey': MISATTRIBUTION, Deloitte's official 2024 survey page contains no such figure. (3) 'Gartner found 67% of offshore projects require significant rework': no Gartner report title, ID or date locatable. (4) 'Only 23% achieve successful offshore partnerships (Accelerance)': source is an offshore brokerage, vendor marketing by definition. (5) '90% of companies fail at offshore development': untraceable marketing copy, published by offshore vendors selling offshore services. (6) Generic 'offshore saves 40-60%' or '70%': no independent basis found. The only traceable dataset measuring realised savings against a prior baseline (Ventoro 2004/2005, 5,231 executives polled, seller-adjacent and self-assessed) found average savings BELOW 10% across all engagements, 19% after excluding self-declared failures, and stated that expecting 50%+ 'is not being realistic'. (7) No headline extra-cost PERCENTAGE exists in Dibbern, Winkler and Heinzl (MIS Quarterly 2008); it is a qualitative six-case study coding extra costs high/medium/low. Any percentage attributed to it is fabricated.
source: Direct fetch and attribution-checking of each claim's cited source, September 2026
note: THE HONEST FINDING for the offshore section: the quantitative claims in this space are almost entirely seller-written and untraceable, and one is attributed to a named report that demonstrably does not contain it. Publishing that absence is the valuable move. Contrast with the genuinely credible peer-reviewed distributed-development literature (Herbsleb, Dibbern, MacCormack), which exists and is good but is dated 2001-2012.

claim: US Government Accountability Office, GAO-06-5, 'Offshoring of Services: An Overview of the Issues', released 28 November 2005, states verbatim: 'Determining appropriate policy responses to the offshoring phenomenon is challenging due to the limited state of knowledge about the extent and impacts of offshoring.' GAO also notes federal statistics provide limited information on the level and effects of offshoring. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics Mass Layoff Statistics series, which tracked relocation of work from January 2004, was DISCONTINUED in 2013, leaving no current equivalent series.
source: GAO-06-5, US Government Accountability Office, 28 November 2005
note: OFFICIAL. An official auditor stating that the outcome data does not exist. This is the cleanest citation for the 'nobody can actually measure this' argument, and it is far stronger than any counter-statistic because it comes from a government body with no stake in the answer.

claim: Michael C. Feathers, 'Working Effectively with Legacy Code' (Prentice Hall PTR, 2004), Preface, verbatim: 'To me, legacy code is simply code without tests. I've gotten some grief for this definition. What do tests have to do with whether code is bad? To me, the answer is straightforward, and it is a point that I elaborate throughout the book: Code without tests is bad code. It doesn't matter how well written it is; it doesn't matter how pretty or object-oriented or well-encapsulated it is. With tests, we can change the behavior of our code quickly and verifiably. Without them, we really don't know if our code is getting better or worse.' Preceding sentence: 'In the industry, legacy code is often used as a slang term for difficult-to-change code that we don't understand. But over years of working with teams, helping them get past serious code problems, I've arrived at a different definition.'
source: Pearson/Prentice Hall official sample pages PDF for ISBN 9780131177055, read directly
note: PRACTITIONER BOOK, quoted verbatim from the PUBLISHER'S own PDF, so page-level attribution is solid (Preface). The reframe that matters for a buyer: an inherited codebase is legacy on day one if it has no tests, regardless of age or how clean it looks. Makes 'is there a test suite' the first due-diligence question, not a nice-to-have.

claim: Ward Cunningham, 'The WyCash Portfolio Management System', OOPSLA '92 experience report, dated 26 March 1992, section 'Consequences', verbatim: 'Shipping first time code is like going into debt. A little debt speeds development so long as it is paid back promptly with a rewrite. Objects make the cost of this transaction tolerable. The danger occurs when the debt is not repaid. Every minute spent on not-quite-right code counts as interest on that debt. Entire engineering organizations can be brought to a stand-still under the debt load of an unconsolidated implementation, object-oriented or otherwise.'
source: Ward Cunningham's canonical page c2.com, read directly; also ACM DL 10.1145/157709.157715
note: PRIMARY, author's own canonical text. The final clause 'object-oriented or otherwise' is usually truncated in secondary retellings. KEY CORRECTION for the article: Cunningham's metaphor was never about sloppy code, it was about code encoding an out-of-date UNDERSTANDING of the problem. That is precisely what a buyer inherits when an agency leaves: not bad code, but someone else's superseded mental model with nobody left to explain it.

claim: Kruchten, Nord and Ozkaya (two of three at Carnegie Mellon SEI), 'Technical Debt: From Metaphor to Theory and Practice', IEEE Software 29(6), Nov/Dec 2012, pp.18-21. Verbatim p.20: 'It's important to keep in mind, however, that technical debt is not only about code and code quality. Code analysis tools will identify a small number of the black elements. Therefore, code analysis tools aren't sufficient for identifying technical debt: more often than not, technical debt isn't related to code and its intrinsic qualities but to structural or architectural choices or to technological gaps. No tool will reveal that, two years ago, the team should have used some tool to internationalize and localize the code.' Figure 1 (p.19), 'The technical debt landscape', splits debt into VISIBLE (new features, defects, low external quality) and MOSTLY INVISIBLE (architectural debt, structural debt, test debt, DOCUMENTATION DEBT, low internal quality, code complexity, code smells, coding style violations).
source: Kruchten, Nord & Ozkaya, IEEE Software 2012, SEI-hosted PDF read directly
note: PEER-REVIEWED / SEI OFFICIAL. The single best citation for 'you cannot see what you are inheriting' and for why running a static-analysis tool over a codebase is NOT technical due diligence. Documentation debt is explicitly named as invisible.

claim: Coelho and Valente, 'Why Modern Open Source Projects Fail', ESEC/FSE 2017, surveyed maintainers of 104 popular deprecated GitHub systems. Failure reasons (Table 2, sums to 110 as projects can fail for multiple reasons): usurped by competitor 27, obsolete 20, lack of time 18, lack of interest 18, outdated technologies 14, low maintainability 7, conflicts among developers 3, legal problems 2, acquisition 1. Grouped: project characteristics 41, project team 39, environment 30. 'Lack of time' and 'lack of interest' attach specifically to THE MAIN CONTRIBUTOR. Developer quotes verbatim: 'I was the only maintainer and there was a lot of feature requests and I didn't have enough time.' (D115); 'My interest began to wane; I moved to other projects.' (D67); 'I was fired by the company that owns the project.' (D65). Of 3 projects that attempted transfer to new maintainers, only 2 actually found a new developer who assumed the project; 69% of respondents reported no funding.
source: Coelho & Valente, ESEC/FSE 2017, arXiv:1707.02327, PDF read directly
note: PEER-REVIEWED. Directly on-topic for 'what happens when the people leave'. Maintenance-practice contrast (failed vs top projects) is the actionable part: contributing guidelines 16% vs 72% (large effect), CI 27% vs 68% (medium). Those are checkable artefacts a buyer can inspect before signing.

claim: Besker, Martini and Bosch, 'Software Developer Productivity Loss Due to Technical Debt: A replication and extension study examining developers' development work', Journal of Systems and Software 156 (2019), pp.41-61. Verbatim from the abstract: 'The analysis of the reported wasted time revealed that developers waste, on average, 23% of their time due to TD and that developers are frequently forced to introduce new TD. The most common activity on which additional time is spent is performing additional testing.' Method for the 23%: longitudinal, 43 developers reporting via weekly web surveys over SEVEN WEEKS, plus 16 interviews. IMPORTANT DISTINCTION: the same paper cites a DIFFERENT earlier study (reference [28], 32 interviews plus a web survey of 258 software practitioners) in which practitioners 'estimate that, on average, 36% of all development time is wasted due to TD'. The two numbers are not interchangeable: 23% is longitudinally REPORTED time from developers, 36% is a one-off retrospective ESTIMATE from practitioners across several roles. A third figure from Martini et al. [29] puts time dedicated to MANAGING TD at about 25%.
source: Besker, Martini & Bosch, JSS 156 (2019). Full PDF read directly from Chalmers research repository.
note: PEER-REVIEWED, read at primary source. SUPERSEDES the blanket 'do not use 36%' caution recorded in cast-crash-cisq-unreachable: the 36% is real but belongs to a different study with a weaker (single-estimate) method, and must never be attributed to the 2019 longitudinal paper. Prefer 23% and state the method, because self-reported weekly logging is markedly stronger evidence than a one-shot recall estimate.

Grewal, Director of Enforcement, verbatim: 'As more and more investors consider using AI tools in making their investment decisions or deciding to invest in companies claiming to harness its transformational power, we are committed to protecting them against those engaged in AI washing.' claim: UK Cabinet Office, 'Contracting For Agile Guidance Note', part of the Digital, Data and Technology Playbook, updated 20 June 2023, cuts against the simple claim that time and materials always protects the buyer. Verbatim: 'Time & Materials (T&M) often seems the most obvious pricing model to employ when contracting for Agile as it offers a high-level of flexibility, which seemingly supports agile principles. However, buyers should be aware that using T&M can drive the wrong behaviours.' The two problems named: 'the Contracting Authority bears the risk of poor quality' and 'T&M may encourage the supplier to sell time, rather than delivery of the required outcome.' On fixed price: 'Those projects with very limited information and a greater level of uncertainty are less likely to achieve the intended outcomes if they use a rigid fixed-price model', mitigated by 'using fixed-price sprints (contracted for in phases) rather than contracting for the entirety of the requirement.' Overall position verbatim: 'There is no one size fits all approach to contracting for agile.' On specification: 'when constructing an agile contract it will almost always be more beneficial to use an outcome-based specification (rather than outputs based).'
source: UK Cabinet Office, Digital, Data and Technology Playbook, Contracting For Agile Guidance Note, updated 20 June 2023
note: OFFICIAL GOVERNMENT, and valuable precisely because it refuses the tidy answer. A government buyer with no stake in selling either model says T&M can drive the wrong behaviours and that fixed-price SPRINTS are the practical middle. This is much more credible than agency content arguing for whichever model that agency prefers to sell.

claim: Flyvbjerg and Budzier, 'Why Your IT Project May Be Riskier Than You Think', Harvard Business Review 89(9), September 2011, pp.23-25. Sample verbatim: 'We examined 1,471 projects, comparing their budgets and estimated performance benefits with the actual costs and results... the average cost was $167 million, the largest $33 billion'. Headline verbatim: 'The average overrun was 27% - but that figure masks a far more alarming one. Graphing the projects' budget overruns reveals a fat tail - a large number of gigantic overages. Fully one in six of the projects we studied was a black swan, with a cost overrun of 200%, on average, and a schedule overrun of almost 70%.' Interpretation verbatim: 'It's not that they're particularly prone to high cost overruns on average, as management consultants and academic studies have previously suggested. It's that an unusually large proportion of them incur massive overages.' MANDATORY SAMPLE CAVEAT, verbatim: 'Our sample drew heavily on public agencies (92%) and U.S.-based projects (83%), but we found little difference between them and projects at the government agencies, private companies, and European organizations that made up the rest of our sample.' Their stress test: can the company absorb its biggest tech project going 'over budget by 400% or more' with 'only 25% to 50% of the projected benefits' realised.
source: Flyvbjerg & Budzier, HBR September 2011; authors' preprint arXiv:1304.0265 read in full
note: The 27% average independently corroborates the ~30% from Jorgensen's table of peer-reviewed surveys, and both are far from Standish's 189%. THREE independent streams converging near 30% while CHAOS sits at 189% is the strongest structural argument available. Always carry the 92% public-sector caveat. The real lesson is distributional, not average: buyers should plan for the fat tail, which is what breaks companies.

If the 95% is used at all it must be attributed as 'a preliminary MIT Project NANDA working report', never as 'an MIT study finds', and the real sample (52 interviews, 153 leaders) must be stated. claim: UK IPO guidance 'Ownership of copyright works' (Intellectual Property Office, published 19 August 2014) on what a buyer actually gets without a written assignment, verbatim: 'in some circumstances, for example when copyright is not dealt with in the contract to commission the work, courts may be willing to find that there is an implied licence allowing the commissioner to use the work for the purpose for which it was commissioned.' The guidance makes clear this is NOT a transfer of ownership but 'a limited non-exclusive licence', and concludes: 'This situation demonstrates the importance of establishing who owns copyright through a contract.' Historical note in the same guidance: before 1 August 1989 commissioned photographs, portraits and engravings were owned by the commissioner, which changed after that date.
source: UK Intellectual Property Office, 'Ownership of copyright works', published 19 August 2014
note: OFFICIAL. This is the practical sting for buyers: without an assignment you may get only a limited non-exclusive licence for the original purpose. That means no right to resell, relicense, or in some readings even to have a different agency extend the work. Pair with Robin Ray v Classic FM (minimalist approach: a licence, not an assignment, will be implied where a licence suffices), which is corroborated but whose judgment text was NOT reached (BAILII and CaseMine both 403).

claim: Software escrow explained in a law review rather than by escrow vendors. Raymond, 'Software Licenses, Source Code Escrows, and Trustee Powers Under 11 U.S.C. Section 365', Journal of Business, Entrepreneurship & the Law (Pepperdine), Vol. I:1, 2007, pp.43-67, verbatim: 'The tension between a licensor's need to limit access to source code and the licensee's need for uninterrupted access to the software can be mediated by a trusted, neutral third-party. The neutral third-party, acting as escrow agent, is charged with administering an escrow account containing the source code deposited by the developer-licensor. The source code is held by the escrow agent unless a release event occurs (i.e., the chef dies), in which case the escrow agent delivers the source code to the licensee.' THE CENTRAL LIMITATION: the article's subject is that US bankruptcy law can override the escrow contract, since the trustee's powers under 11 U.S.C. Section 365(e) bear on whether ipso facto clauses (the standard 'licensor goes bust' trigger) are enforceable. Author discloses he 'was formally employed by a contracts specialist by a commercial supplier of technology escrow services'.
source: Raymond, Journal of Business, Entrepreneurship & the Law (Pepperdine), Vol. I:1, 2007. PDF read directly.
note: LAW REVIEW (student-edited, standard for US legal scholarship), reached at primary source, with author conflict disclosed. The genuinely useful buyer insight is that the most common escrow trigger, licensor insolvency, is exactly the trigger bankruptcy law may not honour. Separately: Mezrich, 'Source Code Escrow: An Exercise in Futility?', Marquette IP Law Review 5(1), 2001, p.117 is the sceptical counterpart but its full text returned 403, so cite its argument at summary level only, with NO verbatim quotes. Escrow-vendor claims about deposits failing verification are rejected (no study, seller interest).

claim: TrustRadius 2024 B2B Buying Disconnect, methodology disclosed verbatim: 'complete, verified responses from 2,164 technology buyers and 243 technology vendors', buyers fielded March 2024 and vendors April 2024, sent 'to professionals who were involved in a software or hardware purchase for their organization in the past year', with 'a nominal incentive ($10 gift card)'. Findings verbatim: 'Of buyers creating short lists, 78% reported selecting products they'd heard of before starting their research process. That number was even higher for enterprise buyers at 86%.' 'Most short lists (63%) include two to three products and 96% include five or less.' Top selection reason 'It met our needs for the best price' at 66% (58% enterprise), while 'The demo blew us away' accounted for only 13% (14% enterprise), against vendors believing demos are the primary win factor.
source: TrustRadius 2024 B2B Buying Disconnect, read directly at the publisher's page
note: VENDOR MARKETING WITH DISCLOSED METHODOLOGY. TrustRadius is a review platform and has the same structural conflict as G2, but unlike G2 it publishes sample sizes, field dates, recruitment and incentive, which is worth crediting and stating. Relevant to agency vetting: buyers overwhelmingly shortlist what they already recognise, and price-fit beats demo polish. CONTRAST: the G2 2025 Buyer Behavior Report PDF contains NO methodology section, no sample size and no field dates anywhere, so it should not be used as a methodologically disclosed source.

claim: US GAO, GAO-25-107852, 'High-Risk Series: Critical Actions Needed to Urgently Address IT Acquisition and Management Challenges', published 23 January 2025. Verbatim: 'Each year, the federal government invests more than $100 billion on IT.' 'Federal IT investments too frequently fail or incur cost overruns and schedule slippages while contributing little to mission-related outcomes.' 'GAO has made over 1,800 recommendations to agencies aimed at improving their management of IT since 2010. As of January 2025, 463 had not been implemented.' Federal IT management has been on the GAO High Risk List since 2015 and in the 2025 assessment the area regressed, with GAO noting OMB 'has not maintained its level of leadership commitment' since the April 2023 assessment.
source: GAO-25-107852, US Government Accountability Office, 23 January 2025

Neither has anything to sell, which is exactly the point for a piece whose thesis is that the information space is written by sellers.

claim: Banerjee and Duflo, 'Reputation Effects and the Limits of Contracting: A Study of the Indian Software Industry', Quarterly Journal of Economics 115(3), August 2000, pp.989-1017. Sample: 230 projects at 125 software firms, interviews in Bangalore, Pune and Hyderabad, winter 1997-98. Verbatim: 'Overruns are frequent (75 percent of the cases), large (23 percent of the estimate on average), and variable (the standard deviation is 30 percent).' THE KEY FINDING, verbatim: 'Firms bear on average 57 percent of the overrun. When they have a fixed-price contract, they bear on average 66 percent of the overrun (the median is 100 percent). When they have a time and materials contract they bear on average 26 percent of it (the median is 0 percent).' Contract prevalence verbatim: 'Time and material contracts are the least frequent (15 percent). Fixed-cost contracts are the most frequent (58 percent).' Attribution of overruns verbatim: 'the client is responsible for 58 percent of the overrun on average (changes and delays in providing critical inputs), and the firm for 29 percent'. Reputation: 'Young firms are significantly more likely to have fixed-price contracts (the probability is 26 percent higher). They also, on average, bear substantially more of the overrun (19 percent more).' 'ISO certified firms... are no less likely to get fixed-price contracts nor to pay less overrun than other firms.' CAUSAL CAUTION, verbatim: fixed-cost contracts show bigger total overrun in the cross section but 'The association however disappears in the fixed-effects regression.'
source: Banerjee & Duflo, QJE 115(3), 2000. Accepted manuscript read in full via MIT DSpace.
note: PEER-REVIEWED, top-5 economics journal. THE central insight for the contracts section: fixed price does NOT transfer the risk it claims to. Nominally the vendor bears 100%, in practice 66%; on T&M where the client nominally pays all, vendors still absorbed 26%. Renegotiation and reputation decide, not contract text. Also note ISO certification bought the buyer nothing. DO NOT claim the paper shows fixed price CAUSES bigger overruns: that association vanishes under fixed effects. Date the fieldwork (1997-98) and the geography (India).

claim: Molokken-Ostvold and Jorgensen, 'A Review of Surveys on Software Effort Estimation', ISESE 2003, Rome, pp.223-230, reviewing TEN surveys. Verbatim: 'Most projects (60-80%) encounter effort and/or schedule overruns. The overruns, however, seem to be lower than the overruns reported by some consultancy companies. For example, Standish Group's Chaos Report describes an average cost overrun of 89%, which is much higher than the average overruns found in other surveys, i.e., 30-40%.' Conclusion verbatim: 'Project overruns are frequent, but most projects do not suffer from major overruns... An average cost overrun of 30-40% seems to be the most common value reported.' Authors' own caveat verbatim: 'Unfortunately, none of the surveys involved a procedure to ensure random samples.' On Standish: 'The have refused to provide these details, claiming them to be business secrets.' From Molokken-Ostvold's 2004 PhD thesis (University of Oslo), a Norwegian survey found 'Public projects had an average effort overrun of 67%, as opposed to the 21% average in private projects' and 'it appears that the use of flexible development models (e.g. incremental, iterative, or agile) leads to a lesser magnitude of effort overruns when compared to the traditional sequential waterfall model.'
source: Molokken-Ostvold & Jorgensen, ISESE 2003, read via the full paper reproduced as Paper I in Molokken-Ostvold's PhD thesis (Simula/University of Oslo, 2004)
note: PEER-REVIEWED. The defensible replacement for Standish: 30-40% average overrun, with 60-80% of projects overrunning at all. NOTE THE PUBLISHED TITLE is 'A Review of Surveys on Software Effort Estimation'; citation aggregators carry a garbled variant. MISATTRIBUTION WARNING: this 30-40% figure belongs to ISESE 2003, NOT to Jorgensen's 'A review of studies on expert estimation of software development effort' (JSS 70, 2004), which contains no such headline figure.

claim: Todd Little (Landmark Graphics), published as 'Schedule estimation and uncertainty surrounding the cone of uncertainty', IEEE Software 23(3), 2006, pp.48-54. Sample verbatim: 'There were 570 total projects in the portfolio. Of these 570 projects, 120 projects were commercial releases... only the 120 commercial releases were considered.' Findings verbatim: 'The ratio of actual over estimate follows a log-normal distribution.' 'The initial project estimate tends to be a target with only about a 10-20% chance of being met.' 'The median project comes in at 75% over the target, and the average (mean) project comes in at 100% over the target.' 'To have 90% confidence, the project estimate would have needed to be 3-4 times greater than the target.' THE HEADLINE: 'This behavior and uncertainty range is nearly identical at all stages in the project lifecycle, in conflict with the cone of uncertainty.' And: 'we do not see a narrowing of the bands as predicted by the cone of uncertainty. Instead, the uncertainty bands remain constant, and at all stages of the project the range of uncertainty is about a factor of four between the p10 and the p90.' Prescription: 'If typical project estimation follows the log-normal pattern that we observed, we should be estimating projects at +100%/-50%.'
source: Todd Little, 'Agility, Uncertainty, and Software Project Estimation', author's own site, same Landmark dataset and conclusions as the IEEE Software 2006 paper (the IEEE version itself is paywalled and was NOT read)
note: Read from the author's companion paper, not the peer-reviewed IEEE version, so mark accordingly. Directly undermines the standard agency promise that estimates tighten as a project proceeds: on real data the band stayed a factor of four throughout. CORRECTIONS: the sample is 120 (not 106); and Little's text gives DeMarco's median as '3.8 to 4.0', not an 'industry median' of 3.8. LIMITATION: Landmark's projects were commercial product releases, not client contract work. Boehm's 1981 'Software Engineering Economics' was NOT reached; cite the cone's band widths only as Little reports them, and never cite a figure number.

claim: 18F, Technology Transformation Services, US General Services Administration, 'De-risking Government Technology: Federal Agency Field Guide', chapter 'Use time and material contract types for custom Agile software development services'. Verbatim: 'CHALLENGE: Firm-fixed-price contracts are not appropriate for custom Agile development.' 'Use time and material (T&M) contracts with a not-to-exceed ceiling.' 'In Agile software development, an agency does not buy a defined product. Instead, it buys development teams (developers, designers, content strategists, etc.) time. Therefore, the most appropriate contract type is T&M.' On attempts to fix-price agile: 'we have seen several programs try to FFP Agile, sometimes in elaborate and complex ways, and none of them have worked well. The most popular method is to FFP a sprint. Another commonly used method is FFP by story points. Both scenarios result in unnecessary gamesmanship and fighting between the contractor and government. The contractor is incentivized to overbill and underdeliver.' Legal hook: FAR 16.601(d)(2), a T&M contract 'may be used only if the contract or order includes a ceiling price that the contractor exceeds at its own risk'. Separately FAR 39.103 on modular contracting: 'Modular contracting is intended to reduce program risk and to incentivize contractor performance while meeting the Government's need for timely access to rapidly changing technology.'
source: 18F/GSA De-risking Government Technology Federal Agency Field Guide (Sept 2020 edition; 18F was shut down in 2025 so archived/mirrored copies are the access route) and FAR 39.103 at acquisition.gov
note: OFFICIAL GOVERNMENT, and the most explicit anti-fixed-price statement found anywhere. IMPORTANT TENSION TO PRESENT HONESTLY: this contradicts the UK Cabinet Office agile contracting note, which warns T&M 'can drive the wrong behaviours' and that suppliers may 'sell time, rather than delivery of the required outcome'. Two governments, neither selling anything, reaching different conclusions. That disagreement is more useful to a buyer than a false consensus. DO NOT reuse the 18F guide's opening '13% of large government software projects are successful': it is footnoted to Standish CHAOS, the undisclosed-methodology source this research rejects. An official document restating a vendor figure does not launder it.

claim: NEVER-USE list for the estimation and contracts section. (1) The '30-40% average overrun' figure must NOT be attributed to Jorgensen's 'A review of studies on expert estimation of software development effort' (Journal of Systems and Software 70, 2004). That paper contains no such headline figure; the figure belongs to Molokken-Ostvold and Jorgensen, ISESE 2003. (2) A '106 projects' sample for Todd Little's cone of uncertainty study is wrong; the verified figure is 120 commercial releases from a 570-project portfolio. (3) 'EQF 4.8 versus industry median 3.8' is imprecise: Little's text says DeMarco reported 'a median value of 3.8 to 4.0' and does not call it an industry median. (4) '13% of large government software projects are successful', as carried by the 18F De-risking guide, traces to Standish CHAOS/'Haze' and must not be used despite appearing in an official US government document. (5) Standish's 89% or 189% average cost overrun is permanently unverifiable: Molokken and Jorgensen asked for the method and were refused, with Standish calling the details 'business secrets'. Cite 89% only as what Standish reported and which peer-reviewed work could not replicate.
source: Cross-checking of primary sources September 2026
note: Guards against five specific errors, one of which (the 13% figure) would otherwise look impeccably sourced because it sits inside a US government publication. That is the exact trap recorded in METHOD.md: official provenance does not make an undisclosed-methodology number citable.

claim: The Ragas framework defines four agent-specific evaluation metrics distinct from its RAG metrics, documented at docs.ragas.io (page last updated 9 December 2025, read 12 September 2026). TOPIC ADHERENCE 'evaluates the ability of the AI to stay on predefined domains during the interactions', requires a reference_topics list, and computes precision, recall and F1 where recall penalises 'queries that were refused and should have been answered'. TOOL CALL ACCURACY 'measures how accurately an LLM agent invokes tools compared to expected tool calls. It evaluates both the sequence of tool calls and the accuracy of their arguments', with a strict-order default and a flexible-order mode, scoring 'Final score = (argument accuracy) x (sequence aligned ? 1 : 0)', so a correct set of tools in the wrong order scores 0.0 in strict mode. TOOL CALL F1 gives 'a softer evaluation' on unordered matching where extra unexpected calls reduce precision and missed expected calls reduce recall. AGENT GOAL ACCURACY is 'a binary metric, with 1 indicating that the AI has achieved the goal', available with a reference outcome or inferring the goal from the conversation.
source: docs.ragas.io agents metrics page, fetched with the scrapling MCP server 12 September 2026
note: THE EVIDENCE FOR THE AGENT EVALUATION POST, and it fills the gap left by the RAG metrics already recorded: those measure retrieval and grounding, these measure whether the agent did the right THINGS. The docs state the selection rule directly, which is the publishable part: use ToolCallAccuracy when you care about exact tool sequence and arguments, ToolCallF1 when you want precision and recall over tool calling, and AgentGoalAccuracy 'when you care about outcome, not the specific tools used'. The worked example given is that for 'Book me a flight to Paris', if you only care that the booking succeeds rather than which intermediate tools were called, use goal accuracy. Pairs with agent-eval-asked-into-a-void, which establishes that people ask this question and get no answer.

Every gap recorded on 11 Sep 2026 still stands, UNCHANGED: Web Bluetooth (api.Bluetooth) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 56; Web NFC (api.NDEFReader) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 89; WebUSB (api.USB) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 61; Web Serial (api.Serial) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 138 (partial); Background Sync (api.SyncManager) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 49; Periodic Background Sync (api.PeriodicSyncManager) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 80; Background Fetch (api.BackgroundFetchManager) iOS NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 74. Confirmed still working on iOS Safari: getUserMedia 11, MediaDevices 11, MediaRecorder 14, Service Workers 11.3, Cache/CacheStorage 11.3, Geolocation watchPosition <=3, Web Share 12.2, Payment Request 11.3, WebAuthn/PublicKeyCredential 13, IndexedDB 8, StorageManager.persist 15.2, Screen Orientation 16.4, MediaSession 15, WebCodecs VideoDecoder 16.4, SpeechSynthesis 7.
source: MDN browser-compat-data npm package @mdn/browser-compat-data v8.1.1, published 2026-09-10, queried from data.json 12 Sep 2026
note: RE-VERIFICATION, NOT A NEW FINDING. Method hardened against the recorded trap: this query reads ONLY the top-level __compat node of each named API path and never a recursive first match, so the api.MediaDevices.getUserMedia false negative (which was the resizeMode sub-feature) cannot recur. getUserMedia re-checked explicitly and is safari_ios 11. CAMERA ACCESS WORKS ON iOS; any claim otherwise is wrong. Minor correction to the 11 Sep record: Web Bluetooth on Chrome Android is 56, not 78. Web Serial Chrome Android 138 is flagged partial_implementation, 'Serial ports are only available if they're provided by Bluetooth RFCOMM serial port emulation', so do not present Android Web Serial as fully general.

claim: NOTHING CHANGED in the last 12 months of Safari releases that closes any gap relevant to the app-versus-website decision. Safari 26.0 (15 Sep 2025) through 26.6 (27 Jul 2026) and Safari 27 beta (WWDC26) were checked feature post by feature post on webkit.org. Across that year the 'Web Apps' and 'Home Screen Web Apps' sections contain only bug fixes, not capabilities: Safari 26.0 'Fixed the "Add to Home Screen" flow failing to load webpage data, preventing users from making new Home Screen web apps. (154655565)' and Safari 26.2 'Fixed an issue where an audio element failed to play when re-opening a Home Screen Web App. (155336513)'. Safari 26.6 is described by WebKit as 'a small refinement to WebAssembly's streaming compilation paths, and delivers eight bug fixes'. The year's substantive additions are rendering and language features, not device or background capability: anchor positioning, scroll-driven animations and WebGPU (26.0), the Navigation API and view transitions (26.2), WebTransport and Keyboard Lock (26.4), the Origin API (26.5), customizable select and the Service Worker static routing API (27 beta). No Safari release in this window shipped Web Bluetooth, Web NFC, WebUSB, Background Sync, Periodic Sync, Background Fetch, or any install prompt.
source: webkit.org feature posts for Safari 26.0, 26.2, 26.4, 26.5, 26.6 and 'News from WWDC26: WebKit in Safari 27 beta'; fetched 12 Sep 2026
note: THIS IS THE ANSWER TO 'WHAT CHANGED', AND THE ANSWER IS NOTHING. That is a publishable finding in itself and it is the opposite of what the competing content implies. Cite it as: checked through Safari 26.6, released 27 July 2026, and Safari 27 beta. The genuine 2026 direction of travel in WebKit is developer ergonomics and rendering, not closing the Fugu device-API gap. Re-check after Safari 27 ships (expected with iOS 27, autumn 2026), because this claim has a shelf life measured in one release.

claim: iOS offers NO programmatic install prompt of any kind, and MDN browser-compat-data records this as an absence rather than a limitation. api.BeforeInstallPromptEvent: iOS Safari NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 44. api.Window.beforeinstallprompt_event: iOS Safari NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 61. api.Window.appinstalled_event: iOS Safari NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 57. api.Navigator.getInstalledRelatedApps: iOS Safari NOT SUPPORTED / Chrome Android 84. So on iOS a site cannot trigger installation, cannot offer a custom install button that works, cannot detect that it was installed, and cannot detect that its native app is installed. Chrome documents the contrasting behaviour: 'when the criteria is met, many browsers will fire a beforeinstallprompt event, allowing you to provide a custom in-app UX that that will trigger the install flow within your app.' Web app manifest support on iOS is correspondingly partial: display, name, short_name, scope, start_url (11.3), theme_color (15), icons (15.4) and id (16.4) are supported, but background_color, description, display_override, orientation, shortcuts, share_target, launch_handler, protocol_handlers and related_applications are all NOT SUPPORTED on iOS while supported on Chrome Android.
source: MDN browser-compat-data v8.1.1 (10 Sep 2026), api and manifests.webapp nodes, queried 12 Sep 2026; web.dev 'Installability criteria' fetched 12 Sep 2026
note: NEW, AND IT IS THE SHARPEST VERSION OF THE INSTALLATION POINT. The 11 Sep research established via WebKit prose that installation is a manual Share-sheet action. This adds the machine-readable proof of the same fact from the other side: the four APIs a developer would reach for to prompt, to detect, or to measure installation are all absent on iOS. Practical consequence for the post: on iOS you cannot measure your own install rate from the page, and any 'install our app' button must be a hand-written instruction to use the Share sheet. The missing share_target member is worth its own line: an installed iOS web app cannot register as a share destination, so it never appears in the iOS share sheet the way a native app does.

claim: A previously broken Home Screen web app capability WAS fixed, and it is the only such fix found in the compat record. Screen Wake Lock (api.WakeLock and api.Navigator.wakeLock) was shipped on iOS Safari in 16.4 but carried, for versions 16.4 through 18.3, the MDN note 'Does not work in standalone Home Screen Web Apps. See bug 254545.' with partial_implementation set. That partial entry was removed as of iOS Safari 18.4 (released 31 Mar 2025), and Wake Lock is now recorded as plain supported. So keeping the screen awake, which matters for kitchen display, checklist, scanning and presentation use cases, works in an installed iOS web app today but did not between March 2023 and March 2025.
source: MDN browser-compat-data v8.1.1 (10 Sep 2026), api.WakeLock and api.Navigator.wakeLock safari_ios entries, queried 12 Sep 2026
note: NEW AND GENUINELY USEFUL, because it is a concrete example of the pattern the post should teach: on iOS a capability can be nominally 'supported' while being broken in exactly the installed-web-app mode the business cares about. Wake Lock was listed in WebKit's own 16.4 announcement under 'New Web API for Web Apps', yet it did not work in standalone Home Screen web apps for two years. The lesson to publish is that 'supported on iOS' and 'works in an installed iOS web app' are different questions, and a build decision should test the second.

claim: Apple's published App Store Small Business Program terms, verbatim: 'It features a reduced commission rate of 15% on paid apps and In-App Purchases'. Eligibility, verbatim: 'Existing developers who made up to 1 million USD in proceeds in the prior calendar year for all their apps, as well as developers new to the App Store, can qualify for the program and the reduced commission.' On crossing the threshold: 'If a participating developer surpasses the 1 million USD threshold in the current calendar year, the standard commission rate will apply to future sales.' On falling back below: 'If a developer's proceeds fall below the 1 million USD threshold in a future calendar year, they can re-qualify for the 15% commission the year after.' Developers must also declare Associated Developer Accounts, so the 1 million USD is measured across all accounts a developer owns or controls, not per app.
source: Apple, App Store Small Business Program, fetched 12 Sep 2026
note: CORRECTS THE MOST COMMON COMMERCIAL ERROR IN THIS GENRE. The reflexive '30% Apple tax' line is wrong for essentially every reader of a small-business agency blog: a business under 1 million USD in annual proceeds pays 15%, not 30%. Write the 15% figure first and the standard rate second, because the 15% is the rate the actual audience would pay. Also note the commission applies to paid apps and In-App Purchases, so a business selling physical goods or services through the app is a different case entirely and should be researched separately rather than assumed to owe commission.

claim: The OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions MOVED out of the main semantic-conventions repository into a dedicated repository, open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai. The old opentelemetry.io page for GenAI spans now states: 'GenAI semantic conventions have moved to the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions repository. This page has moved and is no longer maintained in this repository.' The new repository covers 'spans, metrics, and events for GenAI clients, MCP (Model Context Protocol), and provider-specific conventions'. The agent and framework spans document carries '**Status**: Development', not stable, and the repository README lists its Schema URL as 'TODO'. It defines the operation names create_agent, invoke_agent, execute_tool, chat and embeddings, and 38 gen_ai.* attributes including gen_ai.agent.id, gen_ai.agent.name, gen_ai.conversation.id, gen_ai.operation.name, gen_ai.tool.definitions, gen_ai.usage.input_tokens, gen_ai.usage.output_tokens, gen_ai.usage.cache_read.input_tokens and gen_ai.usage.cache_write.input_tokens. The docs directory shows active development with commits dated 10 September 2026.
source: opentelemetry.io GenAI spans page; github.com/open-telemetry/semantic-conventions-genai README and docs/gen-ai/gen-ai-agent-spans.md, fetched with the scrapling MCP server 12 September 2026
note: TWO PUBLISHABLE FACTS. First, the conventions moved, so any guidance pointing at the old opentelemetry.io location is now stale, and that is most of what is published. Second and more important for honest advice: the agent spans are at Development status with the schema URL still marked TODO, so this is the emerging vendor-neutral answer to 'what should I instrument' rather than a settled one. Recommend it as the direction of travel and say plainly that it is not stable, rather than presenting it as a standard to comply with. The cache_read and cache_write token attributes are directly useful for the agent cost post, since they make the caching saving measurable in a vendor-neutral way.

claim: Apple still publishes its review turnaround statistic and the wording is unchanged as at 12 Sep 2026. Verbatim, under 'Review status': 'On average, 90% of submissions are reviewed in less than 24 hours.' The same page states the review scope: 'We review all apps, app updates, app bundles, in-app purchases, and in-app events submitted to App Store Connect', so EVERY UPDATE is reviewed, not only the first submission. Apple also publishes the leading rejection cause: 'On average, over 40% of unresolved issues are related to guideline 2.1: App Completeness'. Expedited review exists but is discretionary and reason-bound: 'You can request the review of your app to be expedited if you face extenuating circumstances, such as fixing a critical bug in your app or releasing your app to coincide with an event you're directly associated with.' Separately, under common rejection reasons, Apple lists 'Web clippings, content aggregators, or a collection of links' with the text: 'Your app should be engaging and useful, and make the most of the features unique to iOS. Websites served in an iOS app, web content that is not formatted for iOS, and limited web interactions do not make a quality app.'
source: Apple, App Review (developer.apple.com/distribute/app-review/), fetched 12 Sep 2026
note: IMPORTANT NUANCE THAT CUTS AGAINST THE LAZY VERSION OF OUR OWN ARGUMENT, so publish it honestly. Agency posts habitually describe App Store review as a multi-week bottleneck; Apple's own published figure is 90% inside 24 hours, and that figure is current, not a legacy claim. The honest framing is therefore NOT 'review is slow' but 'review is a gate you do not control': median turnaround is fast, yet every update passes through it, the outcome can be rejection rather than delay, and 10% fall outside 24 hours with no published ceiling. The web has no equivalent gate at all, which is a difference in kind, not in speed. Note also that 90% in under 24 hours is Apple's own marketing figure with no published methodology or sample, so attribute it to Apple rather than stating it as independently measured fact. The 'Websites served in an iOS app ... do not make a quality app' line is a second, blunter statement of the 4.2 wrapped-site bar and is worth quoting alongside it.

claim: Apple Pay works on a plain website with no app, documented by Apple itself. Apple's 'Apple Pay on the Web' technology page states: 'Safari supports two JavaScript APIs that let you accept Apple Pay payments from customers on your website', namely the 'Payment Request API, a W3C candidate API' and the 'Apple Pay JS API, analogous to the PassKit (Apple Pay and Wallet) framework for Apple Pay in apps'. The page is marked 'Safari Desktop 10.0+ Safari Mobile 10.0+' and gives availability as Apple Pay JS from iOS 10 and Payment Request API from iOS 11.3. Requirements are only: a compliant website, 'An Apple Developer account and complete the registration', and 'Serve all pages that include Apple Pay over HTTPS'. Corroborated independently by MDN browser-compat-data v8.1.1: api.PaymentRequest is supported on iOS Safari since 11.3. There is NO App Store commission on a web Apple Pay transaction, because the App Store commission attaches to paid apps and In-App Purchases, not to payments taken on a website.
source: Apple, 'Apple Pay on the Web' developer documentation, fetched 12 Sep 2026; MDN browser-compat-data v8.1.1 api.PaymentRequest
note: CORRECTS A VERY COMMON AND COMMERCIALLY EXPENSIVE ERROR. Published app-versus-web comparisons routinely list Apple Pay in the native-only column. It is not: Apple documents two supported JavaScript routes and has since iOS 10 (2016). For a business whose stated reason for wanting an app is 'so customers can pay with Apple Pay', the correct answer is that the website can already do that. Requires an Apple Developer account and merchant ID plus domain verification, so it is not zero-setup, but it needs no app, no review and no commission. Note one real constraint recorded from the same page: in iOS, 'Safari and SFSafariViewController objects support Apple Pay', so Apple Pay on the web is a Safari-engine capability rather than a guarantee inside every in-app browser.
